AMP1001.introduction: This introductory course will provide a conceptual and methodological armature, towards the study of images, and objects. A range of interdisciplinary methods will enable students to annotate objects and images, and their politics across contexts, historical and contemporary. Students will engage with the valence of the image in an age of visual saturation, the circulation of art/objects in the age of globalization, cultural institutions and their role in public culture, and gain an introduction to the immense rupture produced by modernism. Rather than approaching the histories of art and culture as interesting but distant episodes, the course privileges the myriad concerns, and methods that fall under the ambit of what is understood as ‘new’ art history. This critical art history, emerging as it did from the 1970s onwards, bears the imprint of feminism, visual culture, visual anthropology, culture studies, material culture studies, postcolonialism, among others. Brought into its ambit are questions of gender, race, colonial histories, globality, nationalism, and modernity, among others in relation to works of art. As such, the course offers a means of engaging with the histories of art making, and of analyzing contemporary cultures through rigorous visual, historical, discursive, and textual analysis.
AMP1001.learning_outcomes: Students will learn to engage with works of art and contextualise them Students will gain an understanding of art objects circulate and create meaning and resonance in society Students will gain preliminary knowledge of the discipline of art history and its methods, debates and issues
AMP1001.objectives: To introduce students to the history of art through a discussion of select methods, contemporary issues and debates To develop students' skills of close observation and analysis with respect to art objects and images To equip students with an understanding of the circulation of works of art and their shifting meanings To enable students to reflect on how images, objects and experiences, configure our sense of the world, and our place within it.
AMP1001.school: SHSS - School of Humanities and Social Sciences
AMP1001.skill_development: Visual analysis Historical and theoretical contextualization Critical Thinking

AMP1005.introduction: This course provides an introductory exploration of how body, gesture, and performance intersect in the fields of theatre, dance, music, and performance art, with a particular focus on South Asian contexts. It integrates performance theories with practical insights from classical, folk, and contemporary South Asian art forms. Students will critically examine how body and gesture serve as mediums of cultural expression and social commentary, analyzing performances from both traditional and modern contexts. Highlighting the primacy of the Body in dance, this course addresses the many lenses through which the body may be understood in Dance studies. The focus is to address the historical, cultural, and political body through questions around identity, gender, pedagogy, power, and discipline. Through critical readings, the course uses dance to look at how the body is generated and is generative of discourse.
AMP1005.learning_outcomes: 1) Critically examine the politics of the body, with particular attention to questions of race, gender, sexuality, caste, and other intersecting social identities. 2)Define and analyse the processes and mechanisms through which bodies are represented, interpreted, and assigned meaning across diverse performance practices. 3)Understand and critically analyse the concepts of performance, performativity, embodiment, and enactment, and their significance within theatre, dance, music, and performance art. 4)Reflect critically on the social, cultural, and political processes through which bodies are produced, regulated, and experienced in everyday life and performance.
AMP1005.objectives: This course introduces students to the study of the body, gesture, and performance through interdisciplinary perspectives drawn from performance studies, theatre studies, dance studies, and musicology. Focusing on largely South Asian contexts alongside global theoretical frameworks, the course explores how bodies communicate, perform, and produce meaning across theatre, dance, music, ritual, and performance art. Students will develop critical tools to analyse performance as an embodied aesthetic, cultural, and political practice while engaging with questions of identity, representation, and everyday life. Examines body politics through themes of identity, gender, and power, using dance to explore how bodies generate and are shaped by socio-political discourses. It begins to look at dance and movement as a critical dialogue to address the theoretical and political problems of how the body is perceived and produced.
AMP1005.prerequisites: This is a core course for students who want to complete a dance minor course. There are no prerequisites.
AMP1005.program_learning_goals: By the end of this course, students will be able to: - Demonstrate foundational knowledge of key concepts related to body, gesture, performance, embodiment, and performativity across theatre, dance, music, and performance art. - Recognize and compare diverse performance traditions and practices in India and South Asia, including classical, folk, ritual, popular, and contemporary forms. - Analyse how movement, gesture, sound, space, and visual expression work together to create meaning in different performance contexts. - Interpret performances through interdisciplinary perspectives drawn from performance studies, theatre studies, dance studies, and musicology. - Examine how performances engage with questions of identity, culture, memory, gender, caste, politics, and everyday life within South Asian contexts. - Communicate informed and critical responses to live and mediated performances through discussion, presentations, reflective writing, and performance-based analysis.
AMP1005.school: SHSS - School of Humanities and Social Sciences
AMP1005.skill_development: Critical thinking and analytical skills - Visual and embodied observation skills - Research and information literacy - Interdisciplinary Methodological Training - Writing - Cultural Awareness and Interpretation

AMP2002.introduction: Interactive media play a pivotal role in shaping everyday experience and now mediate banking, peer interaction, office work, business, logistics, delegation, navigation, therapy and companionship. This foundational course introduces students to the philosophical, historical, contemporary and future basis of interactive technology. It invites them to view technology as something more fundamental than a succession of devices, and to examine the manner in which tools, interfaces and algorithms reorganise perception, action and social relations. Students will predominantly learn to think with code through hands-on work in generative visual media, motion typography, digital acoustics and interactive data systems. Processing and Pure Data will be used as practical environments through which students can study spatial composition, procedural form, signal flow, interaction and performance. Physical controls and microcontrollers may be introduced as an advanced extension. The course is classified under REAL and DICE because it joins research and applied experimentation with design, innovation and creative problem-solving. Students will conclude the course by producing functioning computational works and by demonstrating a considered understanding of how information, form and behaviour operate together.
AMP2002.learning_outcomes: LO1. Explain key historical, artistic and social contexts that have shaped interactive and algorithmic media. LO2. Construct interactive visual compositions in Processing using geometric primitives, custom vertex forms, three-dimensional space, transformations and trigonometric functions. LO3. Use typography, strings, arrays, loops and per-character operations as materials for motion and interaction. LO4. Build an interactive audio synthesiser in Pure Data by combining oscillators, envelopes, modulation, filtered noise, mixing and user controls. LO5. Load and parse a tabular dataset and produce an interactive visualisation in which visual mapping and hover behaviour communicate information clearly. LO6. Demonstrate technical craftsmanship through legible code, coherent signal flow, file organisation, comments and working documentation. LO7. Make considered aesthetic decisions concerning order, clarity, rhythm, variation, gesture, sound and interaction.
AMP2002.objectives: • To develop conceptual fluency with digital interactivity and procedural systems. • To introduce students to the historical and sociological evolution of interactive technology, computational art and algorithmic culture. • To cultivate algorithmic creativity and procedural literacy across art, design, media, communication and related disciplines. • To train students to construct interactive visual compositions using geometry, typography, transformations, trigonometric logic and user input. • To introduce the principles of digital audio and enable students to build and perform with an interactive software synthesiser. • To develop the ability to load, organise, visualise and interact with data through computational form. • To encourage students to connect digital tools, physical environments and human interaction while attending to questions of ethics, authorship and social consequence.
AMP2002.prerequisites: None. No formal prerequisite. The course is designed as a foundational elective. Familiarity with computers is useful, but prior programming experience is not required.
AMP2002.program_learning_goals: The course contributes to the following programme-level capacities. 1.L(cid:9)ocate art, media and technological practice within historical, social and cultural contexts. 2.D(cid:9)evelop technical and material competency through sustained studio, laboratory and computational practice. 3.U(cid:9)ndertake research, experimentation and applied learning in order to translate ideas into functioning outcomes. 4.U(cid:9)se design methods, creative reasoning and iterative problem-solving to produce original responses to defined situations. 5.E(cid:9)xamine the ethical, social and political consequences of media technologies and algorithmic systems. 6.C(cid:9)ommunicate process, decisions and outcomes through code, visual or sonic demonstration, written reflection and organised documentation.
AMP2002.school: SHSS - School of Humanities and Social Sciences
AMP2002.skill_development: • Procedural literacy and computational thinking • Creative coding in Processing • Geometric composition and three-dimensional transformations • Trigonometric animation and interaction mapping • Motion typography, strings, arrays and iteration • Digital audio synthesis and signal-flow construction in Pure Data • Interface, control and performance design

weekly_modules.1: Interactive Media: Tools, Systems and Society - Introduction to the course and to procedural literacy. Technology is examined as a cultural and social system rather than only as a collection of devices. Discussion considers how contemporary life is mediated through interfaces, computation and algorithms.
weekly_modules.2: Aesthetics of Algorithms and Abstract Modernism - Historical overview of geometric abstraction, Constructivism, the Bauhaus and early computational graphics. Students study order, balance, reduction, repetition and variation as formal principles that can be translated into procedural rules.
weekly_modules.3: Processing Fundamentals and Geometric Construction - Introduction to the Processing environment, the coordinate system, drawing commands, colour, variables, loops and functions. Students work with geometric primitives and custom vertex shapes to understand how a composition can be formally described through code.
weekly_modules.4: Three-Dimensional Space, Transformations and Trigonometry - Use of P3D, translation, rotation, scaling, push/pop matrix and nested transformations. Trigonometric principles - angles, radians, sin(), cos() and related functions - are applied to position, animate and organise geometry in circular, spiral and oscillating structures.
weekly_modules.5: Interaction and Geometric Abstraction- MouseX, MouseY and temporal variables are mapped to movement, scale, spacing, colour and rotation. Students develop a distinctive interactive composition connected to the lineage of abstract modernism while avoiding direct imitation.
weekly_modules.6: Motion Typography as Computational Form - Typography is treated as the primary visual material for an event poster or announcement. Students use text(), font handling, strings, arrays, charAt(), substring(), split(), loops and transformations to animate words, lines and individual characters.
weekly_modules.7: Mid-Semester Development, Testing and Presentation - Supervised refinement of the geometric abstraction and motion typography studies. Emphasis is placed on order, clarity, rhythm, variation, interaction, code comments, executable output and concise screen-recorded documentation.
weekly_modules.8: Introduction to Digital Audio and Pure Data - Fundamentals of digital sound, amplitude, frequency, waveform, signal flow, objects, messages and audio output. Students construct simple tone generators and learn to control parameters through sliders, toggles and number boxes.
weekly_modules.9: Sound Synthesis and Processing(cid:9)- Practical study of oscillators, line-based percussion envelopes, amplitude modulation, Karplus-Strong synthesis, white-noise filtering, basic noise shaping, mixing and output control. Students combine techniques to create a coherent sonic texture rather than a random accumulation of sounds.
weekly_modules.10: Interactive Synthesiser, Gesture and Performance- Design of a playable Pure Data instrument with clear controls and a short performance structure. Attention is given to sonic intent, technical accuracy, control, gesture and interaction. Arduino-based sliders or rotary controls may be explored as an advanced extension.
weekly_modules.11: Data, Tables and Visual Mapping- Introduction to data as a material for interactive media. Students place a CSV file in a Processing project, load a table, parse at least two numeric columns and map values to position, scale, form or other visual properties.
weekly_modules.12: Interactive Data Visualisation(cid:9)- Students design hover or proximity states that alter colour, size, emphasis or textual information. Discussion addresses how motion, proximity and visual cues can guide understanding, and how a visualisation becomes a dialogue between information, form and behaviour.
weekly_modules.13: Final Project Refinement, Demonstration and Reflection(cid:9)- Final testing, file organisation, screen recording, presentation and individual feedback. Students demonstrate their synthesiser and data visualisation, explain their technical and aesthetic decisions, reflect on authorship and AI use, and situate the work within the wider social history of interactive systems.

AMP2004.introduction: This module introduces students to the processes of newsgathering and writing news and features with the environment as a central theme . It aims to develop a critical understanding of editorial processes in news organisations and a working knowledge o
AMP2004.learning_outcomes: i.S(cid:9)tudents will gain knowledge of the broad role of environment journalism and how human activity impacts our environment ii.S(cid:9)tudents will be able to critically distinguish credible sources of information and identify what counts as greenwashing or a public relations exercise by a corporate/government or individual iii.S(cid:9)tudents will gain practical skills of producing multimedia stories, related to the key environmental issues of our times. They will learn elements of design and visual presentation as they create a storytelling piece that will be the capstone of the semester. This could be a written or visual story. iv.S(cid:9)tudents will learn to critique forms of non fiction reporting on the environment and the role of gender, class, caste on reporting.
AMP2004.objectives: This course aims to equip students with interdisciplinary knowledge and real-world experience needed to communicate complex environmental problems in a simple way to audiences -To empower students with the ability to critically analyse environmental issues from the lens of equity and justice - To understand the role of environment journalism as a watchdog and as a tool for storytelling -To familiarse students with the biggest environmental stories of our times from climate change to deforestation and their role in tackling these complex issues
AMP2004.program_learning_goals: Students in this class will learn how to contextualize, critically analyse and formulate narratives on a range of environmental issues. They will learn the skills and techniques they can apply to reporting on environmental issues generally. And they will learn how to think about and explore the many ways in which the environment intersects with nearly every aspect of our society, including health, psychology, architecture and urban design. They will understand what is the Age of the Anthropocene, how human activity is impacting our planet from every facet of our lives from food to air. At a practical level students will learn how to find credible sources for reportage and the distinction between science , activism and public relation releases as forms of communication. Through extensive reading as well as visits with science journalists and researchers studying issues such as ecology, climate change and air pollution, students will learn to how to identify and write compelling stories about the environment

ART342.introduction: The course has four modules. The first module addresses some of the conceptual and philosophical thoughts on photographic time and space to establish the uniqueness of the photographic medium. The second module focuses on the aesthetic and technical aspects of image-making. The third module concerns itself with the burden of representation, colonial photographic gaze, and photography’s troubled relationship with power and knowledge. The final module concentrates on basic studio-training with strobes in varying angles, intensities and permutations.
ART342.learning_outcomes: 1. A critical and conceptual understanding of photographic images 2. Weekly photographic-exercises to test and translate conceptual understandings into a series of images 3. Familiarizing with significant photographic works and contemporary visual trends 4. Experience various forms of image-making
ART342.objectives: Premised on the praxis of thinking and shooting, this course will enable students to cultivate ways of seeing thoughtfully and meaning-making of photographic images. It will expose them to a series of complexities between the real and the represented; the relationship between the viewer, apparatus and the subject; and also grasp a range of new photographic conditions. Daily shooting assignments are designed to improve their sense of composition. Conceptualizing and executing a photo-feature will enable them to work with a narrative structure. Studio-based light-training and editing workshops will familiarize them with new photographic possibilities.
ART342.prerequisites: None; Students pursuing Communications and ART minor will be prefered
ART342.program_learning_goals: Art342 is a comprehensive course that combines conceptual understanding of photographic-image; politics of visual representation; aesthetical and technical aspects of image-making; and basics of lighting and editing.
ART342.school: SHSS - School of Humanities and Social Sciences

BIO2009.introduction: This course integrates classical biochemical principles of bioenergetics and metabolism with contemporary concepts in systems biology, clinical biochemistry, metabolomics, and translational medicine. Emphasis is placed on the molecular basis of energy transduction, metabolic regulation, physiological adaptation, metabolic diseases, clinical diagnostics, and modern analytical approaches used in biochemical research and healthcare laboratories. The course combines lectures, laboratory investigations, case studies, computational analysis, and research-based learning.
BIO2009.learning_outcomes: Upon successful completion, students will be able to: • Explain biochemical thermodynamics and energy transduction. • Analyze enzyme mechanisms and regulation. • Integrate carbohydrate, lipid, amino acid, and nucleotide metabolism. • Explain hormonal regulation and signal transduction. • Interpret biochemical and clinical laboratory data. • Diagnose metabolic disorders using biochemical evidence.
BIO2009.objectives: Develop an advanced understanding of the biochemical principles governing cellular bioenergetics, including the thermodynamics of biological systems, energy transduction, and mitochondrial function. Explain the organization, regulation, and integration of major metabolic pathways involved in carbohydrate, lipid, amino acid, nucleotide, and heme metabolism under normal physiological and pathological conditions. Examine the molecular mechanisms of enzyme catalysis, regulation, and inhibition, and appreciate their roles in metabolic control, biotechnology, and therapeutic intervention. Understand the molecular basis of hormonal regulation and intracellular signal transduction that coordinate metabolism, cellular homeostasis, growth, and adaptation to physiological stress. Apply biochemical principles to the diagnosis and understanding of inherited and acquired metabolic disorders, emphasizing the biochemical basis of disease and the interpretation of clinical laboratory investigations. Develop proficiency in biochemical and clinical laboratory techniques, including enzyme assays, metabolic analyses, clinical chemistry tests, and data interpretation relevant to biomedical research and diagnostic laboratories. Introduce modern approaches in metabolic research, including metabolomics, systems biology, metabolic flux analysis, and computational pathway analysis, and their applications in biotechnology and precision medicine.
BIO2009.skill_development: Technical and Laboratory Skills Perform quantitative biochemical and enzymatic assays using standard laboratory techniques. Measure enzyme activity and determine kinetic parameters (Km, Vmax) and mechanisms of enzyme inhibition. Conduct clinical biochemical analyses, including estimation of glucose, lipids, calcium, urea, creatinine, and liver function biomarkers. Apply spectrophotometric, colorimetric, and enzyme-based analytical methods for biochemical investigations. Maintain laboratory records and adhere to good laboratory practices (GLP), laboratory safety, and quality control procedures. Analytical and Quantitative Skills

BIO302.introduction: Plant biotechnology is an interdisciplinary field that integrates plant physiology, developmental biology, molecular genetics, tissue culture, genomics, and genetic engineering to address challenges in agriculture, food security, and sustainable crop production. This course provides a comprehensive foundation in the principles and applications of plant biotechnology, with emphasis on plant growth and development, tissue culture, genetic transformation, molecular breeding, genome editing, and synthetic biology. The course introduces students to fundamental concepts including totipotency, organogenesis, somatic embryogenesis, micropropagation, protoplast technology, and plant transformation, before progressing to advanced topics such as transformation vector design, Agrobacterium-mediated gene transfer, molecular markers, marker-assisted breeding, transgenic crop development, plant secondary metabolites, and biofertilizers. Contemporary applications in gene regulation and crop improvement are discussed through case studies and current literature.
BIO302.learning_outcomes: Students will have a comprehensive understanding of plant growth and developmental processes including cellular differentiation and dedifferentiation. Students will develop skills in innovative solutions in plant genetic engineering, synthetic biology, genome editing and gene regulation to address real-world challenges. Students will gain practical experience by studying strategies using physiological, biochemical, and molecular techniques to enhance plant responses and adaptations. Students shall also receive hands-on training in important plant biotechnology procedures like plant tissue culture and plant regeneration, plant genetic transformation, and mutant screening based on genotyping pcr Students will Apply innovative approaches in plant genetic engineering, synthetic biology, genome editing, and gene regulation to address challenges related to crop productivity, quality, and stress resilience. Students will critically evaluate current scientific literature and emerging technologies in plant biotechnology and assess their potential applications in research and agriculture. Students will collaborate effectively in team-based research projects, demonstrating skills in experimental planning, troubleshooting, peer learning, and scientific communication.
BIO302.objectives: To provide students with understanding of the principles, instruments, and methods comprehensively, with a heavy focus on experimental design. To enable students develop critical experimental and analytical skills in plant biotechnology through theoretical education and practical methods. To enble students to learn important concepts such as totipotency, organogenesis, and tissue differentiation, molecular markers, breeding in addition to interesting topics such as leaf and root development, floral induction, and reproductive processes. To develop students skills on hands-on training in important plant biotechnology procedures.
BIO302.program_learning_goals: Apply knowledge of biotechnology specialization to the solution of complex biological questions Skills to design, conduct appropriate experimentation, analyze & interpret data, & draw conclusions Apply biotechnology to produce solutions for public health and welfare
BIO302.skill_development: Problem Solving and Critical Thinking Experimental Design and Troubleshooting Analytical and Quantitative Data Interpretation Molecular and Cell Biology Laboratory Techniques Plant Tissue Culture and Regeneration Techniques Scientific Writing and Data Presentation Peer Learning and Collaborative Research

In vitro Culture Techniques: Callus induction and maintenance, suspension cultures, single-cell cultures, factors affecting in vitro growth, morphogenesis, organogenesis, somatic embryogenesis and their applications.

BIO401.introduction: The Research Methodology course aims to equip students with the foundational and applied skills necessary for designing, conducting, analyzing, and communicating scientific research. Students will develop a clear understanding of different types of biologic
BIO401.learning_outcomes: Upon completion of this course, students will have a clear understanding of the principles and types of research used in life sciences, including experimental design, sampling methods, data collection techniques, and ethical considerations related to biological research. They will be able to formulate relevant research questions, design appropriate experiments or field studies, and apply statistical and bioinformatics tools to analyze and interpret biological data. Students will develop the ability to write scientific reports, research proposals, and manuscripts, and effectively present their findings. Throughout the course, they will cultivate a critical, ethical, and responsible approach to conducting research, while demonstrating scientific curiosity, attention to detail, and a collaborative mindset.
BIO401.objectives: • To provide students with a foundational understanding of research types, design, and methodology relevant to the life sciences. • To enable students to identify research problems, formulate hypotheses, and apply appropriate experimental and analytical methods. • To enhance students' ability to critically review scientific literature, interpret biological data, and maintain ethical standards in research practice. • To empower students with the skills needed to write scientific reports, proposals, and communicate findings effectively. • To nurture students to plan and manage research projects, including timeframes, budgeting, and resource allocation.
BIO401.program_learning_goals: 1.D(cid:9)evelop the ability to formulate research questions, design experiments, and apply appropriate methods for data collection and analysis in biological research. 2.C(cid:9)ritically evaluate scientific literature, interpret experimental results using statistical and bioinformatics tools, and adhere to ethical standards in life sciences research. 3.C(cid:9)ommunicate research effectively through well-structured proposals, reports, and presentations, and gain skills in project planning and management.
BIO401.skill_development: This course significantly contributes to the development of core scientific skills essential for life sciences research. It enhances analytical thinking through hypothesis formulation, experimental design, and data interpretation using statistical and computational tools. Students gain hands-on experience in literature review, scientific writing, and research presentation, which strengthens their communication skills. The course also fosters technical competencies in planning and executing biological experiments or fieldwork. In addition, it instills critical soft skills such as attention to detail, time management, ethical decision-making, and the ability to work independently or in teams, preparing students for academic research, industry roles, or advanced studies.

CCC2101.introduction: Course Description: The Nobel Peace Prize recipient, the Dalai Lama, has displayed a lifelong commitment to the promotion of universal values across the globe, and in particular, to equipping younger generations to deal with the complex challenges of the conflict-ridden 21st century. To this end, he calls for a holistic approach to education that cultivates an ethical mindset alongside traditional academic learning. These ethics are grounded not in any belief or religious system, which themselves can be a source of contestation, but in basic human values grounded in common sense, experience, and latest evidence from cutting edge frontiers of economics, evolutionary biology, neuroscience, behavioural psychology and other disciplines and scientific fields. He terms these secular ethics, as they are inclusive of all people—with or without religious affiliation of any kind—and animals. This praxis-based course is designed to explore the idea of secular ethics, not just conceptually but also in practice, with critical self-reflection and exercises designed to test this ethical approach in the laboratory of our own lives. For detailed syllabus and modules, see the relevant section.
CCC2101.learning_outcomes: To know how to apply ethics across all domains of life. To have a transformed attitude to confronting the inevitable challenges of life. To have the skills to navigate challenges and overcome them not only for oneself, but to help others on a larger scale. To voluntarily take up greater responsibility for the well-being of others, as well as animals and the environment, too.
CCC2101.objectives: To develop a detailed understanding of secular ethics and their manifold applications in our daily lives. To equip students to learn about and reflect upon how universal ethics can transform our lives to become more meaningful and happier, for ourselves, our families, our work places, our communities, and the entire world.
CCC2101.program_learning_goals: As a core common curriculum (CCC) course, the idea is to equip students with a foundational course on ethics - the key question of our age - with a secular and universal basis.
CCC2101.school: DEANUG - Office of Dean of Academics
CCC2101.skill_development: The skill to navigate life outside the classroom with all its vicissitues, in order to truly flourish and attain 'A Good Life' in the Aristotelian sense. The skill to not succumb to mental health issues over minor hurdles, but actually gain agency and mastery over one's emotions.

CCC2103.introduction: This course aims to examine non-violence, as a principle and strategy of resistance against a Great Power, using the case of Tibet’s on-going struggle since the 1950s against the CCP, both in exile and within Tibet. “One of the most compelling arguments of the non-violence theorists was that means determine ends” (Hardiman 2013, p. 44). Born of similar conviction, based on the Nalanda philosophy tenets of interdependence and the equality of all beings in their wish not to suffer, and drawing inspiration from Mahatma Gandhi, His Holiness the Dalai Lama has led his people along the Middle Way (Tib. Umay Lam དབུ(cid:3)་མའི(cid:7)་ལམ) of non-violence and non-harm as a response, articulating over the last many decades why such a stance of dialogue and negotiation is critical in building allies and a future democracy (as proposed by non-violence theorists such as Sharp 1973), and why it is the only long-term solution that is likely to succeed (bearing out Chenoweth and Stephan 2011 data on non-violent movements being twice as likely to succeed as violent ones). With no visible results thus far by some measures, however, the Tibetan community in exile and the youth in particular, are restive and divided over the efficacy of such an approach. This course will begin by exploring the literature on non-violence. It will then seek to situate the Middle Way approach, stemming from its own underlying philosophical paradigm, within this body of literature and against the backdrop of historical developments in the Tibetan struggle since 1959. The course will then look in detail at three different Tibetan uprisings of 1956-59; 1987-89; and 2008 (Dorjee 2015) and other ‘strategies’, such as the desperate act of self-immolations, seeking to locate them in a typology of non-violent resistance as categorised by Sharp (1973) and Scott (1990). It will conclude by deliberating on successes, failures and lessons for other movements and struggles vis a vis Great Power modern nation states. For detailed syllabus and modules, see next section.
CCC2103.learning_outcomes: Familiarisation with the principle of, and the literature on, non-violence. Understanding a framework and typologies of non-violent resistance. Inculcating in-depth capacity of how to recognise and categorise various acts of everyday resistance as strategy.
CCC2103.objectives: To equip students with an in-depth understanding of non-violence as principle and strategy in the 21st century context of resistance to a Great Power, using the on-going Tibetan struggle as an empirical case study, but one that is relevant to many other similar conflicts and struggles. To imbue students with a sense of the long-term possibilities and success of non-violence as a strategy. To try to equip students with the futility of, and abhorrence for, violence as a strategy.
CCC2103.prerequisites: Having one's viedo on during online classes is a course prerequisite for getting attendan ce on this course.
CCC2103.program_learning_goals: As a core curriculum course (CCC), this foundational course on non-violent resistance as both principle and strategy in response to asymmetrical Great Power imperialism and hegemony, exposes students to critical literature and thinking in an oft- neglected but increasingly relevant area of 21st century geopolitics.

CCC2103.skill_development: To develop the skill to appreciate and truly value non-violence as the only way. To learn the skill of seeing that with the use of violence, even where one supposedly wins, the costs and cascade effect of an unending cycle of further violence outweigh the gains.

CCC236.introduction: The course aims to develop a critical understanding of pastoralism as a dynamic social and ecological formation rather than a static or disappearing way of life. It introduces students to the anthropological and historical literature of pastoralism in South Asia, focusing on the diverse ways pastoral communities have negotiated mobility, ecology, identity, erasure, and political change. Through comparative and ethnographic perspectives, the course examines pastoralism as a lens through which broader questions of society, culture, and human–environment relations can be understood.
CCC236.learning_outcomes: Students will gain an understanding of the historical and political processes that have shaped pastoral communities in South Asia. They will develop the ability to analyse pastoral worlds through perspectives on ecology, identity, state formation, and social transformation.
CCC236.objectives: The course aims to help students gain an introductory understanding of pastoralism and their multi species world as a dynamic social and ecological formation rather than a static or disappearing way of life. It seeks to familiarize students with some key debates on nomads, mobility, state formation, colonial transformations, and pastoral identities, while encouraging reflection on how pastoral worlds offer alternative perspectives on human and multispecies organization and social life.
CCC236.program_learning_goals: With 2026 designated by the United Nations as the International Year of Rangelands and Pastoralists, pastoral multi-species worlds have gained renewed attention as vital ecological, cultural, and social formations. This course uses this moment to explore pastoralism in South Asia as a distinctive mode of life shaped by mobility, ecological knowledge, social organization, and evolving relationships with states, markets, and landscapes. Nomadic and pastoral communities occupy a unique position in anthropology, offering a critical vantage point from which to rethink settled life, territoriality, property, and ideas of social organization. Rather than viewing pastoralism as a residual or disappearing way of life, the course approaches it as a dynamic formation that illuminates broader questions about human–environment relations, political authority, identity, and belonging. Through historical, ethnographic, and comparative perspectives, the course examines the transformations of pastoral worlds in South Asia, including the effects of colonial rule, agrarian expansion, state-making, and contemporary development processes. It situates South Asian pastoral traditions within wider debates on nomadism and mobility while reflecting on their continuing significance in the contemporary world.

CCC236.skill_development: The course develops skills in critical reading, comparative analysis, ethnographic interpretation, and engaging with interdisciplinary approaches to social and environmental questions.

CCC2503.introduction: This course aims to inform students of the intimate and interdependent connection between our physiology and psychology on the one hand, and lifestyle choices, to include diet, exercise, rest and our exposure to natural and artificial environment on the other, which largely scripts the sense of wellness, or the lack of it, that we experience as “Life”. Students will be introduced to big ideas grounded in recent research that root our wellbeing and resilience in the choices that we can make, as well as in our ability to develop and maintain effective interpersonal relationships in all areas of our lives. The course will equip students with insights and understanding of practical steps they can take, as daily choices, which will enable them to navigate the big challenge of leading a healthy, fulfilled and purpose enriched life. Students will learn through lectures, self-study, and project work centred on changes that they make, and document, in their own daily routines and lifestyle, to witness the value of the concepts in action as they learn. Performance on the course will be assessed through participation and written assignments.
CCC2503.learning_outcomes: On successful completion of the course, students will be able to: a) Understand the underlying drivers of their own behaviour, as well as the behaviour they observe in others. b) Understand the impact of lifestyle choices on our physical and mental health, determining our wellness. c) Understand the role of personality in interpersonal interaction, and aspects they can work on to enhance interpersonal relationships. d) Use creative thinking to improve problem solving in group as well as individual situations. e) Understand the importance of building habits and routines that develop a mindset of serving a purpose of value, which leads to greater fulfilment in life.
CCC2503.objectives: a) To provide students with a framework for understanding how they can enhance their all-round wellbeing, through interventions centred on holistic self-care. b) To inspire students to prioritise wellness as the cornerstone for building the resilience required to overcome life’s challenges and lead a purpose filled life of fulfilment. c) To enhance self-awareness and interpersonal skills to become effective team members and inspiring leaders.
CCC2503.program_learning_goals: a) To provide students with a framework for understanding how they can enhance their all-round wellbeing, through interventions centred on holistic self-care. b) To inspire students to prioritise wellness as the cornerstone for building the resilience required to overcome life’s challenges and lead a purpose filled life of fulfilment. c) To enhance self-awareness and interpersonal skills to become effective team members and inspiring leaders.

Besides the theoretical aspects, students will learn simple steps to reframe situations, break down challenges and set SMART goals. Students will be introduced to key ideas around interpersonal communication, conflict resolution, mindset and leadership.

CCC257.introduction: In general, the existence of elementary particles—such as electrons, muons, quarks, etc.—is well established, and many important phenomena, particularly within the domain of particle physics, high energy physics and astrophysics, can be effectively described using theoretical models based on these fundamental constituents. In this course, however, we will explore a fundamentally different class of emergent particles known as quasiparticles. These entities are indispensable for understanding the rich and often complex phenomena observed in condensed matter physics, a field that underpins much of modern technology. Note that the idea of “emergence” is not limited to condensed matter physics but has also been discussed in the field of biology, literature, economics and more. Very little concentration has been given so far in the field of condensed matter physics, as far as the unique importance of this field for general students is concerned. The present CCC will address the idea of “quasiparticles” and explore the universe of quasiparticles, thus matching the theme “Big Ideas and grand challenges”.
CCC257.learning_outcomes: Upon successful completion of the course, students will be able to: appreciate condensed matter physics beyond Astrophysics and other more popular areas of physics. Such an initiative is highly needed for students, especially when these topics provide a wealth of important physical concepts and are highly beneficial to the betterment of our daily technological lives.
CCC257.objectives: To provide students with the idea of a new area of utmost fundamental and application importance, usually untouched at a popular level so far, unfortunately.
CCC257.skill_development: Students will be able to appreciate condensed matter physics beyond Astrophysics and other more popular areas of physics.

The course content aligns with the theme tackling ‘grand challenges’. The major challenge in industries is the energy crisis to drive heavy machinery to lighter data storage devices. CCC356.learning_outcomes: The first ten classes under this course will focus solely on the writing and editing aspects of print and online media, through a series of classroom exercises and assignments. The remaining six classes will focus on the tools required to cover the news, along with their appropriate application.
CCC356.objectives: To give a beginner-level understanding of the major aspects that contribute towards covering the news, starting from sourcing information to writing and editing a news story. The course delves into minute aspects of writing ledes, giving headlines and straps and writing for space in print media. The course also highlights the significant differences when it comes to writing for the web, where stories are not bound by constraints such as space as seen in print.
CCC356.school: DEANUG - Office of Dean of Academics
CCC356.skill_development: reporting and writing for print and online media, copy-editing, and critical thinking.
CCC356.title_from_outline: News Writing Essentials: Print to Web,

weekly_modules.1: Breakdown of class activity Class 1: Lede writing in Print Media Objective: The lede comprises the opening lines in a piece of journalistic writing. Summarising the most important aspects of an event in a concise manner is crucial to getting the lede right. Students will be given a series of classroom exercises in which they will be required to write a lede based on news events. Specifics and exercises: Students will be shown multiple examples in which well-written and poorly written ledes from news stories – which have been published in print media – will be juxtaposed to give an understanding of what makes a good lede. Apart from the five Ws and one H – what, why, where, when, who and how – students will be required to apply a critical thinking-based approach towards developing a story lede. This is necessary in scenarios where the five Ws and one H cannot be accommodated in totality. This session will comprise example-based interaction and will be followed by a classroom exercise, in order for the students to implement their learnings in real-time. Based on news updates, a total of four story ledes must be formulated by each student.
weekly_modules.2: Class 2: Headlines and straps for Print Media Objective: While one must never start a story with the headline, the headline must communicate the most important part of the story to the reader. Similarly, the strap must communicate additional details about the story that is not mentioned in the lede, in order to give the reader a more detailed inference as to what more lies in the story. Students will be given an exercise to frame headlines and straps based on news events. This will be a classroom-based exercise. Specifics and exercises: The initial half of this session will multiple examples that show neatly done headlines and straps in print media, which will be juxtaposed against examples of those that completely missed the point. Students will then be required to identify the correct and incorrect headlines and straps through a series of examples. These interactive exercises will require them to think critically since space is a major constraint in print media. The remaining half of this session will require students to frame headlines and straps based on the body of stories that will be provided to them.
weekly_modules.3: Class 3: Writing for space in Print Media Objective: This session will focus on writing stories for a given amount of space i.e within a given word count. Regardless of the beat, reporters often struggle to pack information within the prescribed word count, and this continues to be the case in newsrooms even today. Students will be given a writing exercise where they will have to report on a news event within a word count of 300 words, regardless of the complexities surrounding the event. Specifics and exercises: Irrespective of the number of updates that a developing news story may receive, the final copy requires the most crucial details to be incorporated since print media is bound by a word count. After a brief classroom discussion, students will be given multiple news updates to read and analyse, and will be required to draft a news story of 300 words before the end of the class. This exercise is aimed at developing quick and concise writing skills, while keeping the constraint of space in mind.
weekly_modules.4: Class 4: Assignment - I Apart from revisiting the basics that were taught in the earlier sessions, this session will require students to leverage their skills of lede writing, writing for space and giving a headline and strap through one news story (maximum word count: 300 words), which will be based on an event. The grading for the assignment will be based on three factors: quality of the story lede, abiding by the word count while ensuring that key details are included in the story and the level of accuracy in the headline and strap. This assignment carries 25% of the total grade.
weekly_modules.5: Class 5 and Class 6: Differences between print media and online media; Writing for the web and utilising Search Engine Optimisation (SEO) tools Specifics and exercises: The first class of these two sessions (class 5) will focus on drawing distinctions between writing for print and online media. Unlike the former, online media does not have the constraint of space. However, it requires more catchy ledes, and gives room for longer headlines. An industry expert – who has been witness to, and has experienced, the transition from print to online media – will be welcomed to communicate and share insights with the students. Through this interaction, students will get detailed insights on the varying requirements in an online/new media newsroom, which include a basic understanding of search engine optimisation (SEO) tools and how they play a crucial role in terms of story’s overall reach online. The second session (class 6) will see an exercise where story ledes in print and online media will be compared to show minute yet significant differences between the two, an example being that online news outlets require catchy details higher up in the story, not generic details. Other differences in writing style will also be observed. The latter half of this session will see a class exercise where students will work on formulating story ledes based on the requirements for stories in online media. While their knowledge in lede writing for print media will come in handy, this exercise will help students develop the skill of tweaking their writing in a quick and efficient manner for online news portals, thus leaving the students with the skill to write ledes for stories on both platforms i.e. print and online media.
weekly_modules.6: Class 7: Framing a Headline and Strap in online media Unlike print media, online media houses typically indulge in longer headlines that communicate more details about the story. Straps, too, can differ based on the headline and lede, and are often longer than those seen in print media. Specifics and exercises: The differences between framing headlines and straps in print and online will be highlighted through a series of examples. One must note that a strap is not provided in every story that is published in a newspaper due to space limitations, and nor is every headline an elaborate one. However, such limitations are not to be found in online media. The latter half of this session will require each student to formulate six headlines and six straps, based on the body of stories that will be provided to them. This exercise must be completed in class. In addition to this, students will be given an exercise in which they will be required to convert their previously formulated headlines – for print media – into those that are suitable for online media, along with the effective use of keywords. This exercise can be considered as home work and can be submitted before the next class.
weekly_modules.7: Class 8: Writing for space for online media (includes assignment) Having more space does not translate into writing stories that are significantly long, and discourages the reader to indulge further. Though longer, the flow of the story is crucial and it requires the space available to be utilised smartly. While there are no constraints of space in online media, there is the limitation of keeping readers engaged. This means that the core parts of the story have to be mentioned higher up in the body and there must be a smooth flow of details in order to prevent the reader from losing interest. Even if a story has all the required details, it will be irrelevant if the sequencing and flow remains haphazard. Assignment II: An assignment will be given to students where they will be required to write a story for online media that is not more than 350 words. This will be based on news updates. This assignment carries 25% of the total grade.
weekly_modules.8: Class 9 and Class 10: Copy editing for print and online media Specifics and exercises: Apart from writing a news story, it is crucial to have a working knowledge of how to edit the story, which is a core responsibility of the news desk. Editing a news copy requires a thorough check, in terms of facts, numbers, grammar and language, among other elements. Students will be shown examples of poorly written news stories and will be given a step-by-step understanding of how to edit such stories for print and online media – while underlining the differences in the editing required for each medium. Assignment III: At the end of class 10, students will have to edit a 700-word story and bring it down to 450 words while retaining voice, facts and meaning. This assignment carries 25% of the total grade.
weekly_modules.9: Class 11 and Class 12 : Sourcing information and news tracking Specifics and exercises: The primary job of a reporter is to source information that can be possibly converted into a news story. Apart from meeting with government officials, a large pool of information can be sourced through press conferences, gazette notifications and government orders. But journalists continue to remain unaware of the original source of such material. Students will be given a detailed breakdown of how information can be sourced, and how to identify whether such information is newsworthy. Further, maintaining a rhythm where a reporter tracks the news on a regular basis is a necessary exercise to keep oneself up-to-date with what’s making the news. For instance, there have been examples of stories reported in regional publications that have served as a starting point for various reporters in uncovering a larger story. As part of this session, students will be taught best practices in tracking the news, using print and online tools.
weekly_modules.10: Class 13: Fact-checking Specifics and exercises: While sourcing information is an important tool of a journalist, another crucial aspect that must not be overlooked is to verify the information obtained. In the existing news scenario, misinformation is rampant due to hasty procedures that often overlook the basic process of fact checking. Students will be given access to online free use tools that are crucial towards verifying the authenticity of information – this includes reverse image search tools and obtaining the metadata of a file in order to ascertain if it has been tampered with.
weekly_modules.11: Class 14: Media perspectives Specifics and exercises: One of the fundamental aspects of understanding the news, and writing for media, is to build perspective. Through a series of readings and short documentaries, students will be made part of an interactive session that will help build their perspective towards how a news story can be covered. Further, this will assist the students when it comes to critical thinking and building a strong ‘news sense.’
weekly_modules.12: Class 15: Data in journalism Specifics and exercises: Simplifying massive chunks of data into readable and effective language, in a short period of time, is a crucial skill in the newsrooms of today. Data serves as a crucial verification point that adds substance to a claim. Through a series of discussions and reports, students will be guided in a step-by-step manner on how to identify, segregate and utilize data points to enhance the quality of a news story.
weekly_modules.13: Class 16: An introduction to investigative reporting Specifics and exercises: A crucial aspect of a reporter’s training is to break stories that have not been uncovered, and this is executed by closely tracking a subject in every possible angle. Students will be given a beginner-level understanding on how to research, ideate and execute investigative stories. They will also be given a step-by-step breakdown on how some investigative stories in the recent past were brought to life. Assignment IV (final): An assignment that tests the students on their learnings from classes 11 to 16, this assignment carries 25% of the total grade.

CCC527.introduction: Adaptations breathe new life into classics or historical works, ensuring their continued relevance and keeping important stories alive for new generations who might not engage with the original format. Translating narratives from one medium (e.g., a complex novel) to another (e.g., a film or TV series) makes them more accessible to people who may prefer visual storytelling or find the original text challenging. Adaptations are creative acts that involve reinterpretation by new artists, writers, and directors. They can offer fresh, innovative perspectives on familiar characters and themes, exploring previously untold aspects or marginalized voices, such as feminist retellings or different cultural interpretations. Reimagined narratives can address or critique contemporary social and political issues, using the established framework of the original story to comment on modern times and spark relevant cultural conversations. Comic books are adept at presenting complex topics in a simple, accessible manner. Comics offer a more straightforward entry point for young readers and writers by breaking down complex topics like emotions, relationships, or historical events. The combination of visuals and storytelling fosters creativity and aids young people in imagining new worlds and scenarios

CCC685.introduction: CCC_685: Sustainable Buildings is a Common Core Curriculum course from the Department of Civil Engineering. It introduces sustainable techniques, materials, and practices for building design and operation. Students master the fundamentals of building science using thermodynamic principles. Aligned with IGBC guidelines, the course prepares industry-ready professionals for IGBC AP - Associate accreditation Key introductory features: .Inclusive Scope: Targeted at Civil, Mechanical, Electrical, and Design students .Technical Foundation: Imparts knowledge of sustainable design and construction .Scientific Depth: Explores principles regarding heat, air, and moisture .Industry Standards: Utilizes IGBC guidelines to track current trends .Professional Status: Facilitates obtaining IGBC AP - Associate accreditation
CCC685.learning_outcomes: This course is designed in accordance with IGBC/GRIHA/NBC 2017/ECBC guidelines to familiarize students with the current sustainable building trend, help them understand its impact and applications as a practice, and introduce various sustainability concepts associated with building design. Upon completion of the course, students will be: • Having an understanding of core building science fundamentals (basic thermodynamic principles as related to wind, air, moisture, pressure, and heat). • Able to perform some building sustainability concepts (including, but not limited to, site layout, building design, advanced framing, and insulation) • Able to understand and perform some building performance testing At the end of the course, the student will be able to: • Students would be motivated to take advanced courses in Building Energy Efficiency and green and sustainable buildings to become industry-ready. • Opportunity to get accredited as ‘IGBC AP - Associate’.
CCC685.objectives: Students taking this course will attain knowledge of sustainable building techniques, materials, and practices. Utilizing the overall sustainability of various materials and methods, students will learn basic methods of sustainable building design, techniques, documentation, and calculation. Apart from this • Impart knowledge of sustainable concepts in the design, construction & operation of buildings • Exposure to the latest Green Building trends & technologies
CCC685.program_learning_goals: The CCC_685: Sustainable Buildings course provides comprehensive knowledge of sustainable building techniques and practices aligned with IGBC/GRIHA/NBC 2017/ECSBC(Energy Conservation and Sustainable Building Code) guidelines. Students master the fundamentals of building science and thermodynamic principles to analyze heat and moisture flow. The goal is to produce industry-ready professionals prepared for IGBC AP - Associate accreditation. By exploring green building trends, students learn to optimize building design and operation for occupant well-being Key learning goals include: . Mastering building science fundamentals and thermodynamic principles . Implementing water efficiency strategies using the 3R approach . Evaluating energy performance and determining ECBC compliance . Analyzing embodied carbon and the recyclability of building materials . Enhancing indoor air quality and occupant comfort through monitoring
CCC685.skill_development: The CCC_685: Sustainable Buildings course offers technical expertise in sustainable design and operation following IGBC/GRIHA/NBC 2017/ECBC guidelines. Students use building science to improve occupant well-being. This prepares them for industry- ready roles and IGBC AP - Associate accreditation Key skills developed include: . Technical Documentation: Master methods for sustainable design calculations and documentation . Performance Testing: Conduct building performance testing using thermodynamic principles like heat and moisture flow . Compliance: Evaluate ECBC compliance and apply ASHRAE standards for energy efficiency . Resource Management: Use 3R approaches for water and assess embodied carbon in materials . Environmental Monitoring: Monitor air quality and implement strategies to handle urban heat islands

CED305.introduction: This course will cover the basic reinforced concrete design, including topics such as flexural , shear, torsional design of beams slabs, columns, staircase etc. accordance with IS guidelines and limit state of serviceability.
CED305.learning_outcomes: On successful completion of the course, students will be able to: • To give an experience in the implementation of designing concepts (WSM/LSM) which are applied in field of structural engineering • To involve the application of scientific and technological principles of design of buildings according to limit state method of design • To present the foundations of many basic engineering concepts related to the design of structures To understand the various design concepts and analyze and design structural elements such as beams, slabs, columns, and footing under flexure, shear, torsion, and compression.
CED305.objectives: The course aims to make the students learn the analysis and design of safe, serviceable and durable reinforced concrete structures. It has following objectives • To learn about the behaviour of reinforced concrete, materials, and design philosophy (WSM/LSM) as per IS 456:2000. • To perform the design of beams, slabs, columns, foundations, retaining walls, and stairs by means of codal provisions and design tools. • To prepare the reinforcement drawings and structure drawing in accordance with IS 456:2000 and SP 16. • To enhance their skills of problem solving, ethical conduct, and safety, sustainability and durability considerations in structural design

CED412.learning_outcomes: on sucessful completion of this course, the student will able to (1) Explain the principal causes and underlying mechanisms of concrete deterioration, including corrosion of reinforcement, carbonation, chloride ingress, freeze–thaw action, chemical attack, and alkali–aggregate reaction. (2) Identify and categorize common structural damage and defects, and carry out condition surveys and visual inspections of concrete structures (3) Select and apply appropriate destructive and non-destructive testing techniques, and interpret test results for damage and condition rating and reporting (4) Recommend suitable repair, protection, and rehabilitation strategies for deteriorated concrete structures and reinforcement in accordance with accepted engineering principles. (5) Apply sustainability and life cycle assessment tools (e.g., One Click LCA) to evaluate the environmental performance of repair and maintenance options.
CED412.objectives: The primary objectives of this course are to: • Develop an understanding of the causes and mechanisms of deterioration in concrete structures, including chemical, physical, environmental, and design/construction-related factors. • Enable students to identify, classify, and interpret various types of damage and defects in reinforced concrete structures through condition surveys and diagnostic testing. • Introduce the principles and methods of destructive and non-destructive testing (NDT) for the assessment and condition rating of existing structures. • Familiarize students with established principles, materials, and techniques for the repair, protection, and rehabilitation of damaged concrete structures and corroded reinforcement. • Impart working knowledge of sustainability tools, life cycle assessment (LCA), and infrastructure asset management as applied to structural repair and maintenance decisions. • Prepare students to make informed engineering judgments regarding the durability, serviceability, and long-term maintenance of concrete structures.
CED412.skill_development: Through the lectures, tutorials, assignments, and the small project component, students will develop the following technical and professional skills: • Diagnostic and investigative skills: competence in conducting condition surveys, visual inspection, and diagnostic testing of concrete structures. • Analytical and interpretive skills: ability to interpret destructive and non-destructive test data and to perform damage and condition rating. • Technical decision making: capacity to select appropriate repair materials, methods, and protection strategies for a given deterioration scenario. • Sustainability assessment skills: practical familiarity with life cycle assessment and sustainability tools such as One Click LCA for evaluating repair alternatives. • Asset management awareness: foundational understanding of infrastructure asset management principles for long-term maintenance planning. • Reporting and communication skills: ability to prepare structured condition assessment reports and to present repair recommendations clearly and professionally. • Collaborative and project-based skills: teamwork, problem-solving, and practical application of concepts through tutorial assignments and a small project.

weekly_modules.1: Course introduction, scope and relevance of structural repair. Overview of concrete durability. Causes of concrete deterioration: chemical agents (CO₂, acids, salts). Tutorial: discussion of real-world deterioration case studies.
weekly_modules.2: Atmospheric causes (temperature, rain, freezing/thawing); moisture effects (external/internal); fire damage; faulty design, materials and construction. Tutorial: identifying causes from site photographs.
weekly_modules.3: Mechanisms of deterioration – corrosion of embedded reinforcement due to carbonation. Chloride ingress and its role in corrosion. Tutorial: Visula Inspection and methods.
weekly_modules.4: Freeze–thaw deterioration; chemical attack (acids, salts, sulfate attack). Tutorial: photogrammetry methods and software based ranking
weekly_modules.5: Alkali–aggregate reaction and biodegradation. Consolidation of deterioration mechanisms. Tutorial: mechanism-mapping assignment.
weekly_modules.6: Types of damage and defects: construction defects, external/internal cracking, surface scaling, spalling. Tutorial: crack classification exercise.
weekly_modules.7: Corrosion-related damage; mould and moisture damage. Condition survey of buildings and visual inspection of concrete structures. Tutorial: conditional evaluation and distress score, Drone based evalaution
weekly_modules.8: Destructive and non-destructive testing (NDT) methods. Interpretation of test results. Tutorial: interpreting sample NDT data
weekly_modules.9: Damage / condition rating and reporting. Tutorial: preparing a condition assessment report (small project kick-off).
weekly_modules.10: Approach to repair of concrete structures: principles for repair and protection of damaged concrete. Tutorial: selecting repair strategy for a given case.
weekly_modules.11: Principles for protection against reinforcement corrosion; repair materials and methods. Tutorial: repair method selection exercise.

weekly_modules.13: Green area factor, reporting and reflection; introduction to infrastructure asset management. Course review and project presentations. Tutorial: project presentations & wrap-up. (Major exam window)

CED424.introduction: Introduction of the Course It aims to provide students with a deep understanding of quantity estimation for diverse civil engineering projects, including cost analysis for construction work . The course focuses on practical, application-oriented learning to bridge the gap between academia and standard industrial practices . Students are trained to become industry leaders by mastering quantity estimates, construction planning, and project management technologies . This foundational course is open to all disciplines and requires no specific prerequisites . The course covers diverse methods for building estimates. . Students gain expertise in estimating RCC structures, ranging from simple slabs and beams to complex double-story framed buildings . Instruction includes specialized modules on road projects, covering earthwork calculations for hill roads and the modernization of metalled roads . The curriculum introduces advanced project management tools, such as network analysis through PERT and CPM, and the use of management software
CED424.learning_outcomes: Learning Outcomes: Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to: • Learn basic concepts of quantity estimates of various categories of civil engineering projects. • Prepare bill of quantity and cost of all items of work involved in earthwork excavation, plastering, footings, masonry work, RCC work, highway project and irrigations structures. • A complete understanding on the working capital required on a construction project. The students will be well capable in conducting construction planning, project selection using time value of money concept, project planning and network analysis- PERT, CPM, and precedence network.
CED424.objectives: Course Objectives: The objectives of this course are summarized as follows: • To gain an understanding of various aspects of the estimation of quantities of different items of work in civil engineering projects, estimate the costs of necessary items of work, and conduct cost analysis for relevant construction work, and gain insights into construction engineering, technology, and management. • To train and prepare students with all application-oriented curricula, which will help and nurture them in becoming industry leaders in their further career in the industry. • To reveal all standard practices going on in the construction industry during this course curriculum, so that the students will learn how to implement the best engineering and management practices and technologies.
CED424.program_learning_goals: Program Learning Goals The learning goals for CED 307 focus on providing students with a comprehensive understanding of quantity estimation and cost analysis for diverse civil engineering projects . Students are expected to master preparing bills of quantities for various tasks, including earthwork, masonry, and RCC structures . Beyond technical estimation, the program aims to develop proficiency in project management techniques, such as network analysis using PERT and CPM . Ultimately, the course seeks to prepare students for industry leadership by exposing them to standard construction practices, economic decision-making, and modern project monitoring tools like earned value analysis
CED424.skill_development: Skill Development The course focuses on developing a robust technical and managerial skill set for civil engineering students. Participants gain proficiency in preparing detailed bills of quantities and cost analysis for diverse projects, including earthwork, masonry, and complex RCC structures . Beyond technical estimation, the course cultivates expertise in construction planning and economic decision-making using the time value of money concept . Advanced project management skills are developed through network analysis techniques like PERT and CPM, resource scheduling, and the application of project management software . Students also learn project monitoring strategies, such as earned value analysis, to ensure complete industrial readiness . Curriculum modules include specialized estimation for RCC structures, ranging from simple beams and slabs to double-story framed buildings . Students learn to estimate road projects, covering earthwork for hill roads, CC trackways, and the modernization of existing roads . The course introduces construction economics, including cash-flow diagrams, interest tables, and the evaluation of public projects using benefit-cost ratios

CED425.introduction: The following introduction outlines the core components of CED 425: Climate Change and Its Adaptation & Mitigation: . Core Objective: The course provides a comprehensive foundation in climate science, focusing on the mechanisms of the natural climate system and the causes of change. . Earth Systems: Students explore the interactions between the atmosphere, oceans, cryosphere, and terrestrial biosphere, alongside historical climate variability over millions of years. . Energy and Feedbacks: The curriculum examines global energy balances and carbon cycles, specifically how physical and geochemical feedback loops perturb the climate system. . Modeling Frameworks: Learners investigate a hierarchy of climate models to simulate environmental interactions and test the validity of various climate projections. . Future Adaptation: By evaluating emission scenarios, the course prepares students to project 21st-century changes and to develop strategic risk-management plans for adaptation.
CED425.learning_outcomes: Upon Successful Completion Of The Course, the student should be able to: • To Understand The Fundamental Concepts Of Climate Systems, Its Components And Energy Balance. • To Gain Knowledge Of Climate History • To Develop The Concepts Of Climate Balance And Various Types Of Climate Feedback. • To Develop The Concepts For The Climate Change Model • To Develop The Key Concepts For Future Climate Modeling And Scenarios Involved In Future Climate Projection.
CED425.objectives: The overall objective of this course is to understand climate science. • To relate to the natural climate system and causes of climate change. • To predict the vulnerability of the natural system due to climate change. • To understand risk management plan for climate change. • To understand and explore different climate change models. • To understand the concept of future climate change scenarios
CED425.program_learning_goals: The learning goals for the course is to focus on providing students with a comprehensive understanding of Climate Change and its Adaptation & Mitigation The following learning goals have been established: . Comprehend Climate Science: Gain a foundational understanding of the natural climate system, its core components, and the history and mechanisms driving climate change. . Assess Vulnerability and Risk: Predict the vulnerability of natural systems to climate shifts and understand strategic risk management plans for effective adaptation. . Analyze Feedback Mechanisms: Examine global energy balances and the various physical, geochemical, and bio-geophysical feedback loops that perturb the climate system. . Master Climate Modeling: Explore a hierarchy of climate models to simulate environmental interactions and test the validity of climate projections. . Project Future Scenarios: Evaluate emission scenarios and modeling techniques to project 21st-century changes in temperature, precipitation, and carbon cycles.
CED425.skill_development: Students in CED 425 develop a specialized set of technical and analytical skills through the following core competencies: . Climate Modeling Proficiency: Gain the ability to utilize a hierarchy of models, including General Circulation Models, to simulate environmental interactions and validate climate projections. . Risk and Vulnerability Assessment: Develop skills to predict the vulnerability of natural systems and formulate strategic risk management plans for effective adaptation. . Earth Systems Analysis: Master the evaluation of global energy balances and the complex interconnectedness of the atmosphere, oceans, cryosphere, and terrestrial biosphere. . Future Scenario Planning: Learn to interpret and master emission scenarios to project 21st-century changes in temperature, precipitation, and carbon cycles. . Feedback Mechanism Analysis: Acquire expertise in evaluating physical, geochemical, and biogeochemical feedback loops that drive climate system responses to perturbations.
