CHD2002.introduction: The primary objective of a chemical engineer is to design, analyze, and optimize processes that convert raw materials into valuable products. Thermodynamics provides the fundamental framework for understanding energy, its transformation, and the equilibrium behavior of physical and chemical processes, making it one of the core pillars of chemical engineering. This course introduces the fundamental laws of thermodynamics, including the first and second laws, and their application to closed and open systems. Students will learn to apply equations of state to estimate the properties of real gases and gas mixtures, analyze power generation and refrigeration cycles, and understand thermodynamic concepts such as free energy, excess properties, and phase and chemical equilibrium. These principles enable engineers to evaluate the feasibility of processes, predict equilibrium behavior, estimate energy requirements, and analyze the performance of engineering systems. The knowledge gained in this course forms the foundation for advanced topics in chemical engineering, including reaction engineering, separation processes, process design, energy systems, and emerging applications involving biological and biomolecular systems.
CHD2002.learning_outcomes: After successful completion of this course, students will develop a sound understanding of energy and its transformations, the first and second laws of thermodynamics, and the application of thermodynamic principles to closed and open systems. They will learn to apply equations of state for estimating the properties of real gases, analyze power generation and refrigeration cycles, and understand the concept of free energy and its role in determining thermodynamic equilibrium and process feasibility.
CHD2002.objectives: 1. To familiarize students with thermodynamic principles and their relevance to chemical and biological processes 2. To equip students to estimate thermodynamic properties of real systems which are essential for designing of reactors, heat exchangers and other industrial equipment.
CHD2002.skill_development: 1. Apply the first and second laws of thermodynamics to analyze engineering systems. 2. Perform energy and mass balance calculations for closed and open systems. 3. Analyze phase and chemical equilibrium in engineering processes. 4. Estimate the properties of real gases and gas mixtures using equations of state. 5. Evaluate the performance and efficiency of power generation and refrigeration cycles. 6. Assess the thermodynamic feasibility and equilibrium limitations of chemical and physical processes. 7. Calculate and interpret thermodynamic properties, including enthalpy, entropy, Gibbs free energy, and excess properties. 8. Analyze the effects of temperature, pressure, and composition on process behavior. 9. Solve complex engineering problems using analytical and quantitative methods. 10. Develop a strong foundation for advanced courses in reaction engineering, separation processes, process design, and energy systems.

CHD310.objectives: The aim of this course is to make students learn about behaviour of non-ideal reactors and then make use of that understanding to predict conversion and exit concentration in non-ideal reactors for homogenous as well as heterogeneous catalytic reaction.
CHD310.program_learning_goals: Apply the reaction engineering principles to analyze non-ideal reactor behavior using residence time distribution concepts. CHD310.skill_development: It equips students with the ability to analyze and interpret the behavior of non-ideal reactors using the concept of Residence Time Distribution (RTD). CHD318.learning_outcomes: • Describe mass transfer phenomena, including molecular and turbulent diffusion, interphase mass transfer, and mass transfer operations in chemical industries. • Explain and analyze molecular diffusion mechanisms in gases, liquids, and solids, including the estimation of binary diffusivities and understanding their dependence on temperature and pressure. • Convert between different concentration measures (mass fraction, mole fraction, mass/volume, and moles/volume) for process calculations. • Define and calculate average mass velocity, molar velocity, mass (or molar) flux, and diffusion flux, and apply general flux equations for steady-state, one dimensional diffusion problems. • Estimate convective mass-transfer coefficients using dimensional analysis and apply these coefficients in engineering scenarios like flow past flat plates, spheres, cylinders, pipes, and packed beds. • Describe and apply various mass transfer theories (film theory, penetration theory, surface renewal theory, boundary layer theory) to predict mass transfer coefficients. • Analyze interphase mass transfer using equilibrium data, Raoult’s law, Henry’s law, and related concepts for two-phase systems. • Calculate interfacial mass transfer rates using local and overall mass-transfer coefficients and perform resistance analysis for multiphase systems. • Apply the acquired theoretical knowledge to analyze and solve fundamental mass transfer problems relevant to separation and purification processes in the chemical industry, forming the essential foundation for the upcoming Mass Transfer 2 course, where the design and analysis of key mass transfer equipment such as absorbers, distillation columns, liquid-liquid extractors, dryers, and adsorption units will be explored.
CHD318.objectives: To provide students with a fundamental understanding of mass transfer principles relevant to chemical engineering processes. To enable students to describe molecular diffusion mechanisms in gases, liquids, and solids, and explain their industrial relevance. To develop students' skills in analyzing and calculating mass and molar fluxes during steady-state diffusion processes. To provide students with the ability to estimate binary diffusivity using both experimental and empirical approaches. To enable students to understand convective mass transfer, including the concept and calculation of mass transfer coefficients for various flow configurations. To develop students' knowledge of key mass transfer theories (film, penetration, surface renewal, and boundary layer theories) for predicting mass transfer coefficients. To provide students with the competence to evaluate interfacial mass transfer rates using local and overall mass transfer coefficients. To prepare students for designing basic mass transfer equipment and operations essential for separation and purification processes in chemical process industries. To develop students' ability to apply mass transfer concepts to solve real-world engineering problems and support advanced learning in subsequent courses.
CHD318.program_learning_goals: Students acquire fundamental knowledge of molecular diffusion in gases, liquids, and solids, turbulent diffusion, mass transfer coefficients, and interphase mass transfer essential for understanding and analyzing separation and purification processes in chemical industries. Through the understanding of mass transfer theories (film, penetration, surface renewal, and boundary layer theories) and mass transfer coefficients, students can analyze and design basic unit operations such as gas absorbers, dryers, and packed beds. The course encourages the use of dimensionless analysis, analogy methods, and empirical models for problem-solving, providing a foundation for future application of simulation software for mass transfer analysis. Students understand the role and impact of separation and purification technologies in industries related to environmental protection, energy, and sustainable chemical production. Basic understanding of how mass transfer efficiencies affect process design and operational costs is introduced, connecting scientific principles to economic considerations.
CHD318.skill_development: This course contributes to the development of the following skills: • Analytical skills: Ability to analyze mass transfer phenomena and interpret diffusion and interphase transfer data. • Problem-solving skills: Application of theoretical concepts to solve practical mass transfer problems in chemical processes. • Calculation and data handling skills: Performing conversions between different concentration units and calculating fluxes, diffusivities, and mass transfer coefficients. • Fundamental engineering skills: Building a foundational understanding of mass transfer processes necessary for the design of separation equipment in subsequent courses. • Technical communication skills: Developing clarity in explaining physical concepts, process variables, and calculation results relevant to mass transfer.

CHD320.introduction: Most industries operational today aim to automate their processes to the greatest extent. Automatic process control, if programmed and maintained carefully, eliminates the human errors that have led to tragic plant-wide accidents in the past. This introductory course covers basics of process control. The course begins with the introductory concepts, followed by the mathematical modelling. This knowledge base will be beneficial to understand the dynamic behaviour of chemical processes. A major focus will be on the design of feedback controllers, including their tuning and stability analysis. Later, discussions on several advanced control systems will introduce the class to actual systems employed in industries. The course ends with exposing the class with designing practical plant-wide control systems.
CHD320.learning_outcomes: On completion of the course, the students will be able to: Show Block Diagram Of The System. Make The Definition Of Process Control, Know The Concept Of Steady/Unsteady State, And Feed-Back Control. Define The Error Of A System Controlled And Apply It In A Proper Control System. Use The Laplace Method And Solve Differential Equation. Obtain Transfer Functions For First Order Systems Like Mercury Thermometer, Liquid Level, And Mixing Systems. Linearizing The Nonlinear Systems, And Analyse The System Connected In Series. Know Open And Closed Loop Concept While Solving Process Control Problems. Obtain The Transfer Functions Of The Close Loops And Simplify The Transfer Functions Of The Closed Loop. Apply Different Inputs To This Transfer Functions And Find Dynamic Responses Of A Simple Control System. Analyse Stability Of Systems, Know The Stability Concept. Know Methods To Analyse The Stability Of A System, For Example The Routh Theorem.
CHD320.objectives: To provide students with a fundamental understanding of dynamic behavior in chemical process systems, including reactors, heat exchangers, and separation units. To enable students to develop dynamic models of chemical processes using material and energy balances. To develop student skills in formulating linear and nonlinear mathematical models of chemical process dynamics. To provide students with an understanding of Laplace transforms, transfer functions, and their application to chemical engineering systems. To enable students to analyze transient and steady-state behavior of chemical processes and predict system responses to disturbances. To develop student skills in designing and tuning feedback control systems, including PID controllers, for chemical process applications. To provide students with practical knowledge of advanced control strategies relevant to chemical engineering, such as cascade, feedforward, and ratio control. To enable students to use process control software and simulation tools (e.g. Simulink) to analyze and design control systems. To develop student skills in interpreting and designing Piping and Instrumentation Diagrams (P&IDs) for chemical process control systems. To provide students with the ability to evaluate control performance, stability, and safety in the context of chemical plant operations and regulatory requirements.
CHD320.program_learning_goals: Introduction to process control. Then, modelling static and dynamic behaviour will be covered, including the modelling considerations. Followed by, analysis of dynamic behaviour including the linearization of nonlinear systems and Laplace transforms. The above topics will prepare the student to learn transfer functions and input-output models, also covering dynamic behaviour of 1st, 2nd, and higher order systems. The second half of the course will then focus on the design and analysis of feedback control systems and their dynamic behaviour, stability analysis and the design of controller with the help of frequency response analysis. Lastly, the course will finish on the discussion of design and analysis of advanced control systems being used in modern plants today. This discussion will include feedback control of systems with dead time or inverse response, control systems with multiple loops, feedforward and ratio control, adaptive and inferential control systems. Some emphasis will also be put on multivariable processes, meaning design of MIMO control systems for complete plants.
CHD320.skill_development: - Mathematical modeling of chemical process dynamics. - Analysis and interpretation of transient process responses. - Development and use of transfer function models for dynamic systems. - Design, analysis, and tuning of PID controllers. - Stability analysis using classical control techniques (e.g., Routh criterion, Bode plots). - Selection and implementation of appropriate process control strategies (feedback, feedforward, cascade, and ratio control). - (Project work): Simulation and analysis of process control systems using MATLAB/Simulink or equivalent computational tools. - Interpretation of process data and evaluation of controller performance. - Troubleshooting and optimization of industrial process control systems. - Technical communication and teamwork through problem-solving exercises, case studies, and laboratory/simulation activities.

CHY1015.learning_outcomes: Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to: 1. Apply vector analysis and calculus to solve problems in molecular systems. 2. Understand classical mechanics concepts, including harmonic motion, angular momentum, and relativistic effects, and their applications in chemistry. 3. Explain the kinetic theory of gases and statistical distributions relevant to molecular behavior. 4. Analyze the effects of electric and magnetic fields on molecules using fundamental electromagnetism principles. 5. Understand wave phenomena, including interference, diffraction, and polarization, and their significance in chemical studies. 6. Describe the physics of semiconductors, including band gaps, doping, and superconductivity, and their implications for material science. 7. Conduct laboratory experiments to measure optical properties, electromagnetic effects, and mechanical motion, reinforcing theoretical knowledge.
CHY1015.objectives: This course provides fundamental physics concepts essential for understanding chemical principles. It covers vector analysis, classical mechanics, kinetic theory of gases, electromagnetism, wave theory, and semiconductor physics, with applications in molecular and atomic systems. The course also includes hands-on laboratory experiments to reinforce theoretical concepts.
CHY1015.program_learning_goals: The aim of this course is to equip chemistry undergraduate students with a strong foundation in physics, enabling them to comprehend and apply physical principles in chemical sciences. The course emphasizes the role of physics in molecular mechanics, spectroscopy, quantum chemistry, and material science, ensuring students develop analytical and problem-solving skills relevant to their field.
CHY1015.skill_development: Students will develop the skill to perform some primary physics experiments, and they will develop fundamental skills to interpret chemical phenomena using the fundamentals of Physics.

weekly_modules.1: The Importance of Physics for Chemistry Students: Introduction of course: Basics of Vector analysis
weekly_modules.2: Fundamental vector operations, Vector calculus: Gradient, Divergence, Curl and related fundamental theorems of vector calculus, Vector integration (line, surface and volume integrals), Divergence theorem and Stoke’s theorem.
weekly_modules.3: Kinematics of linear and angular motions, Molecular Mechanics, Hooks law and application of Hooks law for molecules. Harmonic motion and periodicity. Applications of harmonicity and anharmonicity in molecules.
weekly_modules.4: Angular momentum and its application of molecular and atomic motions. Molecular Mechanical treatment of oscillators and rigid body rotators. Theory of relativity, relativistic effect in terms of chemistry.
weekly_modules.5: Kinetic theory of gas, degree of freedom, law of equipartition energy, Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution law. Ensembles, Fermi-Dirac and Bose-Einstein Distributions, phase space.
weekly_modules.6: Electrostatics, Charge Density, electric and Magnetic Dipoles and moments, Quadrupole and quadrupole moments.
weekly_modules.7: Continuation of Chemical examples based on electromagnetism. Gauss’ Law and its applications, Impact of Electric Field and Magnetic field on molecules.
weekly_modules.8: Continuation of Chemical examples based on electromagnetism. Fundamental laws of electromagnetics. Induction and Polarization. Electrodynamics.
weekly_modules.9: Maxwell’s equations of Electrodynamics; Impact of electrostatic field on chemical structure and reactivity.
weekly_modules.10: Interference, diffraction, and polarisation of light, Wave nature of Electrons, Sound waves, Doppler’s effect, and its applications.
weekly_modules.11: Elasticity and its applications using examples of molecular mechanical models of molecules.
weekly_modules.12: Physics of Semiconductor: Semiconductors, Band Gaps, Fermi’s Rule, Transistors and diodes, doping, superconductivity, and levitations.
weekly_modules.13: Physics of Semiconductors continuations.

CHY2014.learning_outcomes: A) Use The Instruments And Analyse Data Obtained From A Particular Measurement Efficiently and Precisely. B) Understand And Explain The Fundamental Concepts Of The Foundations Of Various Techniques And Their Role In Research Applications.
CHY2014.objectives: • To provide students with an understanding of the various types of analytical instruments. • To provide students with a working knowledge of instrumental techniques and, the base of characterization of relevant materials of interest. • To develop students’ skills in learning instrument handling through real-life lab experience efficiently. • To develop students’ skills in analysing experimental results.
CHY2014.program_learning_goals: The goal is to familiarize the students with the basic principles of spectroscopy and diffraction. Methods that are instrumental to the analysis of molecules and structures, to give opportunity to get good exposure to the utility of various analytical instruments used for chemical samples.
CHY2014.skill_development: This Fundamental Course Contributes To The Experimental Skills For Performing Meaningful Experiments, Analyse Data, And Interpret Observations.

weekly_modules.1: X-ray Diffraction: What is X-ray? Properties of X-rays, X-ray generation principle; Classification of X-rays; X-ray sources; Lab X-ray source vs Synchrotron-based X-ray source; Diffraction of X-rays, Bragg’s Law; Order of diffractions.
weekly_modules.2: Crystallography: Unit cell, Axes system, Bravais lattices, Lattice rows, Miller indices, Crystallographic planes and directions, Crystal systems, Cubic lattice system, Introduction to reciprocal lattice.
weekly_modules.3: UV-visible spectroscopy: Concept of absorption spectroscopy, atomic vs molecular absorptions, the concept of color, effect of conjugation. Bathochromic, hypsochromic, hyperchromic, and hypochromic shifts. Lambert-Beer’s law.
weekly_modules.4: Photoluminescence spectroscopy: Excited state formation, Jablonski diagram, non-radiative and radiative decay, fluorescence & phosphorescence.
weekly_modules.5: Data Analysis: Uncertainties, errors, mean, standard deviation, least square fit.
weekly_modules.6: Microwave or Rotational Spectroscopy: Principal axes of rotation and three principal moments of inertia, Classification of molecules based on moments of inertia, Rigid (diatomic) rotator model, Rotational energy levels and rotational selection rule and transitions, Rotational spectra of carbon monoxide and water vapor, Basic instrumentation of rotational spectroscopy.
weekly_modules.7: Infra-Red (Vibrational) spectroscopy: Molecular vibrations, Modes of vibration, Factors influencing vibrational frequencies: coupling of vibrational frequencies, hydrogen bonding, electronic effects,
weekly_modules.8: The Fourier Transform Infrared Spectrometer, Calibration of the Frequency Scale, Absorbance and Transmittance scale, intensity and position of IR bands, fingerprint region, and interpretation of IR spectra of simple organic molecules, basic mention of Raman Spectroscopy including the mutual exclusion principle, Raman and IR active modes of CO2.
weekly_modules.9: Thermogravimetric Analysis (TGA), Differential Scanning Calorimetry (DSC). Interpretation of TGA and DSC. Understanding oxidation, reduction, evaporation, and decomposition characteristics of chemical compounds.
weekly_modules.10: Studying phase transition, melting and crystallization events, and thermodynamic properties of chemical compounds.
weekly_modules.11: Mass spectrometry: Introduction to mass spectroscopy: isotope effect, fragmentation patterns. McLafferty rearrangements, chemical ionization.
weekly_modules.12: Chromatography: Principle of chromatography, Thin Layer chromatography (TLC), High-Performance Liquid Chromatography (HPLC),
weekly_modules.13: Liquid Chromatography-Mass Spectrometry (LC-MS), Application of chromatography.

CHY2045.introduction: This course introduces the chemistry of the main-group elements in Groups 13–17 of the periodic table. Students will learn about the periodic trends, electronic structures, bonding, oxidation states, and chemical reactivity of these elements. The course covers the preparation, properties, and applications of important compounds, including hydrides, halides, oxides, etc The course provides a strong foundation for understanding the chemistry and practical applications of p-block elements and highlights the growing importance of main-group chemistry in catalysis and materials science.
CHY2045.learning_outcomes: On Successful completion of the course, students will be able to: A) Understand the chemistry of Group (13-17) elements of the periodic table and their physical properties, reaction of halides, oxides, clusters, occurrence, production, and Applications in real life. B) Explain the fundamental concepts of a redox reaction of the elements involved, redox reactions, and applications. C) Students will perform lab experiments to understand the synthesis and characterization of compounds made up of respective group elements. Students will analyze data obtained from these lab-based experiments efficiently and precisely.
CHY2045.objectives: a) To provide students with an understanding of the physical and chemical properties of group 13-17 elements of the periodic table. b) To provide students with a working knowledge of synthesizing and characterization of relevant materials made up of respective group elements. c) To develop students’ skills through lab experience efficiently. d) To develop students’ skills in analyzing materials of interest. e) To develop analytical and critical thinking ability of the students
CHY2045.program_learning_goals: Understand the chemistry of main group compounds and their properties Fundamental concepts of structure and bonding principles of relevant compounds Synthesis, characterization and analysis of compounds

CHY3041.learning_outcomes: 1. Understand the concept of electrochemistry mechanistically. 2. Application of electrochemistry. 3. Develop a mechanistic understanding of fundamental electrochemical concepts and apply electrochemical principles and techniques to relevant chemical systems.
CHY3041.objectives: 1. General discussion about oxidation and reduction, electron transfer vs. atom transfer, oxidation no. 2. Concept of electrochemistry, Definition: Electrochemical cell, electrodes, salt bridge and its function etc. Battery; types of cell: Electrolytic cell vs Galvanic cell; concentration cell vs chemical cell, How to construct a voltaic cell? 3. Definition: Electrode potential, Std. potential and Formal potential; Physical significance of electrode potential. 4. Types of electrodes: (i) metal electrode, advantage of amalgam electrode; (ii) non-metal electrode, e.g. hydrogen gas electrode, glassy carbon electrode. What is glassy carbon electrode? What is the difference between glassy carbon and graphite electrode? 5. Factors affecting the electrode potential: (i) effect of concentration, (ii) effect of pH e.g. formation of insoluble hydroxide. 6. Application of electrode potential; Latimer diagram. 7. Electroanalytical techniques: Potentiometry, Coulometry, Voltammetry and Amperometry. 8. How to measure electrode potential?; Cyclic voltammetry (CV) 9. Bulk electrolysis.
CHY3041.program_learning_goals: To provide students with an understanding: 1. the concept of electrochemistry; 2. factors affecting the electrochemical processes, mechanistic understanding; and 3. application of electrochemistry and electrochemical techniques
CHY3041.skill_development: Development of practical and analytical skills in electrochemical measurements and techniques, including electrode potential measurement, potentiometry, cyclic voltammetry, coulometry, amperometry, and bulk electrolysis, along with the ability to interpret electrochemical data and apply these techniques to chemical systems.

CSD2003.faculty: Rajeev Kumar Singh, Sheel Sindhu Manohar
CSD2003.introduction: This course provides a comprehensive understanding of the fundamental components that make up a computer system. It begins with the basics of Boolean algebra, logic gates, and the design of both combinational and sequential circuits, forming the foundation for digital logic. Students will explore how computers interpret and execute instructions, delving into machine language, instruction sets, and their processing. The course also covers key elements of computer architecture, including the control unit, arithmetic logic unit (ALU), registers, and pipelining, offering insight into how computers process information efficiently. Different types of memory systems, their organization, and data management techniques will be discussed to understand how memory plays a critical role in computing.
CSD2003.learning_outcomes: On successful completion of the course, students will be able to achieve the following: 1. Understand the evolution and major architectural milestones and their impact on modern computing. 2. Analyze the performance of computer systems using appropriate quantitative metrics. 3. Apply computer arithmetic principles for representing and performing operations on data. 4. Program using assembly language, with emphasis on MIPS programming. 5. Analyze the structure and functionality of the CPU, including datapath design, control unit operation, instruction execution, and register organization. 6. Design and model digital circuits using Verilog for basic computer organization components. 7. Understand the concept of instruction pipelining. 8. Analyze memory organization and hierarchy, including cache memory, main memory, secondary storage, and their impact on overall system performance. 9. Understand and analyze input/output organization.
CSD2003.objectives: This course will enable the students to understand the internal organization of a computer, and analyze its different modules in terms of structure & function. Additionally, the course examines how computers interact with external devices through input/output systems, interfaces, and various communication techniques. Students will gain practical knowledge of interfacing with external devices by learning how hardware and software enable external connections. Overall, this course offers an in- depth look into the internal workings of a computer system and its interaction with the outside world.
CSD2003.skill_development: After completing this course, students will develop the ability to understand, analyze, design, and evaluate the fundamental building blocks of computer systems from digital logic to processor, memory, and I/O organization. Students will develop the following skills: 1. Ability to design and simplify Boolean functions using logic gates, Karnaugh maps, multiplexers, decoders, adders, latches, flip-flops, registers, and counters. 2. Ability to analyze and implement basic combinational and sequential circuits used in computer hardware. 3. Introductory ability to model combinational and sequential circuits using Verilog and understand programmable devices such as PLA, PAL, CPLD, and FPGA. 4. Ability to explain the organization of computer systems, including CPU, memory, buses, I/O devices, datapath, control path, and instruction execution. 5. Ability to perform number system conversions, understand IEEE 754 floating-point representation, and analyze arithmetic circuits such as adders, multipliers, and ALUs. 6. Basic ability to write and analyze MIPS assembly programs and understand instruction formats, addressing modes, registers, and RISC-based execution. 7. Ability to evaluate computer performance using execution time, CPI, clock rate, benchmarking, Amdahl’s Law, and related performance metrics. 8. Ability to analyze memory hierarchy, cache mapping techniques, replacement policies, write policies, hit/miss behavior, and average memory access time.

weekly_modules.1: Definition of computer organization, computer architecture, and their relationship. Basic Components: Input devices, output devices, CPU, memory, storage devices. Binary, octal, decimal, and hexadecimal systems; conversions between all four — binary↔decimal, octal↔binary, hex↔binary, hex↔decimal.
weekly_modules.2: IEEE 754 single and double precision; sign bit, biased exponent, mantissa/significand; normalized form Boolean Algebra — Laws & Theorems: AND, OR, NOT operations; commutative, associative, distributive laws; De Morgan's theorems; duality principle.
weekly_modules.3: Logic Gates & Boolean Function Implementation: AND, OR, NOT, NAND, NOR, XOR, XNOR gates; truth table to gate circuit; gate-level implementations of Boolean functions. Karnaugh Maps & Boolean Minimization: Minterms and maxterms; 2-, 3-, 4-variable K-maps; grouping 1s (SOP) and 0s (POS); don't-care conditions; minimal expressions.
weekly_modules.4: Adder Circuits: Half-adder and full-adder design; full-adder from half-adders; ripple-carry adder; carry propagation delay; sum and carry expressions. Decoders & Encoders: 2-to-4 and 3-to-8 line decoders; enable inputs; decoder expansion; 4-to-2 and 8-to-3 encoders; priority encoder; applications.
weekly_modules.5: Multiplexers & Demultiplexers: 2:1, 4:1, 8:1 MUX; MUX tree expansion; implementing Boolean functions with MUX; 1-to-4 and 1-to-8 DEMUX; data routing applications. Latches — SR, D, and JK: SR latch (NOR and NAND); forbidden state; D latch; JK latch; race condition; enable signal; transparent latch behaviour.
weekly_modules.6: Flip-Flops — SR, D, JK, and T: edge triggering; master-slave configuration; setup and hold time; clock-to-Q delay; excitation tables. Shift Registers — SISO, SIPO, PISO, PIPO: Serial-in serial-out; serial-in parallel-out; parallel-in serial-out; parallel-in parallel-out; bidirectional and universal shift registers; ring counter; applications in serial communication.
weekly_modules.7: Counters — Asynchronous & Synchronous: Asynchronous ripple counter; synchronous counter; mod-N counter design; up, down, and up/down counters; ring counter; Johnson counter; state diagrams. Integrated Review & Problem Solving: Number conversion edge cases; K-map with don't-cares; adder/decoder integration; flip-flop conversion problems; counter + register chain; exam-style MCQs.
weekly_modules.8: Programmable Logic Devices: PLA, PAL, CPLD, FPGA. Modelling combinational and sequential circuits using Verilog Introduction to Computer Architecture: VonNeumann Architecture, Classes of Computers, Moore's Law, Amdahl's Law, Overview of IC Manufacturing, Processor power consumption and performance trends
weekly_modules.9: Processor Performance measurement and Bench marking ISA Fundamentals — Instruction Format & Addressing Modes: What is an ISA; instruction format; opcode and operands; instruction types; addressing modes — immediate, direct, indirect, register, indexed, based, relative.
weekly_modules.10: RISC vs. CISC & Registers: RISC characteristics — fixed-length instructions, load/store architecture; CISC — variable-length instructions, complex addressing MIPS as a Representative RISC ISA
weekly_modules.11: Introduction to MIPS Assembly Language Programming Processor : Data and Control Path
weekly_modules.12: Introduction to the basic pipeling concepts Computer Arithmatic, Basic Adder, Multiplier, Fast Adder, ALU Design & CPU Pipelining.
weekly_modules.13: Memory Systems: Why multiple levels; registers, cache (L1/L2/L3), main memory, secondary storage; locality of reference; cost-speed-capacity tradeoff Cache Memory — Mapping Techniques: Cache hit and miss; hit ratio and average access time; direct mapping; fully associative mapping; set-associative mapping; worked numerical examples for all three techniques. Cache Replacement Algorithms & Write Policies: LRU; FIFO; Random replacement; optimal (Bélády's) algorithm; write-through vs. write-back; write allocate vs. no-write allocate; dirty bit; cache coherence basics.

CSD304.faculty: Shankar Kumar Ghosh, Karnish Nasrin Ahmed Tapadar, Himani Sikarwar
CSD304.introduction: This course will provide a basis in understanding different kinds of computer networks, particularly wired networks. Starting from the very basic of TCP/IP protocol suite, protocols operating from different layers are discussed. Apart from theoretical understanding of different network protocols, basic applications of socket programming and applications of Wireshark will be demonstrated. Basic network security concepts will also be introduced. Fundamental differences in network protocol design between wired and wireless networks will also be discussed.
CSD304.learning_outcomes: On successful completion of the course, students will be able to achieve the following: CO1: Understand the Layered Network Architecture (OSI and TCP/IP), Core Networking Principles, and the functions of various protocols across the Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, and Application layers (DNS, HTTP, FTP, SMTP, Telnet, SNMP and Firewalls). CO2: Analyze and design network topologies and routing strategies using appropriate protocols and algorithms, including IP addressing, Subnetting, Distance Vector and Link State Routing Techniques. CO3: Understand the basic Link Layer Mechanisms (e.g., Error detection and correction, MAC Protocols), Transport Layer Functionalities (e.g., Flow control, Congestion control), and Distinguish between connection-oriented and connectionless protocols. CO4: Apply concepts of socket programming to real world communication scenarios. CO5: Understanding application layer protocols through Wireshark.
CSD304.objectives: 1. To introduce the fundamental types, architectures, and principles of computer networks, emphasizing the layered approach through OSI and TCP/IP models and their comparative merits. 2. To develop a strong theoretical foundation in protocol design, protocol layering, addressing schemes (including classless addressing), subnetting, and routing concepts. 3. To provide detailed insights into the structure and operation of protocols across all networking layers—application, transport, network, and data link—along with packet-level analysis. 4. To equip students with practical skills for designing, configuring, and managing networks using devices such as hubs, switches, and bridges, and to interpret routing entries from topologies. 5. To explore performance optimization techniques, real-world applications, and security considerations involved in the design and maintenance of reliable, scalable networks.
CSD304.program_learning_goals: PLG1: Understand layered network architectures and communication protocols. PLG2: Identify and solve complex network problems using standard algorithms and principles. PLG3: Design and Evaluate reliable and efficient communication systems for real-world needs.
CSD304.skill_development: This course enhances students’ technical skills in network design, configuration, protocol analysis, and Socket programming. It also fosters problem-solving abilities and hands-on experience with industry standard networking tools and services.

weekly_modules.1: Module 1 (Introduction to Computer Networking): Types of Networks (LAN, MAN, WAN, PAN), Network Standards, Protocol Stack, OSI vs TCP/IP protocol suite, Circuit Switching, Packet Switching, Message Switching, Synchronous vs Asynchronous Transmissions.
weekly_modules.2: Module 1 (continued): Physical Layer: Analog vs Digital transmissions, Guided and Unguided Media, Inter-networking Devices: Hubs, Switches, Routers, Gateways, Multiplexing: FDM, TDM, Statistical TDM.

weekly_modules.5: Module 2 (Continued): ARQ Performance in Error-Free & Noisy Channels, MAC Protocols: ALOHA (Pure & Slotted), CSMA, CSMA/CD, Ethernet: Frame Format and Working.
weekly_modules.6: Module 2 (Continued): Wireless MAC: CSMA/CA, RTS/CTS, Backoff Algorithm.
weekly_modules.7: Module 3 (Network Layer): Network Layer Design Issues, Routing Concepts: Forwarding vs Routing, Subnetting, Supernetting.

weekly_modules.11: Module 4 (Continued): TCP: Header Format, Connection Establishment (3-Way Handshake), Flow Control: Sliding Window Mechanism, TCP Congestion Control: Tahoe, Reno, Nagle’s Algorithm, Cumulative ACK, Duplicate ACK, Socket Programming.

CSD311.introduction: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is no longer a niche subfield of computer science; it is the foundational pillar of the 21st-century digital economy. This course introduces undergraduate students to the core concepts, techniques, and paradigms of AI. The course bridges the gap between classical AI—focusing on problem-solving, knowledge representation, and logical reasoning—and modern AI, which is heavily driven by data and machine learning. Students will explore how machines can be engineered to mimic human cognitive functions such as learning, reasoning, problem-solving, and perception. By integrating theoretical foundations with practical Python-based implementations, this course serves as a prerequisite for advanced studies in Machine Learning, Deep Learning, Natural Language Processing, and Computer Vision, ultimately preparing students for the thriving AI startup ecosystem and industry demands in India and abroad.
CSD311.learning_outcomes: • Identify and categorize different types of AI (Narrow, General, Super) and explain the historical milestones leading to modern AI. • Translate complex real-world problems (e.g., route finding, puzzle solving) into state-space representations and implement appropriate search algorithms (BFS, DFS, A*). • Formulate knowledge bases using First-Order Logic (FOL) and apply resolution algorithms to deduce new information and solve logical puzzles. • Develop basic Machine Learning models using Python (e.g., linear regression, decision trees, k-means clustering) and evaluate their performance using standard metrics. • Design, code, and train a simple Artificial Neural Network for a fundamental classification task using standard libraries.
CSD311.objectives: The intent of this course is to: • Introduce the historical evolution, philosophical foundations, and current landscape of Artificial Intelligence. • Familiarize students with the formulation of AI problems as state-space search and equip them to design and analyze uninformed and heuristic search algorithms. • Impart knowledge of Knowledge Representation techniques using Propositional and First-Order Logic, along with automated reasoning and inference mechanisms. • Provide a foundational understanding of Machine Learning, distinguishing between supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning paradigms. • Introduce the basic architecture of Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) and the concept of deep learning as a subset of ML.
CSD311.program_learning_goals: The broader undergraduate program aims to: • 1. Computational Thinking: Develop the ability to formulate, analyze, and solve complex real-world problems using computational principles. • 2. Foundational & Advanced Knowledge: Impart a strong foundation in mathematics, programming, and transitioning to advanced technologies like AI, Data Science, and IoT. • 3. Societal & Ethical Context: Cultivate an understanding of the ethical, legal, and social implications of technology, particularly in the Indian and global socio-economic context. • 4. Employability & Innovation: Bridge the gap between academia and industry by fostering research aptitude, multidisciplinary thinking and problem solving. • 5. Lifelong Learning: Instill the ability to adapt to rapidly evolving technological paradigms through self-directed and continuous learning.
CSD311.skill_development: • Algorithmic Programming: Writing clean, optimized Python code to implement graph searches, logical inference, and ML algorithms. • Data Preprocessing: Skill in cleaning, normalizing, and transforming raw data into formats suitable for AI algorithms. • Model Evaluation: Ability to mathematically and practically validate AI models, understanding concepts like overfitting, underfitting, and cross-validation. • Abstract Problem Formulation: The ability to look at a non-deterministic problem (e.g., "How to play tic-tac-toe optimally?") and abstract it into mathematical states, transitions, and goal tests. • Heuristic Thinking: Developing intuition for creating heuristic functions to optimize computational resources. • Technical Communication: Documenting AI experiments, writing structured reports on algorithmic behavior, and explaining AI limitations to non-technical stakeholders. • Collaborative Debugging: Working in pairs or groups to troubleshoot complex logical errors in AI codebases, mimicking industry Agile workflows.

CSD322.introduction: This course introduces the foundations of modern computer graphics through physically based rendering. Students will learn how geometry, cameras, materials, and light interact to form images, and apply these concepts by building a ray-based renderer in C
CSD322.objectives: To understand how images of virtual 3D scenes are synthesized by modeling geometry, cameras, materials, light, and light transport—and to apply these principles by building a physically based renderer from scratch.
CSD322.prerequisites: Math: Linear algebra, Probability and Statistics Good working knowledge of C++ programing, Object-Oriented Programming (OOP), and some Data Structures. Some work experience with Visual Computing (lmage Processing, Computer Graphics, or Computer Vision) would be helpful. Some work experience with Machine/Deep Learning would be helpful.
CSD322.skill_development: This course develops analytical and conceptual skills by requiring students to move repeatedly between physical phenomena, mathematical models, algorithms, and visual results. Analytical Thinking: Students decompose image synthesis into smaller computational problems—ray generation, intersection, visibility, shading, sampling, and light transport—and analyze their correctness, accuracy, and performance. Mathematical and Physical Reasoning: Students translate concepts from geometry, linear algebra, optics, probability, and numerical integration into working rendering algorithms. Abstraction and Conceptual Modeling: Students learn to represent real-world entities—objects, cameras, materials, and light sources—as computational models and understand the assumptions and limitations of each representation. Problem Solving and Debugging: Building a renderer requires students to diagnose visual artifacts, numerical errors, sampling noise, and performance bottlenecks by reasoning from the generated image back to the underlying algorithm. Connecting Classical and Modern Ideas: By progressing from ray tracing and light transport to NeRF and 3D Gaussian Splatting, students learn how foundational graphics concepts reappear in neural rendering systems.

CSD438.introduction: Distributed systems are ubiquitous and inherently complex, making them challenging to understand and develop. This course comprehensively explores the foundational principles, techniques, and tools essential for analyzing, designing, and building distributed applications and systems. Students will learn the core concepts of distributed computing, including communication and coordination through message passing, and delve into classical distributed algorithms such as logical and vector clocks, leader election, fault tolerance, data consistency, and consensus. Additionally, the course will examine the architecture and design of large-scale distributed systems. Students will gain hands-on experience by implementing many of these concepts through practical assignments and projects, equipping them with practical skills to develop robust and scalable distributed applications.
CSD438.learning_outcomes: 1. Gain the ability to design and develop functional distributed systems while applying key principles and best practices. 2. Learn to create and evaluate algorithms and protocols for various distributed system applications. 3. Transition from thinking in terms of serial programming to designing loosely coupled, asynchronous distributed systems. 4. Acquire the skills to independently design and implement moderately complex distributed systems. 5. Analyze the correctness of distributed algorithms and develop custom solutions for unique scenarios. 6. Gain insights into the design and engineering of contemporary distributed systems, understanding their architecture and operational principles.
CSD438.objectives: • Students get a solid understanding of the principles and practices of distributed computing. • They learn how to design, develop, and manage systems where components located on networked computers communicate and coordinate to achieve common goals. • To enable students with the fundamental concepts such as communication protocols, synchronization, fault tolerance, consistency, and scalability. • By the end of the course, students will be equipped to address challenges in building reliable, efficient, and scalable distributed applications in real-world environments.
CSD438.program_learning_goals: 1. Understand Distributed System Fundamentals 2. Ensure Consistency and Synchronization 3. Evaluate Performance and Fault Tolerance 4. Explore Modern Distributed Technologies
CSD438.skill_development: 1. Learn to evaluate system performance, identify bottlenecks, and optimize distributed applications for scalability, reliability, and resource efficiency. 2. Develop skills in managing concurrent processes, inter-process communication, synchronization, and consistency in distributed environments. 3. Build practical expertise in blockchain to address real-world computing challenges.

CSD457.introduction: An undergraduate-level course on Computer Networks teaches the TCP/IP communication protocol stack and different applications for the Internet. However, all the protocols in TCP/IP protocol stack are mainly designed for efficient data communication and networking. These are not suitable for resource-constrained networking devices and ubiquitous networking. Therefore, a new paradigm of networking has been proposed by the development of IoT. This course is designed to provide information about the core technologies that make up the IoT, and how they are applied in different application domains. It will help to know the components of IoT products and services, including devices for sensing, actuation, processing, and protocols for data communication and networking. Finally, it will help to develop skills and experiences required to design a novel system using IoT.
CSD457.learning_outcomes: Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to: 1. Explain the architecture, protocol stack, and design principles of the Internet of Things (IoT), and distinguish them from conventional TCP/IP-based networks. 2. Identify and describe the key components of IoT systems, including sensors, actuators, embedded devices, gateways, and communication protocols. 3. Explain the operation and applications of IoT communication technologies, including IEEE 802.15.4, 6LoWPAN, RPL, MQTT, and CoAP. 4. Design and implement basic IoT applications using Arduino, NodeMCU, sensors, and actuators. 5. Model, simulate, and evaluate IoT networks using tools such as Cooja and the 6TiSCH simulator. 6. Analyze sensing, actuation, and communication mechanisms involved in IoT-based systems. 7. Explain the role of cloud computing, edge computing, data analytics, and AI/ML in modern IoT applications. 8. Identify security and privacy challenges in IoT systems and discuss possible mitigation strategies. 9. Analyze and propose IoT-based solutions for real-world application domains such as smart homes, healthcare, agriculture, transportation, manufacturing, and smart cities. 10. Design, implement, document, and present an IoT-based solution to address a real-world problem through collaborative project work.
CSD457.objectives: 1.Provide students with a strong foundation in the Internet of Things (IoT), its architecture, layered models, enabling technologies, and applications. 2. Enable students to understand and apply IoT communication protocols and standards, including MQTT, CoAP, 6LoWPAN, and RPL, for resource-constrained networks. 3. Develop students' practical skills in programming embedded platforms such as Arduino and NodeMCU, and interfacing sensors and actuators using standard communication protocols. 4. Enable students to model, simulate, and evaluate IoT networks using tools such as Cooja and the 6TiSCH simulator. 5. Introduce students to emerging technologies, including IoT security, edge computing, cloud computing, and AI/ML for intelligent IoT systems. 6. Encourage students to design innovative IoT solutions through hands-on laboratories, mini-projects, and research-oriented activities.
CSD457.skill_development: This Course Is Designed To Provide Students With A Foundational Understanding Of Core Iot Technologies, Including Sensing, Actuation, Basic Data Processing, And Communication Protocols. Through Lab Sessions and Project-Based Learning, Students Will Gain Practical Experience with IoT Hardware and Software, and begin to develop the ability to design and implement simple IoT-based systems. Through the research based project, students acquire the ability to survey recent literature, design experiments, measure and compare results against a baseline, write in IEEE format, and present their work.

DES1003.introduction: This course make student aware of how society, culture, and design are related to each other. Through theoretical exploration, case studies, and practical applications, students will gain a comprehensive understanding of how societal and cultural contexts shape design choices and how design, in turn, influences and reflects broader societal trends.
DES1003.learning_outcomes: The student should be able to • Define the key terms and concepts related to society, culture, and design • Apply theories such as social constructivism, cultural materialism, and symbolic interactionism to analyse design contexts • Analyse case studies to demonstrate how cultural dimensions’ impact design aesthetics and functionality and develop an understanding of how cultural symbols, rituals, and practices influence design choices • Assess and propose design interventions that respond to current societal challenges • Study and apply of cross-cultural design adaptations and innovations that consider cultural diversity, inclusivity, sustainability and ethics. • Develop capability to foresee Future societal trends
DES1003.objectives: By the end of this course, students should be able to: • Examine the dynamic interplay between society, culture, and design and how they influence one another and identify cultural factors that impact design choices and functionality. • Critically assess the societal consequences of design decisions and innovations, apply relevant theories from sociology, anthropology, and interpret real-world design scenarios. • Provide constructive critiques of design projects, integrating sociocultural insights, and reflect on the ethical implications of design choices. • Develop culturally sensitive design solutions that consider diverse perspectives and respect cultural norms.
DES1003.program_learning_goals: Graduates will exhibit an understanding of socio-cultural contexts and ethical considerations in design decision-making, including sustainability and inclusivity.

DES1004.introduction: This course encourages and engages students to deal with the physicality of the design process and design outcomes. The course involves understanding what the products are made of, how they are made, and why those choices matter. This would provide a lens through which students can examine how the materials and techniques of manufacturing those materials influence lifespans of designed artefacts and lead to a sustainable future. The course would cover the journey from traditional craft based techniques to digital fabrication. This would prepare the students to design objects that not just look and feel good, but also are manufacturable, sustainable, and relevant in a rapidly shifting industrial landscape.
DES1004.learning_outcomes: • Understand, identify and classify a wide range of manufacturing materials and processes. • Demonstrate knowledge of fabrication techniques and their appropriate applications in design. • Apply sustainable practices and lifecycle thinking to material selection and process planning. • Communicate design and manufacturing strategies clearly through visual and written documentation • Apply and integrate material and manufacturing considerations into conceptual and technical development of products.
DES1004.objectives: This course aims to equip students with an understanding of how material choices and manufacturing processes shape design decisions. The course will develop students' foundational knowledge of materials and processes commonly used in manufacturing. The course will engage students in the analysis of real-world applications of manufacturing techniques through case studies. The course will also teach students to critically evaluate the environmental, cultural, and economic implications of material choices.
DES1004.program_learning_goals: The Bachelor of Design (B.Des.) is a 4-year, future-oriented, trans-disciplinary program that uniquely curates knowledge and skills from Social Sciences, Arts, Engineering, and Management into Design. The program aims at nurturing design leaders equipped with the core competencies for the 21st Century and beyond. It provides a choice-based streaming system, allowing students to specialise in Experience Design (UI-UX), Product-System Design, and Visual Communication Design.

DES4001.introduction: The course explores the dialogue between people and interactive products, environments, and systems. Students will examine motion, feedback loops, affordances, and the ethics of behavioural design. It emphasises prototyping high-fidelity interactions that evoke emotional responses and address complex human behaviours in both digital and physical spaces.
DES4001.learning_outcomes: On successful completion of the course, students will be able to: - Analyse the "Five Dimensions" of interaction design (words, visual representations, physical objects, time, and behaviour). - Develop advanced prototypes that demonstrate micro-interactions, transitions, and state changes. - Evaluate the ethical implications of "persuasive design" and "dark patterns" in interactive systems. - Map complex system behaviours using interaction models that go beyond linear user flows.
DES4001.objectives: The course aims to achieve: - Move beyond the functional application of psychology to critically evaluate the ethics of "nudging" and the socio-economic impact of dark patterns in digital ecosystems. - Promote Speculative Responsibility: Encourage students to project the long-term consequences of their design interventions on mental health, social interaction, and environmental sustainability. - Investigate the Politics of the Interface: Explore how design decisions include or exclude diverse populations, addressing the inherent biases in "universal" design standards. - Deconstruct the "Frictionless" Narrative: Challenge the industry standard of seamlessness by exploring how "productive friction" can enhance user agency, transparency, and intentionality.
DES4001.program_learning_goals: The course aims to explore the interaction between humans and products in a more intuitive and hassle-free way. The students learn about the concepts of affordance and feedback, and apply the psychology of designing intuitive products, services, or systems in their projects.
DES4001.school: SHSS - School of Humanities and Social Sciences
DES4001.skill_development: Successful course completion will contribute to following skill development: • • Design + Technology Integration skills • Problem solving skills using electronics, and IoT

DES4002.introduction: The course examines typography as a primary tool for visual communication, identity, and social commentary. While foundational graphic design covers layout, this advanced Typography elective investigates the architecture of the letterform itself and its behaviour across fluctuating media. Students will explore the transition from static print traditions to dynamic, coded, and responsive type systems, focusing on how micro-typographic choices influence macro-level communication and cultural perception.
DES4002.learning_outcomes: On successful completion of the course, students will be able to: • Construct a functional set of custom letterforms using professional font-editing software • Execute complex typographic systems that utilise Variable Fonts (OpenType variations) for responsive environments. • Apply advanced micro-typography techniques to enhance the "deep reading" experience in long-form digital and analogue content.
DES4002.objectives: a. Examine how the physical and digital architecture of a typeface—its weight, axis, and terminal—affects the "voice" of information and the authority of the message. b. Students will be able to understand how screen technologies and AI-driven rendering engines dictate modern reading habits and the "invisibility" of digital type. c. Examine implications of accessibility in typography, moving beyond basic ADA compliance to inclusive, neurodiverse reading experiences. d. Equip students with the technical autonomy to create custom glyphs and variable font systems that respond to environmental or user data.
DES4002.program_learning_goals: Graduates will effectively communicate design intent and strategy using visual, verbal, and written storytelling tools across multiple platforms.
DES4002.school: SHSS - School of Humanities and Social Sciences

DES4007.introduction: Service Design focuses on understanding and improving complex services that involve many touchpoints such as physical spaces, digital platforms, people, and systems. It looks at both what users see and the processes happening behind the scenes. The goal is to make services more useful, efficient, and easy to use, while improving people’s everyday experiences. It uses a human-centred approach to solve problems and create better services through a holistic and multidisciplinary perspective.
DES4007.learning_outcomes: On successful completion of the course, students will be able to: • Analyze existing services using tools such as customer journey maps, service blueprints, stakeholder maps, and service ecologies. • Identify opportunities and design interventions across frontstage (user-visible) and backstage (organizational) elements of a service. • Students will develop a complete service design project with supporting documentation, suitable for a professional portfolio. • Students gain confidence and credibility as they build a research foundation with journey mapping, role-based personas, and service safaris. You'll work with lifecycle maps, ecosystem maps, and service blueprints as you prototype.
DES4007.objectives: It helps to equip students with the mindset, methods, and tools of Service Design to create, improve, and innovate services that are user-centred, operationally viable, and strategically valuable. By focusing on entire service ecosystems (frontstage and backstage), it prepares advanced design students to address complex, multi-channel challenges in sectors such as healthcare, public services, retail, mobility, and sustainability, distinct from the focused interaction or digital product scope of other design electives.
DES4007.program_learning_goals: Graduates will demonstrate the ability to identify and solve complex real-world problems using human-centered problem-solving approach. Graduates will apply systems-level thinking to understand the interconnections between users, technologies, environments, and services. Graduates will exhibit an understanding of socio-cultural contexts and ethical considerations in design decision-making, including sustainability and inclusivity.
DES4007.school: SHSS - School of Humanities and Social Sciences
DES4007.skill_development: Skill of using tools such as customer journey maps, service blueprints, stakeholder maps, and service ecologies.

DES4008.introduction: Designing Games is an introductory course that explores the foundational principles of game design. The course aims to equip students with a conceptual and practical understanding of what constitutes a game and how to craft meaningful play experiences. Throughout the course, students will understand game structure, core loops, game mechanics, player dynamics, and feedback systems. Through the deconstruction and analysis of classic games available in the market, students will develop a critical understanding of how gameplay functions and how engaging game experiences are created.
DES4008.learning_outcomes: • Demonstrate a comprehensive understanding of core game design principles, including gameplay mechanics, systems design, player psychology, motivation, and meaningful play. • Design engaging game mechanics, rules, and systems that create balanced, fair, and rewarding player experiences while differentiating game design from interaction design and user experience design. • Develop compelling game narratives, worlds, characters, and storytelling techniques suitable for both digital and analogue games. • Create and iteratively prototype complete digital or tabletop game concepts using paper prototyping, digital tools, and playtesting methods specifically focused on fun, engagement, and player behaviour.
DES4008.objectives: Students will be equipped to conceptualise and design core gameplay systems, selecting appropriate mechanics based on the intended genre and player experience. A central objective of the course is to explore the concept of "gameness" of a game, what transforms play into a game, and what elements make a game playable and engaging.
DES4008.program_learning_goals: Focuses on play, rules, challenge, reward, and emergent behavior rather than interface micro-interactions or service ecosystems.
DES4008.school: SHSS - School of Humanities and Social Sciences

DES4100.introduction: This course explores the mechanics of visual storytelling across various media, from sequential art and data visualisation to experimental film and interactive environments. While a standard communication design course focuses on the message. Visual Narrative focuses on the structure of the telling. Students will deconstruct how time, space, and perspective are manipulated to guide an audience through a story, focusing on the cognitive and emotional impact of visual syntax.
DES4100.learning_outcomes: On successful completion of the course, students will be able to: • Evaluate the ethical implications of witnessing and representing sensitive or historical events visually. • Synthesise data and abstract information into compelling, human-centric visual stories. • Apply advanced semiotic theory to create layered narratives that reward deep, repetitive engagement from the audience. • Execute a multi-layered narrative project that functions across at least two different media (a physical installation paired with a digital archive).
DES4100.objectives: a. Analyse Non-Linear Architectures: Traditional hero's journey by exploring circular, fragmented, and multi-vocal narrative structures. b. Investigative Aesthetics: Equip students with the tools to use visual storytelling as a form of research and activism to uncover hidden data. c. Deconstruct Narrative Bias: How visual tropes and cliches reinforce cultural stereotypes and analyse the power dynamics.
DES4100.program_learning_goals: Graduates will exhibit an understanding of socio-cultural contexts and ethical considerations in design decision-making, including sustainability and inclusivity. Graduates will effectively communicate design intent and strategy using visual, verbal, and written storytelling tools across multiple platforms.

DOM207.introduction: This course studies the nature, scope, and significance of data science in business and management. In particular, the course offers methods of data science by the use of quantitative techniques (in R and Python) for individual investigation of current problems encountered in business, management, and entrepreneurship. *** This course is a learning-experience, skill-enhancement course. It builds up from very basic stuff and slowly moves on to more advanced, modern topics *** The course is comprehensive and rigorous. You must put in many hours to keep up with the course, especially if you are not yet familiar with subject. Some learners without prior experience in the field have done great in this course, but they did put in a lot of work, asked questions, and after some frustrating but rewarding hours, managed to learn the material and succeed in demonstrating their learning. NOTE: *** Please do NOT use the course as a credit-filler; it will serve NO purpose in that regard. *** Since it’s expected to be a big class, you must keep proper discipline in the class. Disturbing the class by chatting, playing with cellphones, etc. are highly discouraged and may result in expulsion from class. *** The course is based on short surprise class tests (concept-clearing), an endterm, and a # of mini-projects. *** It’s absolutely necessary to participate in class and work with the TA. You must bring your laptops to work in class on short tutorials I'll assign during the lectures

Identify appropriate statistical methods for data science 7. Develop methods to solve problems

DOM306.introduction: In the era where the change is the only constant, the global business landscape is in the perpetual evolution. The enterprises today are navigating through complex challenges and problems. The key to solving these complex problems and responding to the market competition is to unlock the emerging technologies. The businesses, therefore, now witnessing digital shift, enabling them to improve their business performance. However, the landscape of the digitization is continuously evolving and hence, it becomes challenging. The challenge for businesses is, therefore, understanding these digital technologies and select the best fit technology to solve the complex problems. Solving Business Problems in Digital Context (DOM 306) is the course that clearly aligns the business problem with the digital technologies. The course is aimed to provide digital tools and techniques that assists in solving complex business problem. It aimed to make learners future ready for the dynamic world of business.

ECE303.introduction: This course teaches foundational aspects of processor design and straddles the fields of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science. Computer Architecture deals with the specification of “what needs to happen” in a processor and its immediate surrounding ecosystem in order to compute, whereas Computer Organization deals with “how to make it happen” inside the processor. Computer Architecture involves topics like instruction set architectures (ISAs) and compiler support and is essentially a contract with software stating what the processor does. On the other hand, Computer Organization is closer to electrical engineering and describes how exactly it is done, essentially by going deeper and tackling problems like how aggregate components (datapath, memory, controllers, etc) need to be designed and connected together to operate in a precise cadence for the maximal utilization and eƯiciency in delivering on the obligations of the ISA.
ECE303.learning_outcomes: 1) Understand what happens inside a processor when a program is executed, what is meant by pipelining, hazards, parallelism, etc. 2) Come up with an ISA specification. 3) Design the high-level building blocks and their timed and controlled inter-play in order to meet the specifications of the ISA.
ECE303.objectives: 1) To emphasize the electrical engineering aspects of the broad arena of "Computer Architecture and Organization" and therefore focus more on the organization part than on the architecture part. 2) To teach the student the considerations, challenges and techniques in CPU design.
ECE303.program_learning_goals: 1) To enable the student to recognize the software and hardware aspects of processor design. 2) To equip the student with concepts needed to design a generic Instruction Set Architecture (ISA). 3) To equip the student with concepts needed to design the hardware that implements the ISA.
ECE303.skill_development: This course helps develop skills in CPU IP design in the arena of VLSI frontend design.

ECE370.introduction: Wireless Communication is one of the fundamental technologies driving modern digital connectivity, enabling seamless communication between people, devices, and intelligent systems without the need for physical transmission media. It forms the backbone of cellular networks, satellite communications, wireless local area networks (WLANs), the Internet of Things (IoT), autonomous vehicles, smart cities, and next-generation applications such as Industry 4.0 and Integrated Sensing and Communication (ISAC). The rapid evolution from 1G to 5G and the ongoing development of 6G have significantly enhanced data rates, reliability, spectral efficiency, and connectivity while introducing advanced technologies such as OFDM, MIMO, massive MIMO, millimeter-wave communication, and intelligent radio resource management. This course provides a comprehensive understanding of the principles and design of modern wireless communication systems. Students will study wireless propagation mechanisms, large-scale and small-scale fading models, digital modulation techniques, diversity methods, channel capacity, multiple access schemes, OFDM, MIMO systems, and cellular network planning. The course also introduces emerging technologies, including 5G, IoT, Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces (RIS), and AI-enabled wireless networks. Through theoretical concepts, analytical problem-solving, and practical case studies, students will develop the knowledge and skills required to analyze, design, and optimize wireless communication systems for current and future applications in academia, research, and the telecommunications industry.
ECE370.learning_outcomes: • Explain the fundamental concepts of wireless communication systems, including evolution from analog to digital and from 1G to 5G. • Describe and model wireless channel characteristics such as path loss, multipath fading, Doppler shift, and shadowing. • Analyze and compare various modulation schemes (e.g., PSK, QAM, OFDM) and their performance over wireless channels. • Evaluate different multiple access techniques (FDMA, TDMA, CDMA, OFDMA) and their suitability for specific wireless applications. • Apply coding and diversity techniques (e.g., convolutional codes, MIMO, space-time coding) to improve reliability and throughput. • Interpret and simulate wireless communication scenarios using tools such as MATLAB, Simulink, or NS-3 to analyze system performance. • Demonstrate an understanding of wireless standards (e.g., GSM, LTE, 5G, Wi-Fi) and explain their protocols and architectures. • Design basic wireless system link budgets and estimate capacity using Shannon’s capacity theorem and related models. • Discuss current and emerging technologies such as IoT, 5G NR, cognitive radio, and their impact on future wireless networks. • Communicate technical findings effectively through presentations or reports, demonstrating teamwork and problem-solving abilities.
ECE370.objectives: • To introduce students to the basic principles of wireless communication systems and networks. • To understand the historical development and evolution from 1G to 5G (and beyond). • Wireless Channel Modeling: • To analyze the characteristics of wireless channels, including path loss, shadowing, and multipath fading. • To develop mathematical models for wireless propagation and understand their impact on system performance. • To study various digital modulation schemes (e.g., QAM, PSK, OFDM) and their suitability in wireless environments. • To understand error control coding techniques and their role in improving reliability. • To explain and compare multiple access schemes such as FDMA, TDMA, CDMA, and OFDMA. • To explore resource allocation and interference management in shared wireless media. • To familiarize students with contemporary wireless standards (e.g., GSM, LTE, Wi-Fi, 5G NR). • To understand architecture and protocols of cellular and WLAN systems. • To evaluate system capacity under different conditions using Shannon’s theorem and link budget analysis. • To introduce techniques for increasing wireless capacity, such as MIMO and diversity schemes. • To expose students to modern trends like Internet of Things (IoT), cognitive radio, and 5G technologies. • To discuss real-world applications and challenges of wireless communication systems. • To enable students to design and simulate basic wireless communication systems using tools such as MATLAB or NS-3. • To interpret simulation results and apply them in practical scenarios.
ECE370.skill_development: Skill Area Skill Developed Technical Wireless Modeling, Simulation, System Design Analytical Channel Analysis, Capacity Computation, Trade-Off Study Tools & Software Matlab, Ns-3, Sdr, Python Communication Technical Writing, Presentations Teamwork Collaborative Mini-Projects And Term Paper Industry Readiness Knowledge Of Lte/5g, Real-Time Systems Research Aptitude Problem-Solving, Research Project Foundations

weekly_modules.1: Introduction to wireless communication, evolution of mobile systems (1G–6G), electromagnetic spectrum, wireless applications, cellular concept, frequency reuse, duplexing techniques (FDD/TDD).
weekly_modules.2: Radio wave propagation: Free-space propagation, Friis transmission equation, link budget, reflection, diffraction, scattering, large-scale path loss models, shadowing.
weekly_modules.3: Small-scale fading: Multipath propagation, delay spread, RMS delay spread, coherence bandwidth, Doppler spread, coherence time, flat and frequency-selective fading, fast and slow fading.
weekly_modules.4: Statistical channel models: Rayleigh, Rician, and Nakagami fading, power delay profile, channel characterization, channel estimation fundamentals. Review of Random Variables
weekly_modules.5: Digital modulation techniques: ASK, FSK, PSK, QPSK, QAM, signal constellations, BER analysis over AWGN and fading channels.
weekly_modules.6: Diversity techniques and channel capacity: Time, frequency and spatial diversity, selection combining, equal gain combining (EGC), maximal ratio combining (MRC), Shannon capacity, outage probability.
weekly_modules.7: Multiple access techniques: FDMA, TDMA, CDMA, OFDMA, SC-FDMA, introduction to Non-Orthogonal Multiple Access (NOMA).
weekly_modules.8: OFDM systems: Principles of OFDM, orthogonality, cyclic prefix, FFT/IFFT implementation, synchronization issues, peak-to-average power ratio (PAPR).
weekly_modules.9: MIMO communication: SIMO, MISO, MIMO systems, spatial diversity, spatial multiplexing, Alamouti Space-Time Block Coding (STBC), beamforming, MIMO capacity.
weekly_modules.10: Cellular communication systems: Cell planning, handoff strategies, interference management, sectoring, cell splitting, capacity enhancement techniques, LTE architecture overview.
weekly_modules.11: 4G and 5G wireless communication: LTE-Advanced, 5G New Radio (NR), massive MIMO, millimeter-wave communications, beamforming, network slicing
weekly_modules.12: Emerging wireless technologies: Device-to-Device (D2D) communication, Internet of Things (IoT), Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces (RIS), Integrated Sensing and Communication (ISAC), UAV-assisted communications.
weekly_modules.13: Future wireless networks: 6G vision, AI/ML for wireless communications, intelligent radio resource management, quantum communication overview, comprehensive course review and discussion.
