ECE452.introduction: This course covers economic operation of power system, automatic load-frequency control of single and two area systems, power system stability (small signal stability, transient stability and voltage stability) and Sub Synchronous Oscillation. The main objective of this course to know the fundamental concept of power system to communicate power system operation and control efficiently and precisely. This course is useful to improve thinking ability and research ability of students in power system operation and control.
ECE452.learning_outcomes: On successful completion of the course, students will be able to: 1. Use the fundamental concept of power system to communicate power system operation and control efficiently and precisely. 2. Understand and explain the fundamental concepts of power system, physical significance of each concept in real time and the application of these concepts in advance power system. 3. Demonstrate ability to think basic concept of power system by analyzing and creating proofs, examples and counter-examples.
ECE452.objectives: 1. To provide students with an understanding of the detail of economic operation of power system and solve many problems of economic operation of power system. 2. To provide students with an understanding of the detail of automatic load-frequency control of single and two area systems, and the practical application in power system. 3. To provide students with an understanding of power system stability (small signal stability, transient stability and voltage stability) and Sub Synchronous Oscillation. Also, provide the concept of the effect of synchronising and damping torque coefficient in power system. 4. To provide students with an understanding the application of economic operation of power system, load-frequency control concept and the stability problem in power system. 5. To develop students’ skills in communicating the fundamental concept of power system operation and control clearly and efficiently.
ECE452.skill_development: Skill development related to “MATLAB based real time simulation for power system operation and control”.

weekly_modules.1: Economic Operation of Power System: Fundamental of power flow solutions, Power factor correction, Distribution of load between units within a plant, Distribution of load between plants, The transmission-loss equation,
weekly_modules.2: An interpretation of transformation C, Classical economic dispatch with losses, Automatic generation control, Unit commitment, Solving the unit commitment problems.
weekly_modules.3: Load Frequency Control and Control Area Concept: Automatic load-frequency control of single area systems: Speed-governing system, Hydraulic valve actuator, Turbine-generator response, Static performance of speed governor, Closing the ALFC loop,
weekly_modules.4: Concept of control area, ALFC of multi-control area systems (Pool operation): The two area systems, Modelling the Tie-Line, Block diagram representation of two area system, Dynamic response of two area system, Supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA).
weekly_modules.5: Power System Stability Problems: Basic concepts and definitions, Rotor angle stability, Synchronous machine characteristics, Power versus angle relationship,
weekly_modules.6: Stability phenomena, Voltage stability and voltage collapse, Mid-term and long-term stability, Classification of stability.
weekly_modules.7: Small Signal Stability: State space concepts, Basic linearization technique, Participation factors, Eigen properties of state matrix,
weekly_modules.8: Small signal stability of a single machine infinite bus system, Studies of parametric effect: Effect of loading, Effect of KA,
weekly_modules.9: Effect of type of load, Stability improvement by power system stabilizers. Design of power system stabilizers.
weekly_modules.10: Transient Stability: Time domain simulations and direct stability analysis techniques (extended equal area criterion) Energy function methods: Physical and mathematical aspects of the problem, Lyapunov’s method, Modelling issues,
weekly_modules.11: Energy function formulation, Potential Energy Boundary Surface (PEBS): Energy function of a single machine infinite bus system, equal area criterion and the energy function, Multi-machine PEBS.
weekly_modules.12: Sub Synchronous Oscillations: Turbine generator torsional characteristics, Shaft system model, Torsional natural frequencies and mode shapes, Torsional interaction with power system controls: interaction with generator excitation controls, interaction with speed governors, interaction with nearby DC converters,
weekly_modules.13: Sub Synchronous Resonance (SSR): Characteristics of series capacitor -compensated transmission systems, Self – excitation due to induction generator effect, Torsional interaction resulting in SSR, Analytical methods, Counter measures to SSR problems.

ECE453.introduction: Deep learning has become the driving force behind modern artificial intelligence, enabling breakthroughs in computer vision, natural language processing, speech recognition, robotics, scientific computing, and generative AI. This course provides a comprehensive introduction to the theoretical foundations and practical implementation of deep learning models, beginning with multilayer neural networks and progressing to convolutional and recurrent neural networks, representation learning, transformers, large language models, retrieval-augmented generation, multimodal learning, agentic AI, model optimization, Edge AI, reinforcement learning, and federated learning. The course emphasizes both mathematical foundations and hands-on system development using contemporary deep learning frameworks. Students will study recent advances in foundation models and generative AI while gaining practical experience in designing efficient, secure, and scalable AI systems suitable for real-world deployment.
ECE453.learning_outcomes: After successfully completing this course, students will be able to: Explain the principles underlying deep neural network architectures and learning algorithms. Build and optimize convolutional, recurrent, transformer-based, and generative deep learning models. Apply representation learning, fine-tuning, retrieval-augmented generation, and multimodal learning techniques to practical AI problems. Design AI agents capable of reasoning, planning, and tool utilization using modern agentic AI frameworks. Optimize deep learning models using parameter-efficient fine-tuning, quantization, and deployment techniques for edge devices. Analyze security vulnerabilities, robustness issues, and ethical considerations associated with modern AI systems. Implement complete deep learning pipelines from data preprocessing through model deployment and evaluation. Interpret recent research contributions and identify promising directions for future AI systems.
ECE453.objectives: Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to: Understand the theoretical foundations of deep neural networks and modern deep learning algorithms. Design, implement, and train deep learning models for vision, language, sequential, and multimodal data. Analyze transformer-based architectures, foundation models, and generative AI techniques. Develop intelligent AI systems incorporating retrieval, reasoning, tool use, and multi-agent workflows. Evaluate model performance while considering computational efficiency, security, robustness, interpretability, and deployment constraints. Read, understand, and critically evaluate recent research papers in deep learning and generative AI.
ECE453.program_learning_goals: This course contributes to the program by enabling students to: Develop a rigorous understanding of modern deep learning principles, architectures, and algorithms. Apply advanced machine learning techniques to solve complex engineering and data-driven problems. Design, implement, train, evaluate, and optimize deep neural network models for diverse application domains. Critically analyze recent research literature and emerging trends in deep learning and generative AI. Develop practical AI systems using state-of-the-art tools, frameworks, and foundation models while considering efficiency, security, ethics, and responsible AI practices.
ECE453.skill_development: Students completing this course will develop the following technical and professional skills: Deep learning model design and implementation. Programming using modern deep learning frameworks such as PyTorch or TensorFlow. Mathematical reasoning for optimization and neural network training. Natural language processing, and multimodal AI development. Foundation model adaptation, prompt engineering, retrieval-augmented generation, and AI agent development. Model optimization techniques including quantization, LoRA, and parameter-efficient fine-tuning. AI system evaluation, debugging, performance analysis, and deployment. Critical reading of research papers and scientific communication. Team-based project development and engineering problem solving. Responsible AI practices including model security, robustness, fairness, privacy, and ethical AI deployment.

ECO1001.introduction: Microeconomics is the study of how people, firms, and institutions make choices when resources are limited. This course introduces students to the basic concepts and analytical tools of economics through real-world examples, data, graphs, and policy applications. Students will examine how individuals and firms respond to incentives, how markets coordinate decisions, how prices are determined, and why markets sometimes fail. Alongside these foundational ideas, the course will also explore how economic institutions shape behaviour, how inequality emerges and persists, and how issues such as environmental sustainability and public policy influence economic outcomes. Drawing on contemporary evidence and case studies, the course is designed to build economic intuition and emphasise conceptual understanding alongside formal analysis, while encouraging students to connect economic theory to the social and institutional realities of the world around them.
ECO1001.learning_outcomes: 1. Students will be able to apply core economic concepts to analyse individual behaviour, markets, institutions, and policy issues. 2. Students will be able to interpret economic data and graphs, and use logical reasoning to explain real-world economic outcomes. 3. Students will be able to connect theoretical concepts with contemporary economic, social, and policy challenges.
ECO1001.objectives: 1. To build a clear understanding of core economic principles and how markets, incentives, and institutions shape economic outcomes. 2. To develop analytical thinking using examples, graphs, data, and empirical evidence. 3. To prepare students to evaluate economic and public policy questions, including issues of inequality, market failure, and regulation.

ECO4201.introduction: This is an introductory public economics course that focuses on the role of government in the economy. It is designed to provide a basic understanding of reasons for government intervention, the benefits of such policies, and the consequent response of the economic agents. The course begins with an examination of the economic rationale for state intervention in the economy where issues relating to public goods and public choice are reviewed. The taxation component provides an analysis of tax incidence in various forms of markets and market structures, investigates the consequences of taxation on economic efficiency in consumption and in production and considers how taxation affects labour supply.
ECO4201.learning_outcomes: • Develop an understanding of the link between theory and policy. • Develop an understanding of the methods of analysis used to evaluate economic issues pertaining to the public sector. • Provide students with a theoretical understanding of important issues in Public Sector Economics.
ECO4201.objectives: • Explain why the state produces and/or allocates some goods but leaves others to the private market. • Develop the skills appropriate to an economic analysis of the role and effects of government intervention in market economies
ECO4201.school: SHSS - School of Humanities and Social Sciences
ECO4201.skill_development: Undestanding of theoretical model development and optimization to make policy recommendations.

ECO4502.introduction: This course introduces students to Economic Thought as an evolving intellectual tradition shaped by social, political, philosophical and ethical contexts. Rather than treating economic theories as timeless or purely technical constructs, the course situates them within the historical conditions, value commitments and methodological choices that informed their development. Students will examine how economic ideas emerged in response to concrete problems such as industrialization, inequality, colonialism, gender relations, crises and environmental limits. The course adopts a pluralist and critical perspective, engaging with classical, neoclassical, Keynesian, Marxian, institutionalist, gender and other approaches. Special attention is given to debates over methodology, assumptions about rationality, markets, power and the role of the state. By incorporating philosophical foundations and neglected voices, the course highlights how economics has been shaped by normative judgments and contested worldviews. Through close reading of original texts alongside interpretive commentary, students will learn how theoretical choices reflect broader social priorities and epistemological commitments. The course encourages reflection on what is included and excluded in mainstream economic narratives and why certain approaches gained dominance while others were marginalized. Ultimately, the course aims to equip students with historical awareness and analytical tools to critically engage with contemporary economic theory and policy debates.
ECO4502.learning_outcomes: • Explain major schools of economic thought and their historical origins • Analyse how social values, power relations and philosophical commitments shape economic theories
ECO4502.program_learning_goals: • To examine why particular assumptions, methods and models were adopted at different moments in the evolution of economic thought • To cultivate critical thinking about the foundations, scope and limitations of modern economic analysis
ECO4502.school: SHSS - School of Humanities and Social Sciences
ECO4502.skill_development: • Compare and critically evaluate various approaches to economic questions • Apply historical and methodological insights to assess contemporary economic debates and policies

ECO483.introduction: This course introduces students to the design and analysis of surveys for applied research in the social sciences. It focuses on the use of primary data to investigate socio-economic questions through systematic fieldwork, structured survey instruments, and statistical analysis. The course is designed to provide undergraduate students with hands-on experience in formulating research questions, designing questionnaires, selecting appropriate sampling strategies, conducting surveys, cleaning and organizing data, and analyzing survey responses using statistical methods. The course has a strong applied orientation. Students will be expected to move beyond theoretical understanding and engage directly with the practical stages of survey-based research. By the end of the course, students should be able to design and conduct a primary survey, analyze the data collected, interpret the results, and draw meaningful implications for social science research and policy.
ECO483.learning_outcomes: On successful completion of the course, students will be expected to: Gain the ability to formulate research questions that can be addressed through primary data generation. Acquire the ability to design and conduct primary surveys using appropriate sampling strategies and survey instruments. Acquire the ability to clean, collate, and analyze primary survey data using statistical and econometric methods. Develop the ability to interpret survey findings and derive evidence-based policy implications from survey analysis.
ECO483.objectives: This course aims to develop students’ ability to investigate socio-economic research questions through systematic fieldwork (or online surveys), primary data generation, and rigorous survey-based analysis. It is intended for beginning-level researchers interested in applying survey design, sampling strategies, and statistical methods to empirical social science research.
ECO483.program_learning_goals: Develop familiarity with survey design methods, primary data generation, and statistical analysis of survey data for applied social science research.
ECO483.school: SHSS - School of Humanities and Social Sciences
ECO483.skill_development: Students will be able to design structured surveys, collect and organize survey data, apply appropriate econometric methods for survey-data analysis, and derive evidence-based policy implications from the results.

ENF1001.learning_outcomes: By The End Of This Course, Students Will Be Able To: 1. Define And Explain The Core Purposes, Structures, And Environments In Which Businesses Operate. 2. Compare Different Forms Of Business Ownership And Organizational Structures, Including Public/Private And Startup/Established Firms. 3. Describe The Functions Of Key Business Areas—Such As Marketing, Operations, HR, And Strategy—And Explain How They Interact Within A Firm. 4. Apply Basic Strategic Tools (E.G., SWOT, PESTLE, Porter’s Five Forces) To Assess Business Scenarios And Competitive Positioning. 5. Analyze The Role Of Entrepreneurship And Innovation In Creating Value And Driving Economic And Social Change. 6. Evaluate The Impact Of Digital Technologies (AI, Automation, E-Commerce, Fintech) On Business Models And Decision-Making. 7. Demonstrate Awareness Of Ethical Issues, Corporate Social Responsibility, And Sustainability In Business Decision-Making. 8. Discuss Emerging Global Business Trends And Challenges, Such As Climate Change, Supply Chain Shifts, And The Future Of Work. 9. Reflect On Their Own Interests And Strengths In Relation To Future Roles In Business, Finance, Or Policy.

ENG343.introduction: This course is designed to introduce students to some of the most characteristic forms that the novel has taken through the course of its long and continuing evolution and to the range of expressive possibilities that the novel, as a whole, has acquired. The novels that will be studied in this course are (i) Don Quijote (Part 1), one of the earliest novels and one that takes as its central question: what does it mean to read and write novels? (ii) Wuthering Heights, seemingly a ‘domestic novel’ that does what no domestic novel did in the nineteenth century (iii) Disgrace, which raises some of the most pressing questions about the ethics and aesthetics of telling ‘a good story’. (3:1:0)
ENG343.learning_outcomes: 1.Knowledge of the novel form and its development from the 17th to the 20th century 2. Close and contextual reading, literary analysis skills 3. Sharpened critical awareness and knowledge of key debates in women’s writing, book history, authorship, periodical studies, and questions of the representation of gender, race, and class in literature
ENG343.objectives: This course seeks to take the student through some of the major landmarks of the novel form, explain to them how these novels achieve their characteristic effects and enable them to engage with the broader questions of the politics and poetics of novelistic representation.
ENG343.program_learning_goals: PLG 1: Students will be able to apply critical terms and methodology in completing an analysis of literary and cultural texts following cutting-edge conventions in academia as well as industry. PLG 2: Students will be able to locate, apply, and cite secondary materials to further substantiate their reading of texts in a coherent and correct manner. PLG 3: Students will be able to analyze and interpret texts within the contexts in which they are produced as well as appreciate the ethical, political, and aesthetic challenges arising out of situations in which texts are received in varied contexts.
ENG343.school: SHSS - School of Humanities and Social Sciences
ENG343.skill_development: Skills of literary analysis, close reading, the novel form and its varied development from the 17th to the 20th century

ENG440.introduction: In this course we shall look at various forms of fiction including role-playing games (RPG), graphic novels, movies, and TV shows. The intention is to attempt to understand the difference between reading a more or less structured piece of literature, and forms that at this point in time seem more free-flowing and less deterministic.
ENG440.learning_outcomes: 1. Analyse the formal properties of image-text, serial, and interactive narratives using appropriate critical terminology. 2. Evaluate how a given medium's technical and structural aspects (panel and page, episode and season, rule-system, track and album) produce the stories it can tell. 3. Construct sustained written arguments that place literary theory in dialogue with contemporary media forms.
ENG440.objectives: 1. To examine how narrative form and content interact across a range of media, including literary fiction, graphic novels, television, video games, and concept albums. 2. To introduce key theoretical frameworks for reading non-traditional narrative forms, including visual theory, simulation and virtuality, and ergodic or interactive textuality. 3. To develop critical vocabulary for comparing structured literary narrative with more free-flowing, non-deterministic forms of storytelling.
ENG440.program_learning_goals: 1. To equip students with the critical and analytical skills required to interpret texts and narratives across a range of literary and cultural forms. 2. To foster an understanding of how form, medium, content, and context bear upon meaning in literary and cultural production. 3. To develop independent, well-supported critical writing appropriate to advanced study in literary studies and the humanities.
ENG440.school: SHSS - School of Humanities and Social Sciences
ENG440.skill_development: 1. Close reading and visual analysis of image-text and multimodal narratives. 2. Comparative critical writing across disciplines and media, including literature, media studies, game studies, and musicology. 3. Independent research and argument construction, applied in the midterm and endterm assignments.

ENG448.introduction: Proposed by Paul J. Crutzen and Eugene F. Stoermer in 2000 as a new geological epoch marking humanity's imprint on the planet's stratigraphic record, the Anthropocene was formally rejected in 2024 by the Subcommission on Quaternary Stratigraphy (the body responsible for ratifying new geological time units). Yet this rejection has, if anything, sharpened rather than settled the term's critical purchase: freed from the burden of geological precision, "Anthropocene" persists as a contested, generative concept whose scope keeps expanding and whose meanings remain in flux, alongside rival framings like the Capitalocene, Plantationocene, and Chthulucene. Central to this course is a distinction between the forecast and the literary imagination: where climate modeling, policy scenario-planning, and risk assessment seek to render the future calculable and administrable, literary fiction operates through different logics, inhabiting uncertainty, multiplying perspectives beyond the human, and holding open futures that projection forecloses. This course synthesizes anti-, non-, and post-anthropocentric perspectives that challenge the discourses and practices placing humans at the center of the world, with particular attention to what literary studies can offer. Through diverse literary texts and theoretical frameworks, the course examines the complexities of human-environment interaction, asking how literary interventions unsettle established narratives and imagine alternative futures.
ENG448.learning_outcomes: 1. Demonstrate an understanding of the historical development and ongoing debates surrounding the concept of the Anthropocene. 2. Critically evaluate anti-, non-, or post-anthropocentric perspectives and their implications for understanding human- environment relationships. 3. Analyze literary texts and theoretical frameworks to identify representations of human impact on the environment and alternative modes of narrating the Anthropocene. 4. Develop the ability to articulate complex ideas and arguments concerning human-environment interactions, drawing on interdisciplinary insights from literature, philosophy, and environmental studies. 5. Engage in creative and speculative thinking to envision alternative futures and ethical responses to the challenges posed by the Anthropocene. 6. Apply theoretical concepts and critical perspectives to real-world contexts, fostering a deeper understanding of the complexities and ethical dimensions of environmental issues
ENG448.objectives: 1. Trace human impact on the environment through diverse critical vocabularies which seek to reveal the entangled histories of colonialism, capitalism, and ecological precarity. 2. Cultivate sustained attention to plant, fungal, and other non-human life, addressing the tendency toward "plant blindness" and training students to read the environment as active and animate rather than passive backdrop. 3. Introduce embodied methodologies for encountering landscape, extending the practice of attention beyond the page and into direct, first-person environmental experience. 4. Develop the capacity to analyze literary texts as sites where human-environment relations are imagined, contested, and reworked, drawing on ecocritical and posthumanist frameworks.
ENG448.school: SHSS - School of Humanities and Social Sciences
ENG448.skill_development: 1. Analytical & Critical Thinking: - Close reading and textual analysis across genres (fiction, theory, nonfiction nature writing) - Comparative analysis across geographic and cultural contexts - Ability to evaluate and apply competing theoretical frameworks to the same object of study 2. Research & Interdisciplinary Synthesis - Working across disciplinary boundaries (literature, environmental studies, philosophy, critical theory) - Tracing complex, multi-stranded causal relationships (e.g., supply chains linking ecology, economy, and colonial history) 3. Writing & Communication - Constructing and defending sustained written arguments - Translating complex theoretical ideas into clear, accessible language - Group presentation and collaborative research skills 4. Observation & Attention - Sustained, disciplined observation of environment and landscape (via the walking/swimming journal) - Reflective and descriptive writing practice - Counteracting "plant blindness" — developing habits of noticing non-human life

FAC2003.introduction: This core introductory course in finance lays the groundwork for understanding the fundamental principles, concepts, and tools essential in financial management. The course emphasizes practical applications relevant for corporate managers. Students examine major strategic financial decisions, including investment decisions, financing decisions, working capital management, dividend decisions, and capital structure decisions. The course is relevant to general management, strategy, finance, and accounting, and aims to build students' comfort with financial terminology, interpretation, and application.
FAC2003.learning_outcomes: Students will be able to: 1. Comprehend fundamental financial management concepts for informed investment, financing, and dividend decisions. 2. Recognize the strategic significance of financial management in organizational success. 3. Compute cost of capital and devise appropriate financial strategies. 4. Analyze capital structure decisions using relevant models. 5. Discuss implications of dividend policy and make informed financing decisions. 6. Apply financial management tools to case-based, data-based, and experiential managerial decision contexts.
FAC2003.objectives: 1. To build a strong conceptual and practical foundation in financial management for managerial decision-making. 2. To develop students' ability to evaluate investment, financing, working capital, dividend, and capital structure decisions using appropriate financial tools. 3. To strengthen students' ability to apply finance concepts through cases, data-based submissions, MS Excel exercises, and experiential decision-making.
FAC2003.school: SME - School of Management and Entrepreneurship
FAC2003.skill_development: This course develops applied managerial finance skills by training students to interpret financial information, evaluate financial decisions, and communicate finance-based recommendations in business contexts.

FAC313.introduction: This course introduces students to the fundamentals of banking and financial services, with a primary focus on the Indian banking system. Designed for students with no prior background in banking or finance, the course explains how banks and other financial institutions contribute to economic development by accepting deposits, providing loans, facilitating payments, managing savings, and supporting businesses and individuals. Students will gain an understanding of the structure and functioning of commercial banks, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), non-banking financial companies (NBFCs), insurance companies, mutual funds, and other financial institutions. The course familiarizes students with common banking products and services such as savings and current accounts, deposits, loans, digital payment systems, and basic investment products. The course also introduces fundamental concepts of lending, credit evaluation, financial inclusion, banking regulation, and risk management in a simple and application-oriented manner. Students will learn how banks assess borrowers, manage different types of risks, and operate within the regulatory framework established by the RBI and other financial regulators. Recognizing the rapid transformation of the financial sector, the course explores contemporary developments in digital banking, Unified Payments Interface (UPI), mobile banking, financial technology (FinTech), artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, and emerging innovations that are reshaping the banking industry. Through case studies, classroom discussions, practical exercises, and real-world examples, students will develop an appreciation of how modern banking services are delivered and how technology is changing customer experiences. By the end of the course, students will be able to understand the role of banking institutions, evaluate basic banking products and services, interpret current developments in the financial sector, and make informed personal and professional financial decisions. The course also lays a strong foundation for advanced studies in banking, finance, and financial services.
FAC313.learning_outcomes: Upon successful completion of the course, students will be able to: CLO1. Explain the structure, functions, and role of banks and financial institutions in the economy. CLO2. Describe the features and uses of major banking products and financial services. CLO3. Explain the basic concepts of credit, risk management, and banking regulations. CLO4. Discuss the role of digital banking, fintech, and modern payment systems in financial services. CLO5. Apply fundamental banking concepts and ethical principles to simple banking and financial decision-making.
FAC313.objectives: By the end of this course, students will be able to: CO1. Understand the structure, functions, and role of banks and financial institutions in the economy. CO2. Explain the features of basic banking products, financial services, and lending activities. CO3. Understand the fundamentals of risk management and banking regulations. CO4. Describe the role of digital banking, fintech, and modern payment systems in financial services. CO5. Apply basic banking concepts and ethical principles to everyday financial and banking decisions.

FAC405.introduction: Every price you pay, every invoice a business raises, and every balance sheet you will ever read has a tax story inside it. Tax is the single largest recurring transaction between business and the state — and yet most graduates meet it for the first time on the job, unprepared. This course fixes that. Taught from a practitioner's desk, it treats taxation the way the industry actually uses it: how corporate tax and GST liability is computed in India, how firms plan and structure within the law, where the tax authorities and courts push back, and how all of this shows up in real business decisions, financial statements and headlines. The course is anchored in the Indian Income-tax Act, 1961 and the GST law, with a window on the global stage — transfer pricing, tax treaties, and the new global minimum tax. It is deliberately hands-on: worked computations, Excel labs, real disputes from the public record, and a group advisory project. By the end, you should be able to read the tax note in an annual report, follow a Budget speech critically, and hold your own in a Big 4 tax, transfer pricing or in-house finance interview.
FAC405.learning_outcomes: Students will be able to: 1. Describe the structure of India's tax system — direct vs. indirect taxes, the key institutions, and the basic economics of who bears a tax. 2. Compute the corporate tax liability of an Indian company, including choice of tax regime and MAT, and interpret the tax items in published financial statements. 3. Distinguish tax planning, avoidance and evasion, and explain how GAAR and the compliance/assessment machinery constrain corporate behaviour. 4. Explain the arm's length principle and apply basic transfer pricing reasoning to intra-group transactions; describe the global minimum tax at a headline level. 5. Apply the GST framework (supply, place and time of supply, input tax credit) to business transactions and compute GST liability across a simple value chain.
FAC405.objectives: 1. To give students a clear, practical map of India's tax system — what direct and indirect taxes are, who collects them, and why the design matters for business and consumers. 2. To develop working fluency with the computation of corporate tax (including MAT and regime choice) and GST liability under Indian law, through worked examples and Excel labs. 3. To understand how firms manage taxes in practice — planning, compliance, disputes — and where the line between planning, avoidance and evasion is drawn. 4. To introduce the essentials of cross-border taxation — tax treaties, transfer pricing and the global minimum tax — at the level a young finance professional needs. 5. To connect the classroom to industry through cases, current headlines and a group advisory project presented to the class.
FAC405.school: SME - School of Management and Entrepreneurship

weekly_modules.1: Module 1: Setting the Stage — Taxes in Business Life (Sessions 1–3) Session 1: Why Tax Matters: The Lay of the Land Objective: Taxes as the price of the state and the largest recurring 'transaction' of any business; direct vs. indirect taxes with everyday examples; what a company actually pays across a year (corporate tax, GST, TDS, customs); how tax makes headlines — and careers. Session 2: Who Really Pays? The One Piece of Economics You Must Know Objective: Statutory vs. economic incidence, taught through examples: GST on popcorn vs. petrol taxes vs. corporate tax; why 'tax the company' may end up taxing workers or customers; deadweight loss in one diagram. No equations beyond Class-XII intuition.
weekly_modules.2: Session 3: India's Tax System: Institutions, Reforms and the Life of a Dispute Objective: Who does what: CBDT, CBIC, the GST Council, tribunals and courts; the broad arc of reform from licence-raj-era rates to today; the life cycle of a tax dispute — return, assessment, appeal — so later cases make sense. Module 2: Corporate Income Tax — Law, Computation and Decisions (Sessions 4–11) Session 4: The Corporation as Taxpayer Objective: Company, partnership, LLP — how the form changes the tax; residence and source in simple terms; the anatomy of India's corporate rate (base rate + surcharge + cess) and how the ~25% headline compares with the world.
weekly_modules.3: Session 5: From Accounting Profit to Taxable Profit I: Business Income and Depreciation Objective: Why the P&L number is not the taxable number; the 'Profits and Gains of Business or Profession' head; tax depreciation and the block-of-assets system, with worked examples on the board. Session 6: From Accounting Profit to Taxable Profit II: Deductions and Disallowances Objective: The big adjustments in practice: key deductions, the classic disallowances (cash payments, TDS defaults, personal/capital expenses), and a first look at a real company's tax reconciliation note.
weekly_modules.4: Session 7: Computation Lab I: Build a Corporate Tax Computation Objective: Hands-on Excel session: start from a trial-balance-style P&L, make the adjustments, and arrive at taxable income and tax payable. Bring laptops; problem set distributed in advance. Session 8: Capital Gains, Losses and Getting Money Out: Dividends and Buybacks Objective: Capital gains for companies in brief; set-off and carry-forward of losses (why loss-making startups care); how shareholders are taxed on dividends today; dividends vs. buybacks after recent Finance Act changes — a live boardroom question.
weekly_modules.5: Session 9: MAT and the Regime Menu: How a CFO Chooses Objective: Why Minimum Alternate Tax exists (the zero-tax company problem) and how it is computed on book profits; MAT credit; the concessional regimes (22% under s.115BAA; 15% for new manufacturing under s.115BAB) — and the one-way doors involved in choosing. Session 10: Computation Lab II: The Full Picture Objective: Second Excel lab: a fuller computation including losses, MAT and a regime-choice comparison — should this company opt for 115BAA? Teams defend their recommendation.
weekly_modules.6: Session 11: Taxes and Business Decisions: A Practitioner's Tour Objective: Where tax quietly drives strategy: debt vs. equity and the interest shield; leasing vs. buying; timing of income and expenses; group structures and holding companies — illustrated from practice, with war stories. Module 3: Tax Planning, Avoidance and Compliance — Walking the Line (Sessions 12–15) Session 12: Planning, Avoidance, Evasion: Where Is the Line? Objective: The Westminster principle ('every man is entitled to arrange his affairs...') vs. substance-over-form; India's journey through McDowell, Azadi Bachao and Vodafone; why the same structure can be prudent planning in one decade and abusive avoidance in the next.
weekly_modules.7: Session 13: GAAR: The Anti-Avoidance Backstop Objective: India's General Anti-Avoidance Rule in plain language: impermissible avoidance arrangements, the main-purpose test; how advisors 'GAAR-proof' structures in practice; the certainty-vs-flexibility debate. Session 14: The Compliance Year: TDS, Advance Tax, Returns and Assessments Objective: A company's tax calendar from April to March: TDS as collection-at-source, advance tax instalments, return filing, and what happens when the department comes calling; how data (AIS, e-invoicing, TDS trails) has transformed enforcement.
weekly_modules.8: Session 15: Reading the Tax Note: ETR, Deferred Tax and Tax Risk Objective: How analysts read the tax line: effective tax rate reconciliations; deferred tax assets and liabilities in plain English; disputes as contingent liabilities; what a very low ETR signals — efficiency, aggressiveness, or risk? Module 4: International Taxation and Transfer Pricing (Sessions 16–19) Session 16: Cross-Border Basics: Residence, Source and Treaties Objective: Why double taxation arises and how treaties relieve it; permanent establishment — the concept the digital economy broke; treaty shopping and the India–Mauritius route (and its 2016 renegotiation).
weekly_modules.9: Session 17: Transfer Pricing I: The Arm's Length Principle Objective: Why intra-group prices are the biggest tax lever in the world economy; the arm's length principle; the main methods (CUP, cost plus, TNMM) through simple numerical examples; what a TP associate at a Big 4 actually does all day. Session 18: Transfer Pricing II: India in the Dock(et) Objective: India as one of the world's most active TP jurisdictions: the litigation hotspots (marketing intangibles, management fees), and Advance Pricing Agreements and safe harbours as peace treaties.
weekly_modules.10: Session 19: The Global Tax Reset: Profit Shifting and the 15% Minimum Tax Objective: How the Double Irish (with a Dutch Sandwich) worked; the Apple–Ireland and Starbucks UK stories; the OECD response in one lecture — BEPS, and the Pillar Two 15% global minimum tax; India's own experiments (equalisation levy's rise and repeal). Module 5: GST — India's Indirect Tax Revolution (Sessions 20–24) Session 20: From Cascading Chaos to GST: Why 2017 Happened Objective: The pre-GST tangle — excise, service tax, VAT, CST, octroi — and the cascading (tax-on-tax) problem shown with a simple value-chain example; the two-decade road to the 101st Constitutional Amendment; 'one nation, one tax' — slogan vs. substance.
weekly_modules.11: Session 21: GST Design: Dual GST, IGST and the Council Objective: CGST + SGST on intra-state supplies, IGST on inter-state; the GST Council as a Centre–State bargaining table; the rate structure and its 2025 rationalisation to a simpler two-slab system; registration and the composition scheme for small businesses. Session 22: The Machine Room: Supply, Place/Time of Supply and Input Tax Credit Objective: 'Supply' as the taxable event; place and time of supply through examples (goods, services, e-commerce); the input tax credit chain — GST's self-policing genius and its fragility (fake invoicing); e-invoicing and e-way bills.
weekly_modules.12: Session 23: GST Computation Lab Objective: Hands-on Excel session: compute GST liability for a manufacturer, a service firm and an e-commerce seller; trace input tax credit through a multi-state value chain; reverse charge and composition-scheme trade-offs. Session 24: GST in Practice: Compliance Life, Disputes and the Report Card Objective: A business's monthly GST routine (returns, reconciliations, notices); common dispute areas; the report card eight years in — collections, formalisation, and the unfinished agenda (petroleum, real estate). Short structured debate to close the module.
weekly_modules.13: Module 6: Capstone — Round-Up and Presentations (Sessions 25–26) Session 25: Capstone I: Course Round-Up + Group Presentations (Groups 1–6) Objective: A 20-minute integrative recap — the ten ideas to carry into your career (and the exam); then Groups 1–6 present their tax advisory briefs (8 minutes + 4 minutes Q&A each). Session 26: Capstone II: Group Presentations (Groups 7–12) + Closing Objective: Groups 7–12 present (8 minutes + 4 minutes Q&A each); instructor closing on tax careers — Big 4 advisory, transfer pricing, in-house tax, policy — and how to prepare for them from here.

FAC410.introduction: This course provides a comprehensive introduction to financial derivatives markets, instruments, pricing intuition, trading mechanisms, and risk management applications in both Indian and global financial contexts. The course is designed for students with limited prior exposure to derivative instruments and emphasizes conceptual clarity, analytical reasoning, ethical awareness, and practical decision-making rather than advanced mathematical complexity. Students will develop an understanding of the economic rationale behind derivatives, including their role in risk transfer, hedging, speculation, arbitrage, price discovery, and market efficiency. The course covers exchange-traded and over-the-counter derivative instruments such as forwards, futures, options, interest rate swaps, currency swaps, and credit default swaps (CDS), with applications in corporate treasury management, investment portfolio protection, commodity risk management, and foreign exchange risk mitigation. A significant emphasis is placed on the operational mechanics of derivative markets, including margining systems, mark-to-market settlement, clearing corporations, contract specifications, regulatory frameworks, and market infrastructure, particularly within Indian markets (e.g., NSE, BSE, MCX, RBI, SEBI), while also comparing developments across major global exchanges such as CME, ICE, and Eurex. The course introduces the conceptual foundations of derivative pricing, including option valuation logic, put-call parity, Black–Scholes pricing intuition (without advanced derivation), option Greeks, implied volatility, and practical pricing interpretation, enabling students to understand market behavior and derivative pricing drivers without requiring advanced quantitative finance training. Students will also critically examine derivative-based trading and risk management strategies, including portfolio hedging, directional and volatility-based option strategies, institutional hedging practices, and integrated derivatives applications. The course further explores the role of derivatives in systemic risk and financial crises through case studies such as the 1998 LTCM collapse, the 2008 Global Financial Crisis, AIG and CDS failures, the COVID-19 market shock, and recent banking stress events such as Silicon Valley Bank and Credit Suisse. The course integrates ethical reasoning, responsible risk management, global business perspective, applied decision-making, and contemporary market relevance, preparing students for careers in finance, treasury, banking, risk management, consulting, asset management, and financial markets.
FAC410.learning_outcomes: Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to: CLO 1: Explain the Structure and Functioning of Derivatives Markets Demonstrate understanding of the structure, purpose, participants, instruments, and economic significance of financial derivatives markets in domestic and global contexts CLO 2: Differentiate Major Derivative Instruments and Their Applications Distinguish between forwards, futures, options, swaps, and credit derivatives, and evaluate their suitability for various financial and business applications. CLO 3: Analyze Financial Risk Exposure and Risk Transfer Mechanisms Identify different categories of financial risk and analyze how derivative instruments can be used to hedge, transfer, or manage these risks in corporate and investment settings. CLO 4: Apply No-Arbitrage and Pricing Logic in Derivative Valuation Apply conceptual pricing principles such as cost-of-carry, no-arbitrage relationships, put-call parity, and option valuation logic to evaluate derivative pricing scenarios. CLO 5: Interpret Market Risk Sensitivities and Volatility Measures Interpret option Greeks, implied volatility indicators, and market sentiment measures to assess derivative risk exposures and support informed decision-making. CLO 6: Design Basic Hedging and Trading Strategies Using Derivatives Develop appropriate derivative-based hedging, speculation, and portfolio protection strategies using futures and options under different market conditions. CLO 7: Evaluate Corporate and Institutional Applications of Derivatives Assess the use of derivative instruments in treasury management, foreign exchange risk management, interest rate risk management, and institutional portfolio hedging. CLO 8: Critically Assess Regulatory, Ethical, and Governance Issues in Derivatives Markets Evaluate regulatory frameworks, governance mechanisms, ethical challenges, and responsible management issues related to derivatives trading and market participation. CLO 9: Analyze the Role of Derivatives in Financial Stability and Crisis Events Examine how derivative instruments have contributed to or mitigated systemic risk during major financial crises, and assess implications for market stability. CLO 10: Integrate Derivative Concepts to Solve Real-World Financial Problems Integrate conceptual, analytical, and case-based knowledge to solve realistic business and financial decision-making problems involving derivatives.
FAC410.objectives: By the end of this course, students will be able to: CO1. Develop Foundational Understanding of Derivatives Markets Explain the structure, purpose, and economic significance of financial derivatives, including forwards, futures, options, swaps, and credit derivatives, within both domestic and global financial markets. CO2. Analyze Financial Risk and Risk Management Needs Identify and evaluate different forms of financial risk—including market risk, currency risk, interest rate risk, commodity price risk, liquidity risk, and credit risk—and assess the suitability of derivative instruments for risk mitigation. CO3. Apply Derivative Instruments for Hedging and Risk Transfer Design and evaluate practical hedging strategies using derivative instruments for corporate treasury management, investment portfolio protection, and foreign exchange exposure management. CO4. Evaluate Arbitrage, Speculation, and Market Efficiency Analyze the role of derivatives in price discovery, arbitrage opportunities, speculative trading, and market efficiency while distinguishing between productive and destabilizing market behavior. CO5. Interpret Pricing Logic and Valuation Concepts Demonstrate conceptual understanding of derivative pricing principles, including no-arbitrage relationships, cost-of-carry logic, put-call parity, and practical option valuation frameworks. CO6. Utilize Risk Sensitivity Measures for Decision-Making Interpret and apply key risk sensitivity concepts such as Delta, Gamma, Theta, Vega, and Rho to support informed derivatives trading and portfolio risk management decisions. CO7. Compare Indian and Global Derivatives Market Practices Critically compare the evolution, market structure, trading mechanisms, regulatory frameworks, and institutional practices of Indian and international derivatives markets. CO8. Evaluate Ethical and Governance Issues in Derivatives Usage Assess ethical considerations, governance failures, and responsible management challenges associated with derivative misuse, excessive leverage, speculative excess, and systemic financial instability. CO9. Analyze Contemporary Financial Crises and Systemic Risk Examine the role of derivatives in historical and recent financial crises and evaluate their implications for systemic risk, financial stability, and regulatory oversight. CO10. Strengthen Applied Analytical and Strategic Decision-Making Skills Integrate conceptual, numerical, and case-based knowledge to make informed financial decisions involving derivative strategy selection, risk management, and market applications.
FAC410.program_learning_goals: 1. Demonstrate a sound understanding of financial derivatives, their market structure, pricing principles, and applications in modern financial markets. 2. Apply analytical reasoning to evaluate financial risks, derivative strategies, and risk management decisions using qualitative and quantitative approaches. 3. Utilize derivative instruments to support informed business decisions related to hedging, portfolio management, treasury operations, and financial risk mitigation. 4. Evaluate the ethical, regulatory, and governance issues associated with derivatives markets and promote responsible financial decision-making. 5. Analyze the functioning of Indian and international derivatives markets and assess the impact of global financial developments on business and investment decisions. 6. Effectively communicate financial analysis, derivative strategies, and risk management recommendations through case analyses, presentations, and practical assignments.

Derivative Pricing and Trading Interpretation 4. Hedging and Portfolio Risk Management 5. Problem-Solving and Decision-Making 6. Market Data Analysis and Financial Interpretation 7. weekly_modules.1: MODULE I (Sessions 1-5): Foundations of Derivatives Markets and Risk Management Module Objective: This module aims to develop foundational understanding of financial derivatives, their economic rationale, historical evolution, and core market structures. Students will learn how derivatives emerged as tools for managing financial uncertainty and will gain introductory knowledge of forwards and futures, including their practical applications in risk transfer, hedging, and price discovery within Indian and global financial markets. Session No.: 1 Topic: Introduction to Financial Derivatives & Risk Session Objective: To introduce students to the concept of financial derivatives, the economic rationale behind their existence, and the role of derivatives in managing financial risk. Students will develop foundational understanding of hedging, speculation, arbitrage, and different categories of financial risk in modern financial markets. Key Readings: 1. Hull, John C. — Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives, Pearson Education (Chapter 1) 2. Chance, Don M., & Brooks, Robert — An Introduction to Derivatives and Risk Management (Introductory Chapters) Case / Practical Exercise: • Case: Airline Fuel Price Hedging using Futures Contracts • Practical Exercise: Identifying real-life examples of derivatives in commodity, currency, and equity markets Session No.: 2 Topic: Evolution of Derivatives – India & Global Session Objective: To provide students with historical understanding of the evolution of derivatives markets globally and in India, including the transition from commodity derivatives to financial derivatives, the development of organized exchanges, and the rise of modern derivative trading ecosystems. Key Readings: 1. Hull, John C. — Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives (History and Markets Chapters) 2. Varma, Jayanth R. — Derivatives and Risk Management (Indian derivatives market evolution) Case / Practical Exercise: • Case: Evolution of NSE Derivatives Market in India • Practical Exercise: Comparative analysis of NSE, CME, ICE, and MCX trading volumes using exchange data
weekly_modules.2: Session No.: 3 Topic: Forward Contracts – Fundamentals Session Objective: To develop understanding of forward contracts, their structure, customization features, OTC nature, settlement mechanisms, and practical applications in currency and commodity risk management. Key Readings: 1. Hull, John C. — Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives (Forward Contracts Chapter) 2. Chance, Don M., & Brooks, Robert — An Introduction to Derivatives and Risk Management (Forwards and OTC Markets) Case / Practical Exercise: • Case: Exporter–Importer Currency Forward Contract • Practical Exercise: Designing a simple agricultural forward contract between a farmer and trader Session No.: 4 Topic: Forward Pricing & Valuation Session Objective: To introduce students to the pricing logic of forward contracts using the cost-of-carry principle and no-arbitrage framework, along with practical applications in commodity and currency markets. Key Readings: 1. Hull, John C. — Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives (Pricing of Forward and Futures Contracts) 2. Kolb, Robert W., & Overdahl, James A. — Financial Derivatives: Pricing and Risk Management Case / Practical Exercise: • Case: USD-INR Forward Pricing by Indian Banks • Practical Exercise: Gold forward pricing and simple no-arbitrage calculations using spot price, interest rate, and storage cost
weekly_modules.3: Session No.: 5 Topic: Futures Contracts – Fundamentals Session Objective: To provide foundational understanding of futures contracts, exchange-traded derivative structures, standardization, contract specifications, and the functioning of futures markets in India and globally. Key Readings: 1. Hull, John C. — Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives (Futures Markets Chapters) 2. NSE India — Futures & Options Market Educational Material Case / Practical Exercise: • Case: NIFTY Index Futures Trading at NSE • Practical Exercise: Interpretation of futures contract specifications for equity, index, and commodity futures contracts from NSE and MCX websites MODULE II (Sessions 6–10): Futures Markets, Trading Mechanics, and Risk Management Applications Module Objective: This module focuses on operational understanding of exchange-traded derivatives, particularly futures and basic options. Students will develop practical competency in futures trading mechanisms, margin systems, hedging applications, speculative strategies, and arbitrage logic, while also building foundational understanding of option contract structures and payoff behavior. Session No.: 6 Topic: Futures Trading Mechanism & Clearing Session Objective: To familiarize students with the operational structure of futures markets, including margin systems, mark-to-market settlement, clearing corporations, and risk management mechanisms used in exchange-traded derivatives markets. Key Readings: 1. Hull, John C. — Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives (Futures Trading & Margin System Chapters) 2. NSE India — Futures & Options Market Operational Framework and SPAN Margin Guidelines Case / Practical Exercise: • Case: Margin Calls During Volatile Market Conditions • Practical Exercise: Simulating mark-to-market profit/loss and margin calculations for NIFTY futures contracts
weekly_modules.4: Session No.: 7 Topic: Hedging with Futures Session Objective: To develop understanding of how futures contracts are used for hedging financial risk, including commodity price risk, portfolio risk, and market exposure management through practical hedging strategies. Key Readings: 1. Hull, John C. — Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives (Hedging Strategies Chapter) 2. Chance, Don M., & Brooks, Robert — An Introduction to Derivatives and Risk Management (Futures Hedging Applications) Case / Practical Exercise: • Case: Portfolio Hedging Using NIFTY Futures • Practical Exercise: Calculating hedge ratios and designing long and short hedge strategies for commodity and equity portfolios Session No.: 8 Topic: Speculation & Arbitrage in Futures Session Objective: To introduce speculative trading strategies and arbitrage opportunities in futures markets, while helping students understand price convergence, leverage, and the role of arbitrage in maintaining market efficiency. Key Readings: 1. Hull, John C. — Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives (Arbitrage & Futures Pricing Chapters) 2. Kolb, Robert W., & Overdahl, James A. — Financial Derivatives: Pricing and Risk Management Case / Practical Exercise: • Case: Cash-and-Carry Arbitrage in NSE Futures Market • Practical Exercise: Identifying arbitrage opportunities using spot and futures prices under different market conditions
weekly_modules.5: Session No.: 9 Topic: Introduction to Options Session Objective: To introduce students to option contracts, including call and put options, buyer and seller rights and obligations, option market participants, and the fundamental logic of asymmetric payoffs. Key Readings: 1. Hull, John C. — Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives (Options Markets Chapters) 2. Chance, Don M., & Brooks, Robert — An Introduction to Derivatives and Risk Management (Introduction to Options) Case / Practical Exercise: • Case: Retail Investor Using NIFTY Call Options for Bullish View • Practical Exercise: Identifying call and put option positions under different market expectations Session No.: 10 Topic: Options Payoff & Profit Structures Session Objective: To help students understand option payoff and profit structures for long and short option positions, including moneyness, break-even analysis, and payoff visualization under varying market scenarios. Key Readings: 1. Hull, John C. — Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives (Option Payoff Strategies Chapter) 2. NSE India — Educational Material on Option Strategies and Payoff Structures Case / Practical Exercise: • Case: NIFTY Call and Put Option Trading Outcomes at Expiry • Practical Exercise: Drawing payoff and profit diagrams for long call, short call, long put, and short put strategies under different expiry prices
weekly_modules.6: MODULE III (Sessions 11–20): Options Pricing, Risk Management, and Trading Strategies Module Objective: This module develops comprehensive understanding of options pricing, valuation logic, market behavior, and risk management applications. Students will learn conceptual option pricing frameworks, volatility interpretation, Greeks-based risk analysis, and practical option trading strategies used by retail and institutional participants, enabling informed derivatives decision-making without reliance on advanced quantitative methods. Session No.: 11 Topic: Option Pricing Intuition Session Objective: To develop conceptual understanding of the factors that influence option prices, including intrinsic value, time value, volatility, interest rates, and time to expiry, using practical market-oriented interpretation rather than advanced mathematics. Key Readings: 1. Hull, John C. — Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives (Option Pricing Basics) 2. Chance, Don M., & Brooks, Robert — An Introduction to Derivatives and Risk Management (Option Valuation Concepts) Case / Practical Exercise: • Case: Weekly NIFTY Options and Rapid Time Decay • Practical Exercise: Analyzing NSE option chain data to identify intrinsic and time value components Session No.: 12 Topic: Put-Call Parity & No-Arbitrage Session Objective: To introduce the concept of no-arbitrage relationships in options markets and help students understand synthetic positions, put-call parity, and basic arbitrage opportunities in derivative pricing. Key Readings: 1. Hull, John C. — Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives (Put-Call Parity Chapter) 2. Kolb, Robert W., & Overdahl, James A. — Financial Derivatives: Pricing and Risk Management Case / Practical Exercise: • Case: Synthetic Long Futures Using Options • Practical Exercise: Identifying arbitrage opportunities using put-call parity relationships
weekly_modules.7: Session No.: 13 Topic: Conceptual Foundations of Option Pricing Models Session Objective: To provide students with intuitive understanding of why option pricing models are required and how uncertainty, expected outcomes, and probability-based thinking influence derivative pricing decisions. Key Readings: 1. Hull, John C. — Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives (Introduction to Option Pricing Models) 2. Chance, Don M., & Brooks, Robert — An Introduction to Derivatives and Risk Management Case / Practical Exercise: • Case: Pricing Expectations Before Major Corporate Announcements • Practical Exercise: Simple expected outcome analysis under different market scenarios Session No.: 14 Topic: Black–Scholes Model – Conceptual Framework Session Objective: To introduce the Black–Scholes option pricing framework conceptually, focusing on its assumptions, economic intuition, and importance in modern derivatives markets without advanced mathematical derivations. Key Readings: 1. Hull, John C. — Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives (Black–Scholes Framework Chapters) 2. Chance, Don M., & Brooks, Robert — An Introduction to Derivatives and Risk Management Case / Practical Exercise: • Case: Why Black–Scholes Changed Modern Finance • Practical Exercise: Interpreting the impact of volatility, time, and interest rates on option premiums using online pricing calculators
weekly_modules.8: Session No.: 15 Topic: Black–Scholes Applications Session Objective: To help students apply Black–Scholes pricing intuition in practical market settings and interpret how various factors influence option prices and market behavior. Key Readings: 1. Hull, John C. — Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives (Applications of Black–Scholes Model) 2. NSE India — Educational Material on Option Pricing Case / Practical Exercise: • Case: Pricing NIFTY Options Under Different Volatility Conditions • Practical Exercise: Using Excel or online calculators to estimate option premiums and compare market prices Session No.: 16 Topic: Option Greeks Session Objective: To develop practical understanding of option Greeks as risk management tools and explain how option prices respond to changes in underlying asset prices, volatility, time, and interest rates. Key Readings: 1. Hull, John C. — Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives (Option Greeks Chapters) 2. NSE India — Option Greeks Educational Material Case / Practical Exercise: • Case: Delta and Theta Behavior in Weekly NIFTY Options • Practical Exercise: Interpreting Delta, Gamma, Theta, Vega, and Rho using real option chain data
weekly_modules.9: Session No.: 17 Topic: Implied Volatility & Market Sentiment Session Objective: To help students understand implied volatility as a measure of market expectations and sentiment, including volatility smile, skew, IV crush, and volatility-based trading behavior. Key Readings: 1. Hull, John C. — Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives (Volatility & Implied Volatility Chapters) 2. CBOE / NSE Educational Notes on VIX and Implied Volatility Case / Practical Exercise: • Case: India VIX During Elections or RBI Policy Announcements • Practical Exercise: Comparing historical volatility and implied volatility for selected NSE stocks Session No.: 18 Topic: Bull & Bear Option Strategies Session Objective: To introduce directional option trading strategies used under bullish and bearish market expectations and evaluate their payoff, risk, and reward characteristics. Key Readings: 1. Hull, John C. — Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives (Trading Strategies Chapters) 2. NSE India — Option Strategy Educational Modules Case / Practical Exercise: • Case: Bull Call Spread During Market Recovery Phase • Practical Exercise: Constructing payoff diagrams for covered call, protective put, bull spread, and bear spread strategies
weekly_modules.10: Session No.: 19 Topic: Neutral & Volatility Strategies Session Objective: To develop understanding of non-directional and volatility-based option strategies used during uncertain or event-driven market conditions. Key Readings: 1. Hull, John C. — Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives (Advanced Option Strategies Chapters) 2. Chance, Don M., & Brooks, Robert — An Introduction to Derivatives and Risk Management Case / Practical Exercise: • Case: Straddle Strategy During Union Budget or Election Results • Practical Exercise: Designing straddle, strangle, butterfly, and iron condor strategies under different volatility expectations Session No.: 20 Topic: Advanced Option Applications & Institutional Hedging Session Objective: To expose students to institutional applications of options in portfolio protection, volatility management, and advanced risk management practices used by mutual funds, hedge funds, and corporate treasury teams. Key Readings: 1. Hull, John C. — Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives (Risk Management Applications Chapters) 2. CFA Institute Readings on Portfolio Hedging and Options Applications Case / Practical Exercise: • Case: Mutual Fund Portfolio Protection Using Index Options • Practical Exercise: Designing a basic protective hedging strategy for an equity portfolio using NIFTY options
weekly_modules.11: MODULE IV (Sessions 21–23) : OTC Derivatives and Corporate Risk Management Applications Module Objective: This module introduces over-the-counter (OTC) derivative instruments used by corporations, financial institutions, and governments for managing financial risks. Students will develop an understanding of interest rate swaps, currency swaps, and credit default swaps (CDS), and appreciate their role in managing interest rate, foreign exchange, and credit risks in domestic and international financial markets. Session No.: 21 Topic: Interest Rate Swaps Session Objective: To introduce students to the concept, structure, and applications of interest rate swaps, enabling them to understand how organizations use fixed-for-floating interest rate exchanges to manage borrowing costs and interest rate risk. Key Readings: 1. Hull, John C. — Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives (Interest Rate Swaps Chapter) 2. Chance, Don M., & Brooks, Robert — An Introduction to Derivatives and Risk Management (Interest Rate Swaps) Case / Practical Exercise: • Case: Corporate Borrowing Strategy Using Fixed-to-Floating Interest Rate Swaps • Practical Exercise: Design the cash flows of a fixed-for-floating interest rate swap and compare the borrowing costs before and after entering into the swap agreement. Session No.: 22 Topic: Currency Swaps & FX Risk Management Session Objective: To develop understanding of currency swaps and their applications in foreign exchange risk management, multinational treasury operations, and cross-border financing decisions. Key Readings: 1. Hull, John C. — Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives (Currency Swaps Chapters) 2. RBI Educational / Regulatory Material on Foreign Exchange Risk Management Case / Practical Exercise: • Case: Indian Company Managing USD Borrowing Exposure through Currency Swaps • Practical Exercise: Designing a simple INR–USD currency swap structure for an exporter/importer scenario
weekly_modules.12: Session No.: 23 Topic: Credit Default Swaps (CDS) & Credit Risk Transfer Session Objective: To introduce students to credit derivatives, particularly credit default swaps (CDS), and explain how CDS instruments are used for credit risk transfer, hedging, and speculative purposes in financial markets. Key Readings: 1. Hull, John C. — Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives (Credit Derivatives Chapters) 2. Kolb, Robert W., & Overdahl, James A. — Financial Derivatives: Pricing and Risk Management Case / Practical Exercise: • Case: AIG and CDS Exposure During the 2008 Global Financial Crisis • Practical Exercise: Calculating CDS payoff under default and non-default scenarios using simplified numerical examples MODULE V (Sessions 24–26): Regulation, Financial Stability, and Integrated Applications Module Objective: This module develops awareness of governance, regulation, ethical considerations, and systemic implications of derivatives markets. Students will critically evaluate the role of derivatives in financial crises, understand contemporary regulatory frameworks, and integrate course concepts through real-world case analysis and applied problem-solving. Session No.: 24 Topic: Derivatives Regulation, Clearing & Governance Session Objective: To develop understanding of the regulatory framework governing derivatives markets, including the role of exchanges, clearing corporations, regulators, and governance mechanisms in ensuring market integrity, transparency, investor protection, and financial stability. Key Readings: 1. Hull, John C. — Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives (Regulation and Market Structure Chapters) 2. SEBI / RBI Guidelines on Derivatives Market Regulation and Clearing Mechanisms Case / Practical Exercise: • Case: SEBI Reforms in Indian Derivatives Markets and Margin Regulations • Practical Exercise: Comparative analysis of Indian and global derivatives regulatory frameworks (SEBI vs CFTC/BIS)
weekly_modules.13: Session No.: 25 Topic: Systemic Risk, Financial Crises & Derivatives Misuse Session Objective: To critically examine the role of derivatives in financial crises, systemic risk transmission, excessive leverage, and market instability, while evaluating the ethical and governance issues associated with derivative misuse. Key Readings: 1. Hull, John C. — Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives (Credit Crisis and Systemic Risk Discussions) 2. Selected Reports/Articles on the 2008 Global Financial Crisis and Derivatives Markets Case / Practical Exercise: • Case: AIG, Lehman Brothers, and CDS Exposure During the 2008 Financial Crisis • Practical Exercise: Group discussion analyzing how leverage and derivatives amplified systemic risk during major financial crises Session No.: 26 Topic: Integrated Applications, Capstone Cases & Exam Readiness Session Objective: To integrate concepts learned throughout the course and apply derivative instruments to realistic business, treasury, investment, and risk management scenarios through comprehensive case analysis and problem-solving exercises. Key Readings: 1. Review of Selected Chapters from Hull, John C. — Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives 2. Instructor-provided integrated case materials and market examples Case / Practical Exercise: • Case: Integrated Hedging Strategy for an Export-Oriented Company Using Futures and Options • Practical Exercise: Capstone case analysis involving derivative selection, hedging strategy design, and portfolio risk management under changing market conditions

FAC415.introduction: Part A - Regulatory, Compliance & Ethical Risks The Regulatory and Ethical Risk Management Framework course is designed to provide students with a comprehensive understanding of the regulatory environments and ethical considerations that impact modern businesses. The course covers topics such as major regulations affecting industries, the role of ethics in compliance, risk management strategies, and case studies of regulatory failures. Students will gain practical knowledge to manage and mitigate risks within an organization effectively. Part B – Third Party Risk Management An effective third party risk management program should be embedded across various functions like Procurement, Sales, Compliance, etc. so as to become an integrated part of the company's overall risk framework. This module provides an overview of third party risk management principles and ensures students gain a strong grounding in the risk management discipline and provides them with the knowledge and skills appropriate for managing these risks. The course is intended to provide students with a high-level understanding of the concept of TPRM which includes a definition of third parties, different risks associated with third parties and ways to manage and mitigate these risks.
FAC415.learning_outcomes: Students will be able to: 1. Understand and recall the fundamental concepts of regulatory frameworks and ethics in business. (mapped to PLO – 6.1) 2. Analyze and apply key regulations impacting various industries.(mapped to PLO – 6.2) 3. Evaluate the consequences of non-compliance on business operations and reputation 4. Understand strategies for managing regulatory and ethical risks. 5. Understand the fundamental concepts of Third Pary Risk management frameworks in business 6. Understand the third-party lifecycle and issues and challenges in implementing TPRM. 7. The students would be able to evaluate and prepare an analysis of high risk third parties for different industries and learnings from past penalties paid by various companies
FAC415.objectives: Part A1. To provide a thorough understanding of the regulatory frameworks and their significance in business operations. 2. To equip students with the skills to analyze and manage ethical risks within various industries. 3. To enable students to evaluate the impact of non-compliance on business sustainability. 4.To develop the ability to apply theoretical knowledge to real-world scenarios through case studies and practical exercises. Part B 1.Students will be able to understand the concepts of third-party risk management and understand how to make effective decisions under conditions of risk and uncertainty. 2.Equip students to implement robust third party risk management strategies in the real world. 3.Ability to optimize business strategies through managed risk-Case studies + Workshop. 4.Ability to assess third party risk, manage exposure and develop a proactive approach to managing risk from third parties in a comprehensive manner.
