weekly_modules.1: Module objective: To provide students with a foundational understanding of ethics, compliance and regulatory risk in business. The module helps students distinguish between legal, illegal, compliant and ethical behaviour; identify stakeholders; understand the role of the Ethics and Compliance function; and appreciate how regulatory and ethical failures affect business reputation, sustainability and stakeholder trust. Session 1 Introduction to Ethical, Regulatory and Compliance Risks Duration: 2 Hours Session objective: Understand the importance of ethics, compliance and regulatory risk in business decision-making. Students will discuss why profit-making is acceptable, but the manner in which profits are earned is important. Readings: Institute of Business Ethics – Business Ethics Framework: https://www.ibe.org.uk/business-ethics-framework/ Class Activity: Expectation-setting exercise: What does ethics mean to you? Is compliance enough for a sustainable business? Session 2: Ethics versus Legal Duration: 2 Hours Session objective: Understand the difference between legal, illegal/criminal, civil, compliance and ethics. Students will examine whether conduct that is legal is always ethical and how ethical standards change over time. Readings: Material for internal circulation – GRMI’s Copyright IP content Markkula Centre for Applied Ethics – A Framework for Ethical Decision Making: https://www.scu.edu/ethics/ethics-resources/a-framework-for-ethical-decision-making/ Class Activity: Discussion on examples of: legal now but once illegal; illegal now but once legal; ethical once but now unethical; unethical once but now ethical.
weekly_modules.2: Session 3: Ethical Theories and Ethical Decision-Making Duration: 2 Hours Session objective: Understand basic ethical approaches such as utilitarianism, deontology, virtue ethics, ethical relativism and social contract theory. Students will apply these approaches to simple business dilemmas. Readings: Markkula Centre for Applied Ethics – Ethical Decision Making: https://www.scu.edu/ethics/ethics-resources/ethical-decision-making/ Class Activity: Prepare a simple ethical decision-making tree for a workplace or business dilemma. Session 4: Stakeholder Mapping and Ethics Function Duration: 2 Hours Session objective: Identify internal and external stakeholders and map them into the circles of control, influence, and concern. Students will understand how the Ethics and Compliance function interacts with business, regulators, employees, customers, investors and other stakeholders. Readings: UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights: https://www.ohchr.org/sites/default/files/documents/publications/guidingprinciplesbusinesshr_en.pdf Class Activity: Stakeholder mapping for Dr Reddy’s / Byju’s / Blinkit / Maruti / Amul.
weekly_modules.3: Session 5: Ethical Risk Case Study – Cerelac / Nestlé Duration: 2 Hours Session objective: Apply stakeholder mapping and ethical decision-making to a real-world business case. Students will analyze how a product may be legally compliant but still raise ethical concerns. Case Study: Cerelac / Nestlé baby food sugar-content issue, Readings: Material for internal circulation – GRMI’s Copyright IP content WHO – Guideline: Sugars Intake for Adults and Children: https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241549028 Class Activity: Map stakeholders and propose short-term, medium-term and long-term ethical strategies. Session 6: Regulatory Risk and Major Regulations Impacting Organizations Duration: 2 Hours Session objective: Understand regulatory risk, its sources and its impact on business operations, profitability, reputation and strategic decisions. Students will discuss major regulations impacting organizations in India. Readings: ISO 31000:2018 Risk Management – official ISO page: https://www.iso.org/standard/65694.html Competition Commission of India – Legal Framework: https://www.cci.gov.in/legal-framwork/act India Code – Environment Protection Act, 1986: https://www.indiacode.nic.in/bitstream/123456789/4316/1/ep_act_1986.pdf Class Activity: Students identify one regulation, its objective, affected industry and potential business impact.
weekly_modules.4: Session 7: Regulators, Powers of Regulators and Consequences of Non-Compliance Duration: 2 Hours Session objective: Understand the role and powers of regulators, including standard setting, authorization, supervision and enforcement. Students will evaluate the consequences of non-compliance, including legal, financial, criminal, reputational and business continuity risks. Readings: OECD – Risk and Regulatory Policy: Improving the Governance of Risk: https://www.oecd.org/gov/regulatory-policy/risk-and-regulatory-policy-9789264082939-en.htm Reserve Bank of India – Notifications and Regulatory Directions: https://www.rbi.org.in/Scripts/NotificationUser.aspx SEBI – Legal Framework: https://www.sebi.gov.in/legal.html Class Activity: Discussion on how regulatory action can affect business continuity, reputation and stakeholder trust. Module 2: Regulatory Risk Framework and Anti-Bribery Compliance Module objective: To enable students to understand and apply a regulatory risk management framework and relate it to anti-bribery and corruption compliance. Students will learn how organizations identify regulations, map obligations, assess risks, implement controls, monitor compliance, encourage speak-up culture and respond to bribery and corruption risks. Session 8: Regulatory Risk Management Framework – Components and Governance Duration: 2 Hours Session objective: Understand the components of a regulatory risk management framework, including risk identification, risk assessment, risk mitigation, monitoring and reporting, governance and oversight, board accountability, tone at the top, escalation protocols and control implementation. Readings: Material for internal circulation – GRMI’s Copyright IP content COSO Enterprise Risk Management Framework: https://www.coso.org/guidance-erm U.S. DOJ – Evaluation of Corporate Compliance Programs: https://www.justice.gov/criminal/criminal-fraud/page/file/937501/dl?inline= Class Activity: Prepare a basic compliance risk matrix showing likelihood, impact, control gaps, ownership and monitoring mechanism.
weekly_modules.5: Session 9: Building and Implementing a Regulatory Risk Framework Duration: 2 Hours Session objective: Learn the practical steps for building a regulatory risk framework: identify laws, map obligations, evaluate risks, implement controls, monitor and report, and audit and review. Students will understand implementation challenges such as weak tone at the top, unclear ownership, poor documentation and weak escalation culture. Readings: Material for internal circulation – GRMI’s Copyright IP content OECD – Good Practice Guidance on Internal Controls, Ethics and Compliance: https://legalinstruments.oecd.org/public/doc/258/body-text.en.html IRM – A Risk Practitioner’s Guide to ISO 31000:2018: https://www.theirm.org/media/6884/irm-report-iso-31000-2018-v2.pdf Class Activity: Draft a simple regulatory risk framework for a selected industry. HIS1001.introduction: In this course, we shall look at the history of making of the Indian economy with respect to the rest of the world. In many ways, the colonial experience played an instrumental role in defining, delimiting and shaping the Indian economy. The course, by looking at this history of colonialism, and connecting it to the histories before and after, will try to shed light on how the contemporary issues of production and distribution, measurements of national income, poverty and exploitation, fiscal and monetary policies, progress, growth and development, governance and policy-making have antecedents in the past experiences of colonial domination and postcolonial aspirations. Moreover, the course will try to map the location of India in a global landscape of economic progress and the challenges faced thereof. This course should encourage the students to take up some of these questions forward as they move in the programme and make sense of the contemporary in the light of the past.
HIS1001.learning_outcomes: Understanding the Indian economy historically; Reflecting on the relationship between the Indian economy and global historical processes; studying the impact of colonialism both on India and the world; understanding the historical processes that contribute to making and unmaking of policies and institutions
HIS1001.objectives: To offer a history of the development of the Indian economy in different phases in history To provide an analysis of the impact of colonialism on Indian economy To trace the histories of various institutions and structures of Indian economy in its colonial past and nationalist aspirations To examine the policies and programmes taken by the colonial state and the post-colonial nation-state in terms of their significance and impact To locate the growth of the Indian economy vis-à-vis the developments in the world economy

HIS102.introduction: HIS 102 is a 100 level course designed to introduce students to the discipline of history. People have always told and preserved the stories of their past. However, a telling and retelling of stories is distinct from the academic discipline of History. The discipline of history writing, as we recognise it today, emerged out of the post - Enlightenment universities and academies in Europe. In this course, we trace the emergence of the discipline of history writing, examining its relationship to the Enlightenment and European modernity. We look at the debates around history writing in South Asia, in the backdrop of colonialism. In the final part of the course, we discuss the making of the archives as the primary tool of history writing. The course seeks to introduce the students to the discipline through its history and critically engage with the In this course we will discuss the emergence of History writing, looking at its relationship to the Enlightenment and European modernity. We will look at changes in the debates around history writing in South Asia, especially in the backdrop of colonialism. The third part of the course deals specifically with the question of the Archives. course has three main parts: In Part One, we discuss the emergence of History as a discipline in the post Enlightenment Academies of Europe. In Part Two, we explore the emergence of History as a discipline in Colonial India. Part Three: Introduces the students to the Archives and the discussions around the making of the Archive. In this course, we discuss the emergence of History as a discipline in the post Enlightenment Academies of Europe and its emergence and early struggles in colonial India. The third part of the course introduces the students to the Archives and the discussions around it.

HIS312.introduction: Landscape is a fashionable word. It is used by engineers, architects, designers, artists, historians and archaeologists, among many other disciplines. Specialists in all these fields approach landscapes differently, although, as we will learn in this course, all these conceptions are mutually intelligible to a trained archaeologist. In this course you will be introduced to archaeological and anthropological understandings of landscapes. We will address the following themes: 1) origins and historiography of the sub discipline of Landscape archaeology 2) the various themes investigated by anthropological archaeologists employing a landscape approach (through case studies) a. Cultural ecology b. Phenomenology c. Ideational perspectives 3) Use of Landscape archaeology in the South Asian context 4) Intersections of Landscape archaeology with other approaches to studying the past, particularly intensive, object-based studies. 5) Engagement with the current conceptions of the Anthropocene.
HIS312.learning_outcomes: a. Students will appreciate how archaeologists know what we know about the past. b. The methods employed by archaeologists, especially while studying ‘landscapes’, will introduce students to a novel analytical and interpretive framework, that is different from what historians do. c. In addition, students will hone writing, analyzing, and presentation skills. d. The course will be geared towards engaging with archaeological materials from different areas of the world and as such students will learn to appreciate diversities inherent in these archaeological data.
HIS312.objectives: The course is designed to give theoretical and conceptual tools to students to undertake basic analyses of a broad-scale archaeology. They will engage in independent, critical thinking and writing regarding such approaches to doing archaeology.
HIS312.program_learning_goals: 1) Students will learn about an important thematic research component of archaeology; 2) students will understand how archeology and allied disciplines such as environmental sciences, humanties come together in this important theme; 3) skills such as GIS and remoe sensing for archaeological and/or planning landscapes will come in handy as a research and practical skill.

HIS323.introduction: The course explores the histories of photography and archaeology to demonstrate the importance of noting the practices of ‘seeing and knowing’ in the scholarship of History and Archaeology. It provides a survey of the cultural histories of the Visual and Material and of the ways in which field based scholarship build upon transcriptions of vision. Histories of field photography illuminate aspects of the evidentiary realm. Practices of archaeological fieldwork are usually premised upon our abilities of seeing the field, and the understanding of a visual reality nurtures the premise of valid evidence. The course highlights some of the ways in which the non-present past and ideological notions are given tangible forms. Additionally, it creates a regard of the politics of seeing, especially in histories of imperialism. It highlights the possibilities of archaeology's visual histories, and of the historiography, and guides students to engage with photographs and photographic collections and archives as objects of archaeological knowledge.
HIS323.learning_outcomes: Students will learn about: • The Importance of Visual Histories • Histories of Photography and Archaeology in India • The Photographic Collections of the Archaeological Survey of India • Field Photography of the Monuments of India • Photography and Heritage Making • Histories and Practices of Archaeological Photography

Why photographs and historic photographic collections aid careful and reflexive scholarship The importance of reflecting critically on Classifications and Categories, which the Visual implores us to look at

HIS326.introduction: Histories of medieval and early modern South Asia are dominated by the stories of kings and queens. Historical and political practices map these periods through their person, lives and works. In turn, historical change is imagined as individual acts, influenced and shaped by the belief systems, assertion of power and personal whims of monarchs. However, this approach allows us only a partial glimpse of the ideas, processes and structures of authority in the making of pre-modern states. In this course, we will move away from the persona of the kings and look at monarchy as an institution in the early modern period. We will focus on significant political formations of early modern South Asia like the Mughal Empire. The course will follow three main sites of articulation and conceptualisation of kingship: a. Akhlaq: In this section we will examine the ideological and legal conceptions of state and sovereignty and explore the limits of king’s powers. b. Darbar: The royal court signified both the seat of power as well as the site of disputation. It was both a space for the enactment of imperial authority as well as an institution where multiple networks of power and patronage converged. We will look at the royal court through paintings and literary descriptions. c. Shahr: The early modern period saw the making of cities, planned and built with royal impetus. However, once built and inhabited, these cities acquired a dynamism of their own. Most urban centres of early modern south Asia evolved their own relationship with political power. We will explore these themes through an study of the evolution of Shahjahanabad (Delhi)— conceived as a grand capital, but where the space of the city became an alternative to the palace.
HIS326.learning_outcomes: • Understand state formation in the medieval and early modern period in South Asia. • Analyse, in their historical context, concepts of kingship, sovereignty and juridical authority. • Critically read and parse a range of archives from textual material to visual sources.
HIS326.objectives: • To help students understand the institution of kingship and sovereignty in the early modern period. • To develop an understanding of the processes of the formation of authority and power in history. • To help the students read the relationship between political authority and challenges to it in the urban space. • To help students engage with primary archival material. • To help students trace the linkages between contemporary political and social institutions and the early modern past.
HIS326.prerequisites: The course is designed for 200 – 400 level History majors and advanced History minors, who have some knowledge of the history and debates of pre-modern South Asia.

HIS326.skill_development: Students will learn to: Read and write. Engage with art and the visual archive. Use visual and digital media in their presentations.

HIS331.introduction: How do historians write histories that transcend the nation-state? How have empires, commodities, migration, law, science, humanitarianism, and environmental change connected societies across the world? Rather than treating Europe as the sole centre of historical change, this course examines the nineteenth and twentieth centuries through interconnected histories spanning South Asia, Africa, Europe, the Americas, and the Indian Ocean world. Introducing students to the methods and debates of Global History, the course explores how colonialism, capitalism, and mobility reshaped societies across continents. It foregrounds scholarship that situates South Asia and Africa as sites from which global historical processes can be understood, while critically engaging with questions of power, inequality, circulation, and comparison. Students will encounter influential approaches, including connected histories, commodity histories, global legal history, environmental history, and histories of science and humanitarianism, through case studies that reveal how people, ideas, objects, and institutions moved across borders and oceans. The course also examines critiques of Global History, asking whose histories become "global," how historians negotiate the relationship between local archives and global narratives, and whether Global History can be written from the Global South.
HIS331.learning_outcomes: On successful completion of the course, students will be able to: • Explain major concepts and debates in Global History. • Analyse interconnected historical processes across regions. • Critically evaluate historical scholarship and primary arguments.
HIS331.objectives: Introduce the methodological and theoretical approaches of Global History Understand the critiques and possibilities of Global History Gain insights into regions beyond South Asia
HIS331.program_learning_goals: To familiarise students with new scholarly and methodological trends in the field of Modern and Contemporary History; Provides comparative approaches and insights into regions beyond South Asian history; Provides insights for students across the Humanities and Social Sciences to engage in interdisciplinary learning.
HIS331.school: SHSS - School of Humanities and Social Sciences

IHS1002.introduction: As an introductory course placed in the first year of learning, the course aims to address the sub-fields in philosophy that form the basis of knowledge necessary for pursuing various courses in the multi-disciplinary branch of knowledge such as liberal arts. To that end, the course is designed to facilitate students to explore the nature of reality, knowledge, ethics, and human existence through major works of philosophy in a historical timeline. The course is developed to cover themes such as logical thinking, theories of knowledge acquisition, the nature of reality, meanings of human existence and ethics. The last component introduces students to themes in ancient Indian philosophical tradition. The objectives of the course are (a) analysing and evaluating philosophical arguments and theories; (b) applying philosophical concepts to real-world issues and problems; and (c) developing critical thinking, reading, and writing skills. Some of the learning outcomes include being able to compare and contrast multiple approaches to understand texts, actions and events, understanding fundamental questions of ethics and their contexts and communicating arguments and views in a cogent manner. The course will also have space for experiential learning where the students will be introduced to complex ideas and concepts through thought experiments and simulations of real-world problems. Classroom teaching will use not only linguistic texts but also audio-visual material ranging from artworks, films, music and other forms of expression.
IHS1002.learning_outcomes: On successful completion of the course, students will be able to: (a)compare and contrast multiple philosophical approaches to understand texts, actions and events. (b)understand fundamental questions of ethics and their contexts. (c)communicate ideas and arguments in a cogent and intelligible manner. (d)study a real-world problem in its complexity and approach it with rigour, care and confidence.
IHS1002.objectives: (a)Introducing students to methods of analysis and evaluation of philosophical arguments and theories (b)Teaching them how to apply philosophical concepts to real-world issues and problems (c)Helping them develop critical thinking, reading and writing skills (d)Introducing complex ideas through means of experiential learning like thought experiments and simulations of real-world problems

IHS1003.introduction: This course is an introduction to the discipline of history. The course has three rubrics: 1. Key words In this rubric we examine three important concepts: Time, Memory and Periodisation. Each of these terms represents a concept, and has been the subject of thought and writings in philosophy, economics etc. We will look at these terms through the writings of historians. The idea is to explore how each of these terms go towards making a conception of what is history and its relationship to collectives of communities, countries and nations. 2. Emergence of history writing as a discipline Through this rubric, we follow the history of Europe in the period of early modernity. Starting from mid 14th century, we discuss four moments in European history: Renaissance, Reformation, Scientific Revolution and the Enlightenment. In each of these, we will explore the new intellectual debates and how they link to what is later called European Modernity. This will form the backdrop to our discussion on the emergence of history writing as a discipline in the European academy. The final part of this discussion will be on the emergence of the discipline of history in the colonies. We will specifically look at South Asia in the colonial period. 3. Archives All history writing draws upon the traces of the past. The archives are the repositories of these traces. In this section we will examine the archives, entering questions of their formation, and look at how historians have critically engaged with the archival material. We will also look at the silences in the archive. In this rubric, the class will read some original archival material. The section on the Archives will end with a discussion on Digital Humanities.
IHS1003.learning_outcomes: Students will learn to think critically, using basic concepts from social sciences. Students will be able to identify and understand the historical processes behind the making of their world.
IHS1003.objectives: This course will:Introduce students to the key terms, methods and debates in the discipline of history writing. Introduce students to reading and analysing primary archives of history writing. Encourage students to use the tools of history writing to critically engage with contemporary social issues.

IHS1003.skill_development: Student will develop the skills of Reading and Writing Work with digital humanities Working with different media like the visual, material and archival objects.

INT1001.introduction: ‘Understanding how the world works.’ This is a simple but challenging way of describing one of the key goals of studying international relations. The pursuit of this goal is made difficult by the sheer enormity of our world: billions of people who are divided into hundreds of societies that practise thousands of cultures and follow dozens of ideologies. There are hundreds of states and non-governmental organizations, numerous social movements, a plethora of rivalries, and pressing challenges of war, development, governance, justice, and the environment. To this is added the confusion created by an ever-enlargening body of new and fast-changing data that get generated as states and other international actors interact with one another. The international arena is full of complexity, and in its face, we are likely to have many questions: Is there a way of making sense of it all? Should we focus on just one aspect of international relations? What is worth focusing on? Should we privilege our national standpoint while studying international affairs? Is any other standpoint even possible or desirable? This course will equip students with the tools with which they can begin to think about these questions systematically. It will do this by introducing students to the academic discipline of International Relations (IR). In this course, students will learn about the nature of IR as a social science. They will become familiar with the key concepts and theories that form the spine of the discipline. And they will take first steps towards connecting theoretical learning with understanding of the real world in terms of its key contemporary problems. If students do the course well, they will get a decent sense of, as an IR scholar once put it, ‘What makes the world hang together’.
INT1001.learning_outcomes: On successfully completing this course, students should: 1. Become familiar with IR as a scholarly field. 2. Be able to understand, analyse and critique the key dynamics of contemporary international relations. 3. Be able to speak and write systematically and knowledgeably about international relations.
INT1001.objectives: The course aims to build a firm scholarly foundation for those who are studying for a major or a minor in IR. To those students who opt for it as a UWE, it offers a rich overview of the subject as well as basic analytical skills, which they can employ in their own academic or professional fields.
INT1001.program_learning_goals: The course fulfills the primary goal of the programme, that is, training of students into the discipline of International Relations. It also sets the tone for the rest of the programme, orientating students and offering a 'shadow of the future'.

INT2003.introduction: The on-going wars, global greed for rare earths, and the Covid-19 pandemic have brought in their wake a flurry of international attention and domestic activity on environmental challenges. That the IPCC and other global environmental/biodiversity/freshwater assessments, with their knowledge and policy outputs had sought but failed to achieve this scale and intensity of attention marks our entry to this course. In the midst of discussions on carbon ‘trading’ between nation states, instruments of governance for a sustainable planet, and sustainable development goals, there are demands to leave fossil fuels underground, movements demanding environmental justice, end of extinction of species, degrowth and a feminist post- growth global order. Governments (in developed and developing countries) bargain over international, regional, national, and local options to address the climate crisis. As governments decide how to govern the environment, we ask if there is a new ‘eco- state’? Do concerns about their sovereignty, economic growth, options for sustainable development, conflict resolution, peace and human rights remain as we know them through IR theory? Or through development economics or Keynesian/ ecological economics theories? Given that the economy is an important sub-set within our limited ‘spaceship earth’, a robust understanding of the relationships between the environment and the economy is central to local, national, and international decision making. This course explores the concepts, and theoretical frameworks that help us understand the environment and the economy; the global economy, national economies and sectoral/regional economies. It explains how in the evolution of nations and their economies since the first industrial revolution, one particular framing of the economy and of nature became central to governing economies and ecosystems. But knowledge and ways of knowing human evolution from one ecosystem to another, understanding, controlling and using exo-somatic resources for economic and social gain, seems inadequate to govern our limited environment or planet. We need to understand the politics of this knowledge and governance. We explore the origin and evolution of the environmental social sciences that have attempted to reformulate our knowledge of planetary, national, sectoral and niche ecosystem sustainability. The environmental social sciences have contributed knowledge and capacities to redesign the relationships between the environment, society and the economy. Despite these advances, the knowledge politics evident in concepts like ecosystem services, permissible limits, and even planetary boundaries, bring decision making back to square one; one particular framing of the economy. Whether within or between sovereign governments, international organizations or transnational networks, an alternative ecological lens is necessary and possible to govern the environment and the economy. The course presents such alternatives, imbued with social and ecological security, equality and fraternity, democratic values and processes drawing from the environmental social sciences, with evidence of changes in governance mechanisms. It enables a critical understanding of nature, time and justice to make decisions using inter-and trans disciplinary social-ecological economics and ensure sustainability and resilience.
INT2003.learning_outcomes: On successful completion of the course, students will be able to: Understand the economy as a sub-set of a limited environment or bio-geophysical system. Understand and express clearly, the fundamental concepts and frameworks that inform our strategic decisions about the environment, our production and consumption activities, and our social systems. Distinguish between disciplinary and inter-and trans-disciplinary framings, and national and global decision making that shape sustainable and resilient ecosystems and economies
INT2003.objectives: To give students a preliminary exposure to the relationships between the environment and the economy at the local, national and global levels, with insights into contributions from IR and IPE to address environmental challenges; To equip them with fundamental concepts as used in ecology/environmental sciences, in economics, and in a range of environmental social sciences; To develop an appreciation of the use of these concepts in the governance of economic activities, economies and economies; To develop capacities to articulate and analyse tensions between the environment and development; and explore alternatives or opportunities for new relationships between ecosystems and economies.

weekly_modules.1: Week 1: Introduction to the course: Politics of the Anthropocene: Global Risks and Nation States, International Relations theory and international environmental politics-state-capital; The environment in economic thought - Carbon trading, Sustainable development, Climate change mitigation and adaptation - Forest conservation, Coastal zone regulation, Pesticide toxicity limits, Payment for ecosystem services, Waste treatment, Climate refugees.

weekly_modules.3: Weeks 3 and 4: Economy/Ecosystem and Economics/Ecology: Ecology: definition, emergence, evolution, governance: Beginning with Haeckle, Darwin, and studying Odum’s fundamentals of ecology. Environment – the basic natural sciences; and Ecology – the ‘link between the natural and social sciences’. Stocks and funds. Flux and dynamic systems. Different energy systems – production and consumption in the bio-physical system
weekly_modules.4: Weeks 3 and 4: Economy/Ecosystem and Economics/Ecology: Economics: definition, emergence, evolution, entry in governance (politics, planning, development, markets). Schools of thought- Classical, Neo-classical, Marxist, Development, Institutional – production, consumption, energy and environment in different schools of thought. Concepts, analytical units and theories: of value; of energy, labour, capital, types and assumed typologies of capital, substitutability of natural resources with capital.
weekly_modules.5: Week 5: The economics of ‘spaceship earth’: Environment as resources for economic growth. Understanding throughput and social metabolism. Matter, Energy, Information. Models of economy-environment relationships: (i) Resource and Scarcity (ii) Embedded sub-set and Balance. Energy, economic myths and social metabolism: Stocks, funds and flows - Evolution of knowledge politics, national and international systems since the industrial revolution.
weekly_modules.6: Week 6: Sustainable Development, Sustainability and Resilience: Concepts and features of Sustainability and Resilience. Origin and evolution of sustainable development – 1970s-2010s. Two discursive shifts (i) limits (ii) technology. Four environmental politics transitions. Yet, prevalence of one economic framework. How? Environmental Kuznets Curve (an example). Why? Ways of knowing.
weekly_modules.7: Week 7: The environmental social sciences: Ecological economics: study of relationships between nature’s households and human households mediated by social systems. Evolution of Ecol. Econ. Nature, Justice, Time. LCA, MEFA, MuSIASEM– recap of matter, energy and information on spaceship earth.
weekly_modules.8: Week 8: Political ecology (drawing from Development Geography and Cultural Ecology): study of relationships between ecosystems people and people with capital (in coal mines, sand mining in river beds, nuclear waste disposal, relocation of polluting industries to the Third World). Evolution of Pol Ecol. Questions of social and environmental justice, radical ecological democracy.
weekly_modules.9: Week 9: Environmental history: Crisis and lessons from history about reorientation and creative response of people, nations, international organizations/networks. Complex relationships between history and environment, national cultures and political processes. The centralizing state and environmental movements (of marginal people); power, state and regional/global actors.
weekly_modules.10: Week 10: Environmental /Conservation Sociology, Industrial Ecology, Agroecology and Human Ecology, Urban ecology, Environmental humanities- a peep into these inter-disciplinary arenas, their evolution.
weekly_modules.11: Week 11: Environmental Governance: conceptualizing risk, uncertainty and ignorance, and complexity. Concepts and measures: Social metabolism (MEFA)/ Ecologically Unequal Trade (TIVA/PTB)/ Sustainable Development (SDGs)/ Ecological justice (HANPP/ecosophy/ feminist ecology) Environmental social sciences – move to STS questions, asking ‘how’ we know, and how does what we know relate to how we make decisions about the environment and the economy. Environment and Development in India – Planning, Maintaining status quo WGEEP and HLWG
weekly_modules.12: Week 12: Ecosystem services: from eye-opener to agenda-setting governance mechanism. Green accounting, national income accounting, social metabolism. National and global environmental conflicts, payment for ecosystem services, carbon trading and other governance mechanisms. Weak sustainability and strong sustainability – decision making for sustainable development (growth as a key pillar), green growth, degrowth and post-growth. Recap- Models of economy-environment relationships: (i) Resource and Scarcity (ii) Embedded sub-set and Balance
weekly_modules.13: Week 13: From ecosystem services to social-ecological systems: Sustainability and resilience with security, prosperity and wellbeing. IR theories, revisiting global economy and environmental challenges, Global Risk Report, New local, national and global/planetary order.

INT3032.introduction: The course begins with an overview of the prevalent agrarian-cum-environmental crises in the world. Changes in the nature and content of agriculture since the 1950s, internationally and domestically, as given in development studies/economics and IPE/IR literature. The population and food security questions (of the 1960s) are pitched against the prevalence of hunger and food sovereignty agroecology questions (of the 2000s). Leading on to the major debate on agriculture and climate change, and a summary of the status of agriculture today, the course introduces students to the options for reframing the relationship between agriculture (primary production) and the environment (local as well as planetary boundaries that host and enable all economic activities). Given the importance of food security and environmental security and justice to the nation state, non-state actors, a range of international actors and the planet, the course helps students delineate different disciplinary and trans-disciplinary approaches to analysing the agriculture-environment relationships. Theorisation of, empirical evidence on and options for a wide range of alternatives, of agriculture in the environment are discussed and analysed, especially with reference to the six planetary boundaries (limits) that modern agriculture has transgressed. Addressing the knowledge politics, policies and decentralized democratic capabilities needed to support agroecological alternatives is more crucial than investing in farmer’s practices.
INT3032.learning_outcomes: On successful completion of the course, students will be able to achieve the following: Learn to articulate why different actors have different agricultural understandings and purposes (the actors include the nation state, local governments, farmers, consumers, traders, industrial corporations, input producers, agricultural scientists, bankers and other production service providers, agro-processors, nutrition experts, environmental organizations, international financial organizations, trade blocks); and the semantics and politics of national and planetary boundaries. Clearly explain the national and global agricultural system and its impacts on the environment, the planet – land/soil, water, biodiversity, atmosphere and other planetary systems. Identify and assess the interlocking structures of prevalent agriculture-environment relationships, and possible alternatives, especially agroecological transitions to ensure food, nutrition and environmental security and sovereignty.
INT3032.objectives: To enable students to distinguish the multiple relationships between agriculture and the environment (planetary limits), as mediated by the interlocking structures of knowledge, security, finance and production, in the national economy, local social systems (their capital, labour and technology), the nation state and the international state. To help intellectual engagement and integration of IPE/IR with global agri-environmental problems to ensure local food sovereignty, nutritional security, environmental security and justice, without breaching planetary limits.
INT3032.program_learning_goals: On successful completion of the course, students will be able to achieve the following: Learn to articulate why different actors have different agricultural understandings and purposes (the actors include the nation state, local governments, farmers, consumers, traders, industrial corporations, input producers, agricultural scientists, bankers and other production service providers, agro-processors, nutrition experts, environmental organizations, international financial organizations, trade blocks); and the semantics and politics of national and planetary boundaries. weekly_modules.1: Introduction to INT232/ four modules This course is designed as an exploration, IR/IPE engagements with an alternative politics and governance of agriculture. That agriculture is at the crossroads of climate induced and economically foreordained changes, and that we have to make some significant political choices as nation states, producers and consumers AND as multilateral forums, international organizations and markets, is the key message. But how we make these choices is not and cannot be prescribed. The course helps us explore the interactions between agriculture and the environment (what we call natural resources), as mediated and governed by the nation state and the international state, as we confront questions about agricultural and food systems that do not violate planetary boundaries. Module 1: Agriculture, Crisis and the Environment Lecture1: Introduction to the course. Why do we need to know about agriculture? How is industrial agriculture different from other types of agriculture? And why do nation states support industrial agriculture? Tutorial1: Introducing Planetary Boundaries, interactions, evolution of agricultural crises. Discussing The Journey of Food (UNEP 2023); 8 stages of the journey, exploring interactions between the interlocking structures of security, finance, production and knowledge, EAT Lancet Commission (2019 and 2026) Reading 1: Lang (2010) Crisis, Planetary, Global, International, National and Local + Power, States, Markets.
weekly_modules.2: Week 2: Reading 1. Contd. + Reading 2. Bene and Devereux (2023) (2 chapters) Sustainable agriculture (production-distribution-consumption, and knowledge), Resilience, Knowledge politics, Policies and decentralized democratic capabilities. Exploring the structures; the theorisation and institutionalization of particular models of agricultural development and the governance challenges they pose. Tutorial2: Interlocking structures, Susan Strange 2021 (1988)- why should we theorise planetary boundaries, nation states and agricultural crisis? Reading 3: Clapp and Cohen (2011) (two chapters) Reading 4: Strange (1988) We will read Susan Strange’s chapters and discuss these two chapters during the Tutorial hour. Please pick to major processed foods that you are familiar with. Let us discuss how the four domains of security, production, finance, and knowledge are interlocked. What happened to the institutions/norms that once governed agricultural knowledge, production systems, financial and other support services? Did they lead to food security? Questioning international technological and market/financial frameworks. Seeking interlocking structures and explanations.
weekly_modules.3: Week 3: Module 2: The Nation State and Planetary Limits Reading 4. Clapp 2014 and Reading 5. Friedman and McMichael 1989 Why is the international so important in agriculture and agrarian crises? How are the linkages and options for action created, opened up and curtailed? The modern nation state has little or no capability to address the agricultural/food crisis. Tutorial3. INT354.learning_outcomes: On successful completion of the course, students will be able to:  Acquaint themselves with the historical positionality of nuclear issues in world politics and learn to critically engage with key issues and concepts in nuclear strategy, non-proliferation, and the nuclear social world.  To understand the nuclear fuel cycle activities and understand their interface with global politics, security, and society.  Learn various mainstream and critical approaches in nuclear politics, including anti-nuclear and peace narratives and their contemporary significance.  Critically identify and evaluate technological capabilities and limitations of deterrence as a policy instrument.  Assess nuclear security as a “sub-discipline” within the International Relations field and prepare for the world of peace and policy advocacy.
INT354.objectives: The course aims to help students reach a broader understanding of the nuclear issues in global politics. It seeks to illuminate the positionality of nuclear science and technology in international politics as well as in our social lives. The overall aim is to show why history matters and how it connects the past with present challenges and future atomic imaginaries.
INT354.program_learning_goals: Since the discovery of atomic radioactivity in the early 20th century, nuclear technologies have shaped our world in multifaceted ways and have proven consequential to everyone, from medical practitioners to military planners. While medical practitioners used radiation to treat wounded soldiers, strategic planners resorted to the logic of deterrence to prevent the outbreak of a great war. The atomic age thus engendered a world divided between doctrines of “mutually assured destruction” (MAD) alongside the campaigns for a “world free of nuclear weapons”. Throughout the Cold War, nuclear strategic thought rationalised the possession of atomic weapons, while the political economy of atomic energy enabled the commercial race to construct nuclear power plants. The strategic utility of atomic weapons, together with peaceful atomic energy applications, has been the defining element of the post-war global nuclear order. The course aims to go beyond the narrow conceptions of nuclear order defined merely in terms of the power distribution among states to engage with questions of justice and equity in the nuclear world. To tackle the concerns of order and justice in the nuclear realm, the course will devote attention to both the essentialisation of atomic weapons as well as contestations grounded in agency, identity, and representation to discuss peace campaigns, the effects and affects of radioactive exposure, the tropes of “coloniality”, “domination”, and “control” in the nuclear order. In doing so, the course will explore perspectives on radiation protection, atomic warfare, non-proliferation regimes, nuclear social movements, and gender and intersectionality in a nuclear world. Through its interdisciplinary focus and eclectic coverage of issues and perspectives, the course aspires to offer a comprehensive introduction to global atomic politics, enabling students to develop their core interest areas and prepare them for advanced learning and research.

INT363.introduction: Images play a crucial role in defining perceptions of an international event and our understanding of global politics. Following the ‘visual turn’ in the discipline of IR and treating the visual as the site of power and representation we will examine not only how political narratives and conflicts shape what images people see and how they make sense of them but also how the political field itself is visually constituted. The objective of this course will be to examine how visual sources- photographs, maps, cartoons and films – influence international political phenomena. We will also take up fundamental theoretical questions about the place of affect and the senses in political life.
INT363.learning_outcomes: To understand and evaluate how the focus on the ‘visual’ began to intervene in the discipline and what prompted this intervention in knowledge production. • Critically examine how what is seen/unseen shape international organizations, states and security dynamics. • Understand and draw on visual evidence to present a critically engaged argument on world politics.

Use derivatives to find local maxima and minima and apply them to curve sketching and optimization problems. 5. Understand definite integration as capturing the notion of area, and be able to calculate or estimate integrals 6. Set up and solve separable first order differential equations.

MAT2004.introduction: Probability is the means by which we model the inherent randomness of natural phenomena. This course introduces you to a range of techniques for understanding randomness and variability, and for understanding relationships between quantities. The concluding portions on Statistics take up the problem of testing our theoretical models against actual data, as well as applying the models to data in order to make decisions.
MAT2004.learning_outcomes: By the end of the course, students will be able to: 1. Apply basic principles of probability to solve problems involving events and sample spaces. 2. Work with discrete and continuous random variables and their distributions. 3. Compute and interpret expectation, variance, and covariance. 4. Analyze standard probability distributions such as Binomial, Poisson, and Normal. 5. Apply Central Limit Theorem and basic estimation techniques, including MLE. 6. Construct and interpret confidence intervals for population parameters. 7. Perform hypothesis testing and interpret results using p-values and significance levels. 8. Use statistical reasoning and computational tools to analyze data-driven problems.
MAT2004.objectives: 1. Introduce the fundamentals of probability, including sample spaces, events, and axioms. 2. Develop understanding of random variables and common probability distributions. 3. Build skills in computing expectation, variance, and covariance. 4. Study standard distributions such as Binomial, Poisson, and Normal. 5. Introduce statistical inference, including estimation and MLE. 6. Enable construction and interpretation of confidence intervals. 7. Develop understanding of hypothesis testing and p-values. 8. Apply statistical methods to solve problems and use basic computational tools.
MAT2004.skill_development: This course helps students develop the following skills: 1. Problem-solving skills in probability and statistical reasoning. 2. Analytical skills for modeling uncertainty using random variables and distributions. 3. Computational skills for evaluating statistical measures and performing inference. 4. Data interpretation skills through estimation, confidence intervals, and hypothesis testing. 5. Application skills using statistical tools such as Excel and R. 6. Logical thinking and mathematical reasoning for real-world data analysis problems.

MAT230.introduction: Ordinary Differential Equations (ODEs) constitute one of the fundamental mathematical tools for describing dynamical processes in nature, engineering, economics, and the life sciences. They provide mathematical models for systems whose behaviour changes with respect to time or space, including population growth, mechanical vibrations, electrical circuits, chemical reactions, and disease transmission. This course introduces both the theoretical foundations and practical solution techniques for ordinary differential equations. Students will learn analytical methods for solving first-order and higher-order differential equations, systems of differential equations, power series solutions, and Laplace transform techniques. The course also emphasizes qualitative analysis of dynamical systems and mathematical modelling, enabling students to connect mathematical theory with applications in physics, biology, engineering, and other scientific disciplines.
MAT230.learning_outcomes: Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to: LO1. Solve first-order ordinary differential equations using analytical techniques including separable, exact, integrating factor, and Bernoulli methods. LO2. Explain the concepts of existence and uniqueness of solutions and interpret their significance in mathematical modelling. LO3. Solve higher-order linear differential equations using complementary functions, particular integrals, variation of parameters, Euler–Cauchy methods, and undetermined coefficients. LO4. Determine linear independence of solutions using the Wronskian and construct general solutions of linear differential equations. LO5. Analyze systems of ordinary differential equations using eigenvalue methods, phase plane analysis, equilibrium points, and stability concepts. LO6. Obtain series solutions of differential equations using power series and Frobenius methods. LO7. Apply Laplace transform techniques to solve initial value problems involving ordinary differential equations. LO8. Formulate and interpret mathematical models of real-world phenomena using ordinary differential equations and critically evaluate the resulting solutions.
MAT230.objectives: The objectives of this course are to enable students to: Understand the mathematical theory underlying ordinary differential equations and the existence and uniqueness of solutions. Master analytical techniques for solving first-order and higher-order ordinary differential equations. Develop the ability to formulate mathematical models for problems arising in science and engineering. Analyze systems of differential equations using qualitative methods, phase plane analysis, and stability theory. Apply power series and Frobenius methods to obtain solutions near ordinary and singular points. Use Laplace transform techniques to solve initial value problems efficiently. Develop mathematical reasoning, analytical thinking, and problem-solving skills through theoretical and applied examples.
MAT230.program_learning_goals: Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to: Develop a rigorous understanding of the theory and methods of ordinary differential equations. Apply mathematical reasoning to formulate, analyze, and solve real-world problems arising in science and engineering. Select appropriate analytical techniques for solving first-order, higher-order, and systems of differential equations. Interpret qualitative behaviour of dynamical systems using mathematical concepts such as equilibria, stability, and phase portraits. Build mathematical models for physical, biological, and engineering systems and critically evaluate their assumptions and limitations. Develop logical thinking, quantitative reasoning, and problem-solving skills essential for advanced studies in mathematics and allied disciplines.
MAT230.skill_development: The course develops the following academic and professional skills: Mathematical modelling of real-world systems. Analytical and logical reasoning. Quantitative problem solving. Mathematical proof and rigorous reasoning. Interpretation of dynamical systems. Scientific computing readiness. Critical thinking and abstraction. Communication of mathematical ideas through written solutions and presentations. Independent learning and collaborative problem solving during tutorials and assignments.

MAT360.introduction: MAT360: Linear Algebra–II is an advanced undergraduate course that develops the structural theory of finite-dimensional vector spaces and linear transformations. Building on the introductory linear algebra course, it moves from computational techniques such as row reduction and matrix manipulation to an abstract treatment of vector spaces over arbitrary fields. The course studies how a linear transformation can be represented, simplified, and classified through a suitable choice of basis. Particular emphasis is placed on dual spaces, determinants, invariant subspaces, characteristic and minimal polynomials, primary decomposition, rational canonical form, and Jordan canonical form. The final part develops the theory of finite-dimensional inner product spaces, adjoint operators, unitary and normal operators, and the finite-dimensional spectral theorem. Throughout the course, abstract results will be supported by explicit matrix computations, proof-based exercises, and problem-solving tutorials. The course therefore provides both the theoretical foundation and computational techniques required for advanced courses in algebra, analysis, differential equations, numerical analysis, operator theory, and related areas.
MAT360.learning_outcomes: On successful completion of the course, students will be able to: 1. Solve systems of linear equations using row reduction and interpret their solution sets in terms of rank, nullity, consistency, and affine subspaces. 2. Work with abstract vector spaces, subspaces, bases, coordinates, dimensions, and direct-sum decompositions over arbitrary fields. 3. Determine the kernel, range, rank, and nullity of a linear transformation and construct its matrix relative to prescribed bases. 4. Analyse how the matrix of a linear transformation changes under a change of basis and recognize similarity as the matrix form of basis independence. 5. Work with dual spaces, double duals, linear functionals, transpose transformations, and dual bases. 6. Define and compute determinants and apply their principal properties to questions of invertibility, eigenvalues, and characteristic polynomials. 7. Identify invariant subspaces and determine whether a family of operators is simultaneously triangularizable or diagonalizable. 8. Compute characteristic and minimal polynomials and use them to analyse the spectral and algebraic structure of a linear transformation. 9. Apply the primary decomposition theorem and the theory of cyclic subspaces to obtain rational and Jordan canonical forms. 10. Work with inner products, orthogonality, orthonormal bases, adjoint operators, and unitary transformations. 11. Characterize normal, self-adjoint, and unitary operators and apply the finite-dimensional spectral theorem. 12. Present clear, logically complete proofs and combine abstract arguments with explicit matrix computations
MAT360.objectives: The course is designed to: 1. Develop an abstract understanding of finite-dimensional vector spaces over arbitrary fields. 2. Strengthen students’ understanding of linear transformations and their matrix representations relative to different bases. 3. Introduce dual spaces, double duals, transpose transformations, and their relationships with the original vector space. 4. Develop the determinant systematically using permutations and its defining algebraic properties. 5. Study invariant subspaces and polynomial methods for analysing linear transformations. 6. Establish the primary decomposition theorem and use cyclic subspaces to derive rational and Jordan canonical forms. 7. Develop the structure of finite-dimensional inner product spaces and the theory of adjoint, unitary, self-adjoint, and normal operators. 8. Prove and apply finite-dimensional spectral theorems. 9. Improve students’ ability to construct rigorous mathematical arguments and connect abstract theory with concrete matrix calculations.
MAT360.program_learning_goals: • Generalise the concept of vectors in R^n to a more abstract framework. • Define the elementary concepts of linear span, dimension, and subspace in the context of an abstract vector space. • Recognize that linear transformations are generalization of matrices. • Important facts in inner product spaces are established.
MAT360.skill_development: The course develops students’ abstract reasoning, computational proficiency, and proof-writing skills in linear algebra. Students learn to analyse linear transformations, perform change-of-basis and canonical-form computations, interpret spectral properties, and connect abstract theory with concrete matrix problems. Tutorials and group discussions further strengthen problem-solving, mathematical communication, and collaborative learning skills.

MAT494.introduction: This course provides a rigorous introduction to Deep Learning from a mathematical perspective. Rather than treating neural networks as black-box computational tools, the course develops the underlying mathematical principles governing learning algorithms, optimization, representation learning, and modern neural architectures. Beginning with the foundations of artificial neurons and multilayer networks, the course explores the role of linear algebra, calculus, probability, and optimization in understanding deep learning models. Topics include feedforward neural networks, backpropagation as an application of the chain rule, gradient-based optimization, regularization methods, convolutional neural networks, recurrent models, autoencoders, and generative architectures. The emphasis is on mathematical formulation, derivation of algorithms, geometric interpretation of learning, and implementation of deep learning models using computational frameworks. The course bridges theoretical foundations and practical applications in computer vision, sequence modeling, and scientific data analysis.
MAT494.learning_outcomes: After completing this course, students will be able to: 1. Explain the mathematical foundations of neural networks o Represent artificial neurons and multilayer networks using linear algebra. o Interpret neural networks as nonlinear function approximators. o Understand the role of activation functions and network depth. 2. Derive and analyze learning algorithms o Derive the backpropagation algorithm using multivariable calculus and the chain rule. o Explain gradient descent and variants from an optimization perspective. o Analyze loss functions and convergence behavior. 3. Understand optimization principles in deep learning o Formulate training as a high-dimensional optimization problem. o Compare stochastic gradient descent, momentum methods, and adaptive optimization algorithms. o Understand challenges such as saddle points, vanishing gradients, and exploding gradients. 4. Apply mathematical ideas behind deep architectures o Explain convolutional networks using linear operators, filters, and feature maps. o Analyze recurrent networks using dynamical systems concepts. o Understand representation learning and dimensionality reduction. 5. Understand regularization and generalization o Explain overfitting and model complexity. o Analyze regularization techniques including dropout, weight decay, and normalization. o Connect deep learning with statistical learning principles. 6. Develop computational implementations o Implement neural networks from mathematical formulations. o Translate equations into Python-based computational models. o Experiment with model training, evaluation, and visualization. 7. Explore advanced mathematical viewpoints o Interpret deep networks through geometry and transformations. o Understand energy-based and generative models. o Relate modern deep learning to approximation theory and optimization.
MAT494.objectives: **Course Objectives (Deep Learning – Mathematical Approach)** By the end of this course, students will be able to: 1. **Understand the mathematical foundations of deep learning** through concepts from linear algebra, calculus, optimization, probability, and information theory. 2. **Analyze artificial neural networks mathematically**, including perceptrons, multilayer networks, activation functions, loss functions, and learning mechanisms. 3. **Derive and implement learning algorithms** such as gradient descent, stochastic optimization, and backpropagation using mathematical principles. 4. **Study the approximation and representation capabilities of deep neural networks** and understand their theoretical foundations. 5. **Explore major deep learning architectures** including convolutional neural networks, recurrent neural networks, and autoencoders from both theoretical and applied perspectives. 6. **Apply regularization and optimization techniques** to improve model performance, stability, and generalization. 7. **Develop the ability to connect deep learning models with real-world applications** while critically evaluating their limitations and interpretability.
MAT494.skill_development: **Skills Developed** On successful completion of this course, students will develop the ability to: 1. **Mathematical Modeling Skills** * Formulate machine learning problems using concepts from linear algebra, calculus, optimization, and probability. 2. **Algorithmic Thinking and Problem-Solving Skills** * Understand, derive, and design learning algorithms based on mathematical principles. 3. **Computational and Programming Skills** * Implement neural network models, optimization methods, and deep learning architectures using modern computational tools. 4. **Data-Driven Decision-Making Skills** * Analyze datasets, extract meaningful patterns, evaluate models, and make evidence-based predictions. 5. **Optimization and Analytical Skills** * Apply gradient-based methods, loss minimization techniques, and regularization strategies for solving complex problems. 6. **AI Model Development Skills** * Build, train, validate, and improve deep learning models for applications involving images, text, signals, and structured data. 7. **Research and Innovation Skills** * Read and interpret contemporary deep learning research and extend mathematical ideas to new AI problems. 8. **Critical Evaluation Skills** * Assess model accuracy, robustness, limitations, generalization ability, and ethical implications of AI systems. 9. **Interdisciplinary Application Skills** * Apply deep learning techniques across domains such as science, finance, healthcare, engineering, and digital humanities.

MED2001.introduction: This course introduces the fundamental relationships between the structure, properties, and performance of engineering materials. It covers crystal structures, atomic arrangements, and techniques used to determine material structures, along with various crystal imperfections and their influence on material behavior. The course also examines phase diagrams and phase transformations that govern the development of microstructures in materials. Students learn the mechanisms of diffusion, nucleation, and grain growth, as well as the principles of plastic deformation in crystalline solids. Finally, the course explores key strengthening mechanisms, including grain boundary strengthening, solid-solution strengthening, precipitation hardening, and strain hardening, which are used to enhance the mechanical properties of materials. Through these topics, students develop a foundational understanding of how materials can be engineered for specific applications.
MED2001.learning_outcomes: Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to: • Explain the crystal structures, atomic bonding, and crystallographic concepts of engineering materials, and interpret structural information obtained through X-ray diffraction techniques. • Analyze the role of crystal defects, dislocations, and diffusion processes in influencing the physical and mechanical properties of materials. • Interpret and apply phase diagrams and phase transformation principles to predict phase evolution, microstructure development, and material behavior under different processing conditions. • Evaluate the mechanisms of plastic deformation and strengthening in crystalline materials, and relate microstructural features to the mechanical performance of engineering materials.
MED2001.objectives: • To provide students with a fundamental understanding of the crystal structure, atomic arrangement, and bonding in engineering materials, and their influence on material properties. • To enable students to analyze crystal imperfections, including point defects and dislocations, and understand their role in determining the mechanical behaviour of materials. • To provide students with knowledge of phase diagrams and phase trans-formations, enabling them to predict microstructural evolution during material processing and heat treatment. • To enable students to understand the mechanisms of diffusion, nucleation, grain growth, and plastic deformation in crystalline materials, and their effects on material performance. • To provide students with an understanding of the various strengthening mechanisms used in engineering materials and the ability to relate microstructure to mechanical properties for materials design and selection.
MED2001.program_learning_goals: (1) Competent mechanical engineers with sound fundamental knowledge of material science concepts (2) To enable students apply material science concepts in solving real world problems (3) To enhance skill-set of students and equip them with cutting-edge research and strategic capabilities
MED2001.skill_development: (1) This course helps students in designing or selecting materials for a specific application such as aerospace, biomedical, electronics etc. (2) Trains the students in failure analysis i.e understanding why a particular material or product failed and how to improve it. (3) Provides hands-on training on various instruments and synthesis techniques.

MED2004.introduction: Fluid Mechanics is the study of fluids either at rest (fluid statics) or in motion (fluid dynamics). The aim of the course is to present enough fundamental concepts and applications so that the student develops an interest to move into the specialized fields of science of flow. The course mainly deals with the three basic approaches for analysis of arbitrary flow problems: control volume (integral), differential, and experimental analyses. The concepts discussed in the classroom can be verified experimentally in the laboratory. Students will be evaluated through multiple theory exams and a lab exam.
MED2004.learning_outcomes: On successful completion of the course, students will be able to: • Analyse fluid flow systems by using principles of conservation of mass, momentum and energy. • Apply the concept of dimensional analysis and similarity for experimental modelling of a scaled system.
MED2004.objectives: The course aims to equip students with basic principles and methodologies for carrying out analysis of engineering systems with fluid dynamical sub-systems. The following are the major objectives of this course: • To provide a strong foundation of the basic principles and governing equations of fluid mechanics. • To provide the intuition necessary for the correct application of fluid mechanics principles in engineering systems. • To provide experiential learning through verification of the basic fluid mechanics principles in the laboratory.
MED2004.skill_development: On successful completion of the course, students will be able to: • Analyse fluid flow systems by using principles of conservation of mass, momentum and energy. • Apply the concept of dimensional analysis and similarity for experimental modelling of a scaled system.

MED303.introduction: Heat is defined as the flow of energy due to a temperature gradient. The science of heat transfer is concerned with estimating the rate at which heat is transported, the time of heating and cooling for a specific heat duty. There are three distinct modes in which heat transmission can take place: conduction, radiation and convection. The course emphasizes both analytical and practical aspects, preparing students to apply heat and mass transfer concepts in real-world engineering problems. Students would learn the fundamentals of the subject during the class hours. Students would be evaluated based on their performance in quiz, practical exam, viva-voce, mid-term and end-term examinations of the subject.
MED303.learning_outcomes: On successful completion of the course, students will be able to: (Knowledge based) • Explain the fundamental concepts of heat and mass transfer • Apply the fundamental knowledge of heat transfer mechanisms, namely conduction, convection and radiation to analyse different engineering applications. • Design and evaluate the performance of heat exchangers. • Apply the fundamental knowledge of mass transfer
MED303.objectives: • To cover the basic principles of heat and mass transfer • To provide students with engineering examples from the real world to illustrate how heat transfer is applied in engineering practice. • To apply the principles of mass transfer in various engineering applications. • To design and evaluate heat exchangers and other thermal systems
MED303.program_learning_goals: 1. Develop competent Mechanical Engineers with a strong foundation of knowledge. 2. Foster transformed individuals who are not just informed, but capable of applying their knowledge strategically
MED303.skill_development: Analytical skills for heat transfer analysis will be developed. Skills to experiment on heat transfer equipment will be devoped.

MED403.introduction: The global demand for energy is projected to nearly double by 2050. However, the finite reserves of fossil fuels will be insufficient to meet this growing demand in a sustainable manner. Furthermore, the extensive use of fossil fuels has significant adverse impacts on the environment, including greenhouse gas emissions and climate change. Therefore, there is an urgent need to develop and promote renewable energy technologies that are both cost-effective and highly efficient. Among the various renewable energy sources, solar energy is one of the most promising due to its abundance, sustainability, and minimal environmental impact. Harnessing solar energy plays a vital role in achieving global energy security and environmental sustainability. Solar Energy is offered as an elective course by the Department of Mechanical Engineering. The course provides students with both theoretical knowledge and practical exposure to solar energy systems. Classroom lectures are complemented by visits to relevant solar energy installations and facilities, enabling students to gain hands-on experience with real-world applications. Students' performance in the course will be evaluated through mid-term and end-term examinations, along with other assessment components as prescribed by the department.
MED403.learning_outcomes: On successful completion of the course, students will be able to: • Explain the fundamentals of solar radiation, solar geometry, and the potential of solar energy as a renewable energy source. • Identify and describe the working principles, components, and applications of solar thermal and solar photovoltaic (PV) systems. • Analyze the performance of solar energy systems using appropriate engineering principles and performance parameters. • Evaluate the techno-economic feasibility and environmental benefits of solar energy systems compared to conventional energy sources. • Conduct experiments on solar energy devices, interpret experimental data, and prepare technical reports. • Demonstrate awareness of current trends, policies, and challenges in the deployment of solar energy technologies for sustainable development.
MED403.objectives: This course aims to: • Provide students with a fundamental understanding of solar energy resources, solar radiation, and their significance in sustainable energy systems. • Introduce the principles, technologies, and applications of solar thermal and solar photovoltaic (PV) energy conversion systems. • Develop students' ability to analyze, design, and evaluate basic solar energy systems for residential, commercial, and industrial applications. • Familiarize students with the performance characteristics, economic aspects, and environmental benefits of solar energy technologies. • Enhance practical knowledge through laboratory experiments, field visits, and case studies involving solar energy systems. • Promote awareness of national and global renewable energy policies, challenges, and opportunities related to solar energy deployment. • Encourage students to apply engineering knowledge to develop sustainable and energy-efficient solutions using solar technologies.
MED403.program_learning_goals: By the end of the course, students will be able to: Understand Solar Energy Fundamentals Demonstrate a sound understanding of solar radiation, solar geometry, and the principles of solar energy conversion technologies. Analyze Solar Energy Systems Analyze the performance of solar thermal systems using engineering principles and performance metrics. Design Solar Energy Solutions Design and size solar energy systems for residential, commercial, agricultural, and industrial applications based on energy demand and local climatic conditions. Apply Modern Engineering Tools Develop Problem-Solving Skills Identify and solve real-world renewable energy challenges by integrating scientific knowledge with engineering design methodologies.
MED403.skill_development: After completing the Solar Energy course, students will be able to: Solar Resource Assessment Measure, interpret, and analyze solar radiation data for different geographical locations. System Design and Sizing Design and size solar thermal systems based on energy demand and climatic conditions. Performance Analysis Evaluate the efficiency and performance of solar collectors, and complete solar energy systems using engineering principles. Simulation and Software Skills Experimental and Laboratory Skills Conduct experiments, collect data, analyze results, and prepare technical reports on solar energy systems. Problem-Solving and Optimization Identify technical issues in solar installations and recommend appropriate solutions to improve system efficiency and reliability.

MED410.introduction: Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) is the science of predicting the behaviour of a fluid flow through the numerical solution of the equations of motion that govern the flow. This course will focus on the terminology, principles and methods of CFD. It can be applied in many areas of engineering, including aerodynamics, hydrodynamics, air-conditioning, combustion, minerals processing, etc. The objective of this course to make students become coders and knowledgeable users of CFD software.
MED410.learning_outcomes: On successful completion of the course, students will be able to: • Know how to create mathematical model of a given problem for CFD related solution. • Develop skills to write codes for the mathematical model derived. • Develop attitude to make proper choices and judgement based on sound principles for simulating CFD model. • Develop skills to understand and work on CFD software.
MED410.objectives: • To provide students with information on how to derive basic equations of the model to be used for CFD analysis. • To provide students with basic knowledge of CFD modelling and simulations. • To provide students with knowledge about how to write codes for solving the mathematical model for CFD problem. • To provide students with knowledge about how to use CFD software like FLUENT.
MED410.skill_development: On successful completion of the course, students will be able to: • Know how to create mathematical model of a given problem for CFD related solution. • Develop skills to write codes for the mathematical model derived. • Develop attitude to make proper choices and judgement based on sound principles for simulating CFD model. • Develop skills to understand and work on CFD software.
