MED416.introduction: This course is meant to give students the basic skills needed to understand robot motion along with the ability to put together the hardware and software and integrate it into a working robot that performs a specific task.
MED416.learning_outcomes: On successful completion of the course, students will be able to: • Build a robot. • Write the code to control that allows it to perceive its environment and autonomously plan and execute motion to achieve the goal.
MED416.objectives: This course is meant to be a continuation of “Industrial automation” course and is meant to impart in-depth understanding of robot motion. The general framework necessary to understand a vast majority of industrial and mobile robots is covered. The project and practical are clubbed into one unit. Teams composing of 4 members each will execute the project; they will simultaneously attend practical sessions that support their project. Being a hands-on course requiring constant input from instructors there will be little difference between practical’s and project. Exercises on individual aspects of the robot both hardware and software will be covered in practical’s. Skills acquired in these sessions will be tested continuously in the form of experiments administered on a weekly basis during the practical’s. Also the application of these skills in the different stages of project will also be evaluated through a series of presentations delivered on the project.
MED416.program_learning_goals: Robotics finds applications through the entire spectrum of the manufacturing industry. The course is offered as an elective as part of the "Robotics and Automation" specialization track offered by the department. It also serves as an integral course in the interdepartmental specialization "Cognitive Robotics"

MGT211.introduction: The course is set in the context of renewable resource extraction, pollution generation, and nonrenewable resource depletion and the role of industries in sustaining them without affecting future generations' needs. This course aims to provide students with the necessary skills to make well-informed judgments and take immediate action that will conserve the environment while being economically viable. The principles of sustainability will be reviewed, and their application to energy, climate change, urban planning, transportation, water use, ecosystem services, and social equity will be considered. Examples from both developed and developing economies will be discussed and compared.
MGT211.learning_outcomes: Knowledge: Students Will Be Able To: 1.Explain Core Concepts Of Sustainability, Including Ecological Limits, Systems Thinking, Planetary Boundaries, Circular Economy, Pollution Management And The Un Sustainable Development Goals (Sdgs). 2.Analyze The Interdependence Of Environmental, Social, And Economic Systems In Local, Regional, And Global Contexts. 3.Evaluate Sustainability Challenges Such As Climate Change, Biodiversity Loss, Resource Depletion, And Social Inequity Using Interdisciplinary Frameworks. 4.Identify Regulatory Frameworks, Policies, And Instruments That Promote Sustainable Development. 5.Understand Life Cycle Thinking And The Environmental Impacts Of Products, Processes, And Behaviors From Cradle To Grave. 6.Understand Industrial Efficiency Relevant To Sustainable Development. Skills 1.Apply Systems Thinking Tools (Causal Loop Diagrams, Material Flow Analysis, Sankey Diagrams) To Map And Assess Sustainability Issues. 2.Conduct Sustainability Assessments, Including Carbon Footprint, Life Cycle Assessment (Lca), Water Footprint, And Sustainability Audits. 3.Communicate Sustainability Findings Effectively Through Written Reports, Visualizations, And Public Presentations Tailored To Diverse Audiences. Attitudes: 1.Demonstrate A Commitment To Ethical And Responsible Action For Sustainability And Intergenerational Equity. 2.Develop A Mindset Of Innovation And Adaptability To Address Complex Sustainability Problems.
MGT211.objectives: 1.To enable students to describe Socio-Political Information Related To The field of Environmental Sustainability. 2. To develop student skills in identification of information related to the field of Environmental Sustainability. 3. To enable students to investigate sustainable development issues in India. 4. To enable students to summarize the role of industries in Environmental Sustainability. 5. To enable students to discuss various paths to sustainable development locally and globally.

MGT211.skill_development: 1.Apply Systems Thinking Tools (Causal Loop Diagrams, Material Flow Analysis, Sankey Diagrams) To Map And Assess Sustainability Issues. 2.Conduct Sustainability Assessments, Including Carbon Footprint, Life Cycle Assessment (Lca), Water Footprint, And Sustainability Audits. 3.Communicate Sustainability Findings Effectively Through Written Reports, Visualizations, And Public Presentations Tailored To Diverse Audiences. Develop analytical framework helpful to identify and resolve ethical issues in business 3. Practice decision making on ethical issues, scripting solution and managing them. 4. MGT301.program_learning_goals: This course is a study of ethical problems in business and the foundations for decisions involving ethical issues. Topics include ethical concepts, personal integrity, company loyalty and responsibility conflicts as they impact on the decision process in the functional areas of business. This course is designed to inform and stimulate thinking on the ethical issues encountered in business and to help prepare students recognize and manage these issues in their future career. Using a rich mix of case studies, articles, role playing exercises, video, movie clippings and contemporary examples this course explores the ethical challenges of a global business environment from the perspective of a manager and business leaders. Students will develop a sense of critical thinking and appreciate alternative approaches and perspectives on managing ethical issues in business and in different organizational and social set ups.

MKT402.introduction: Effective communication with target audiences is crucial for brand success. Rapid technological change, digital platforms and evolving consumer behaviour have transformed the marketing communication landscape. Organizations today must integrate multiple communication tools such as advertising, sales promotion, digital media, public relations and direct marketing to deliver consistent brand messages. This course focuses on planning and managing Integrated Marketing Communication (IMC) strategies. Students learn how organizations design communication campaigns, select appropriate media, develop persuasive messages and evaluate promotional effectiveness using managerial frameworks.
MKT402.learning_outcomes: Students will be able to: 1. Explain the concept and strategic role of Integrated Marketing Communications in marketing management. 2. Analyse consumer behaviour and cultural influences while developing communication strategies 3. Evaluate traditional and digital media alternatives in marketing communication planning. 4. Develop strategic communication recommendations using analytical frameworks. (mapped to PLO – 3.2)
MKT402.objectives: 1. To develop a clear understanding of Integrated Marketing Communications and its role in building consistent and effective brand messages. 2. To enable students to analyse and integrate traditional, digital and emerging communication tools for strategic decision-making. 3. To Develop the ability to make strategic communication decisions regarding media, messaging and promotional tools.
MKT402.program_learning_goals: 1. Develop effective communication abilities to thrive in a collaborative environment 2. Develop a reasoning ability using analytical and logical thinking skills to provide solutions to existing problems in an integrated environment 3. Develop an entrepreneurial ability to create, innovate, and provide solutions to an existing problem in an integrated environment. 4. Analyze assumptions by evaluating evidence for effective business decision-making 5. Understand new technologies and their importance in driving innovation for future growth opportunities 6. Sensitize towards legal, ethical & sustainability aspects of decision- making for positive business outcomes and social impact

MKT409.introduction: In today's rapidly evolving digital ecosystem, social media has become a strategic marketing tool that shapes how organizations engage with customers, build brands, and create business value. Social media marketing has evolved far beyond creating content, increasing follower counts, or mastering individual platforms. It now operates at the intersection of consumer behavior, technology, data analytics, culture, ethics, and managerial decision-making. This course provides a comprehensive foundation in social media marketing by equipping students with the knowledge and skills to design, implement, manage, and evaluate effective social media marketing strategies while addressing the strategic, ethical, and technological challenges of today's dynamic digital environment.
MKT409.learning_outcomes: CLO1: Ensure the students understand the fundamental concepts, frameworks, and strategic role of social media marketing. CLO2: Design and implement integrated social media marketing strategies by developing target audience personas, creating engaging content, selecting appropriate social media platforms, and leveraging influencer marketing and emerging digital technologies. CLO3: Analyze the performance of social media marketing campaigns using relevant metrics and analytics, and recommend improvements while considering ethical and responsible marketing practices.
MKT409.objectives: This course aims to develop the following learning objectives: 1. Understand the evolution of social media and its role in modern marketing. 2. Design and implement effective social media marketing strategies by identifying target audiences, creating engaging content, selecting appropriate platforms, and integrating social media with broader marketing objectives. 3. Evaluate the effectiveness of social media marketing through several performance metrics and support data driven managerial decisions. 4. To understand the ethical, legal and emerging technological considerations to develop responsible and innovative social media marketing solutions for business challenges.
MKT409.program_learning_goals: 1. To develop a comprehensive understanding of social media marketing. 2. To learn how to design and execute integrated social media marketing strategies. 3. To strengthen analytical and decison making skills.
MKT409.school: SME - School of Management and Entrepreneurship
MKT409.skill_development: Through this course the students will develop the following skills: 1. Strategic Thinking. 2. Develop social media marketing strategies to meet marketing objectives. 3. Learn how to create social media pages and how to design ad campaigns.

PHY305.learning_outcomes: Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to explain the fundamental principles of quantum mechanics, apply the formalism of linear algebra to analyse quantum systems and their state descriptions, solve problems involving quantum measurements and time evolution, and interpret the counterintuitive features of quantum theory. They will also be prepared to undertake advanced courses where quantum mechanics forms the theoretical foundation.
PHY305.objectives: This course aims to follow up on the development in Introduction to Quantum Mechanics (PHY202) with more advanced topics in the fundamental subject of Quantum Mechanics, such as the Schrödinger, Heisenberg, and Interaction (Dirac) pictures; Theory of Angular Momentum; Time-Independent Perturbation Theory and the Variational Principle. It starts with reviewing the basic concepts and surprises in Quantum Mechanics (QM). This course, together with the next advanced course (PHY306: Quantum mechanics – II), would ideally prepare students at a Graduate QM level, ready to go into research, and is ideal for students interested in going into the 4th-year extension into B.Sc. Research. It can also be of interest to certain students in Chemistry, Mathematics or some branches of Engineering, provided they have the necessary background.
PHY305.program_learning_goals: The goal of this course is to introduce the technical and conceptual aspects of quantum mechanics. Starting from the very basic formalism of quantum mechanics based on linear algebra, the course will gradually train the students in some advanced techniques of quantum mechanics.
PHY305.skill_development: This course will develop the problem-solving and analytical skills required for quantum mechanics. Students will be able to identify the counter-intuitive aspects of quantum mechanics, solve basic problems involving quantum measurements and dynamics using tools from linear algebra, and ultimately prepare themselves for higher studies and research in physics, where quantum mechanics is an essential tool.

PHY307.introduction: PHY307: Electronics-II introduces the fundamental principles and practical implementation of digital electronic systems. Building upon the concepts of analog electronics covered in PHY206, the course focuses on number systems, Boolean algebra, logic gates, combinational and sequential logic circuits, counters, registers, multiplexers, converters, and digital logic families. The course integrates theoretical concepts with extensive laboratory practice, enabling students to understand, analyze, design, and implement digital electronic circuits used in modern computing, communication, instrumentation, and embedded systems.
PHY307.learning_outcomes: After successfully completing the course, students will be able to: 1: Explain digital number systems, logic levels, Boolean algebra, and logic gate operations. 2: Analyze and simplify complex digital circuits using Boolean algebra and Karnaugh Maps. 3: Design combinational logic circuits including adders, parity generators/checkers, multiplexers, demultiplexers, and comparators. 4: Design and analyze sequential logic circuits including latches, flip-flops, counters, and shift registers. 5: Explain the operation of A/D and D/A converters and compare various digital logic families such as TTL and CMOS. 6: Construct, test, and troubleshoot digital electronic circuits using laboratory equipment and integrated circuits.
PHY307.objectives: The course aims to: • Introduce the principles of digital electronics and their advantages over analog systems. • Develop proficiency in Boolean algebra and logic simplification techniques. • Enable students to design and analyze combinational and sequential logic circuits. • Familiarize students with memory devices, counters, registers, multiplexers, and converters. • Provide hands-on laboratory experience in designing and testing digital circuits. • Prepare students for advanced courses in embedded systems, microprocessors, digital communication, and computer architecture.
PHY307.program_learning_goals: On successful completion of the Physics undergraduate program, students will be able to: 1. Develop a strong foundation in fundamental concepts of physics and electronics. 2. Apply mathematical and scientific principles to analyze and solve engineering and physical science problems. 3. Design, analyze, and troubleshoot analog and digital electronic circuits. 4. Develop experimental skills using modern laboratory instruments and electronic components. 5. Communicate scientific ideas effectively through technical reports, presentations, and teamwork.
PHY307.skill_development: Upon completion of the course, students will acquire: Technical Skills • Boolean logic implementation • Digital circuit design • Circuit simplification • IC identification and testing • Digital troubleshooting • Timing analysis • Digital system design Laboratory Skills • Breadboard implementation • Oscilloscope usage • Logic probe utilization • Signal generation • Digital IC interfacing • Experimental verification Analytical Skills • Logical reasoning • Problem-solving • Circuit optimization • Error analysis • Hardware debugging Professional Skills • Teamwork • Technical documentation • Experimental reporting • Scientific communication • Engineering design thinking

PHY560.introduction: The high energy particle physics is the subject where we explore the subatomic structure of nature as relativistic quantum theories. The lecturer introduces critical experimental results and theoretical concepts in this course. A highlight is the theoretical and empirical foundations of the standard model of particle physics. This course is offered for first-year graduate students and 4th-year undergraduate students, and thus, knowledge of quantum field theory (QFT) is NOT assumed as a prerequisite. Key points are explained during this course.
PHY560.learning_outcomes: 1. Gain a basic understanding of the fundamental structure of high energy physics 2. To be able to perform basic calculations on relativistic many-body quantum transitions, which is part of the basis for understanding the applications of particle reactions at high energies (e.g. Cosmology, Astrophysics, Nuclear Physics, etc.)
PHY560.objectives: 1. To undersntand fundamental concepts in high energy physics 2. To know how to calculate relativistic many-body problems 3. To be able to approximate physical quantities for various reactions. Especially, learn in detail about reactions in quantum electrodynamics
PHY560.program_learning_goals: This course will teach you the fundamentals of formalism necessary to understand quantum physics at high energy scales of approximately 1 GeV and above, going beyond a qualitative understanding to enabling you to perform specific quantitative probability calculations in the case of electromagnetic interactions. The knowledge you will acquire in this course will be useful in understanding quantum phenomena in general, where many particles interact at high energies (such as signals in high- energy accelerator experiments, fundamental particle reactions in celestial bodies and the early universe, etc.).
PHY560.skill_development: 1. Basic Calculation Of Relativistic Quantum Many-Body Systems 2. Applications Of Special Relativity

PHY565.introduction: The classical gravitational interaction is an integral part of the physical description of macroscopic objects, the full description of which was given by Einstein as the general theory of relativity. This theory is also a fruit of extensively pursuing an important viewpoint in physics, namely that the intrinsic properties of physical systems are independent of the choice of coordinate system. Not only does this theory include a theoretically interesting geometrisation of the laws of gravity, but the complete description of classical gravity provided by this theory is an indispensable tool for an accurate understanding of the stellar structures, the celestial motions, the time evolution of the universe and even the now widely used GPS system. The aim of the course is to cover the basics of General Relativity and to discuss its applications. The necessary mathematical tools will first be provided after a brief review of the prerequisite special relativity. Next, the core ideas of general relativity are introduced, and the Einstein equations are derived, which give an accurate description of classical gravity. Under specific conditions, we also confirm that the results are in approximate agreement with the conventional Newtonian gravity. In the remaining time, some of the important physical phenomena described by general relativity will be explained as time permits. Since this course deals with relatively advanced content (although no formal exercise time is planned), it assumes a reasonable amount of preparation and review by the students outside of class time. Grading will be based on the results of multiple homework assignments and two regular examinations (report submission, in-class examination or presentation, depending on progress and other factors).
PHY565.learning_outcomes: 1. The student can acquire important concepts in modern physics, such as the description of physical quantities in general coordinates and the geometrical description of gravity. 2. This course provides the necessary theoretical background, particularly for astrophysics, cosmology, and associated astrophysical/cosmological phenomena in high-energy physics.
PHY565.objectives: 1. To understand the methodology for describing physical systems in general coordinates. 2. To acquire the core ideas of general relativity and the methodology of its consequence, the complete description of classical gravity. 3. To understand some mathematical aspects of general relativity and some physical phenomena that general relativity can accurately discuss.
PHY565.program_learning_goals: Building upon a solid understanding of special relativity, students will grasp how extending its principles to the general realm leads to a precise description of gravitational interactions, along with the necessary mathematical tools for such a description. Furthermore, through several concrete examples, students will understand that general relativity becomes indispensable when gravity is strong.
PHY565.skill_development: 1. Basics Of Tensor Analysis In General Coordinate Systems 2. Its Applications To Gravitational Systems

SOC323.introduction: Welcome to "SOC 323: Kinship and Relatedness" for the Monsoon 2026 semester! What are the ties that bind and the ties that tear? How do we make families, friendships, and enemies? Indeed, how do ways of relating constitute ourselves and organize the world? This course takes up these fundamental questions through a captivating combination of classical and contemporary studies of kinship and relatedness. We will begin by exploring the classical foundational trends in the sociology and anthropology of kinship, grounding ourselves in a selection of widely renowned and relevant scholarly works. From there, the course shifts focus toward modern horizons, offering selections that examine new ways of relating, marriage, adoption, and diverse paths of family making. In our final segment, we will venture into the formation of friendship and animosity through theoretical studies and recent ethnographies. Our ultimate aim is to introduce you to the emerging debates and lively deliberations surrounding our changing notions of relatedness—particularly as they are reshaped by new technologies of communication. Together, we will look beyond traditional boundaries to discover how human connection is being fundamentally redefined in the modern world.
SOC323.learning_outcomes: 1. To be able to analyze how models of human connection have shifted from classical, structural kinship systems to modern, alternative ways of family-making and adoption. 2. To be able to evaluate the social mechanisms behind how we form families, friendships, and animosities, and how these relationships actively organize society. 3. Going forward, equipped to examine how modern communication technologies and emerging global debates actively alter, expand, and redefine the boundaries of human relatedness.
SOC323.objectives: To critically examine how human relationships—from classical family structures to modern digital networks, friendships, and animosities—shape individual identity and organize the social world.
SOC323.program_learning_goals: The program aims to transform how students understand the fundamental ties that organize human society. It guides students from classical structural and biological definitions of family toward contemporary, global perspectives on intimacy. Ultimately, the program challenges students to critically analyze how cutting-edge technologies, non-normative identities, and even interspecies relationships actively redefine what it means to belong.
SOC323.school: SHSS - School of Humanities and Social Sciences
SOC323.skill_development: Read and evaluate best known anthropological texts to extract core arguments about how diverse cultures build social ties. Connect broad theoretical concepts about family to real-world dynamics like digital communication and modern relationships. Trace and map how interpersonal networks—from friendships to animosities—shape broader social structures.

SOC414.introduction: Contemporary social and political theory has increasingly turned to the question of life itself. Building on the ancient Greek distinction between zoē (biological life) and bios (political or lived life), philosophers and anthropologists have asked how modern forms of power govern, value, and differentiate human life. This course traces these debates through the work of Michel Foucault, Lisa Stevenson, Hannah Arendt, Giorgio Agamben, João Biehl, Peter Locke, and Angela Garcia. The first half of the course examines the emergence of biopolitics and explores how governance extends into the management of bodies, populations, care, and abandonment. Moving from Foucault's analysis of biopower to Stevenson's ethnography of care in the Canadian Arctic, students examine the affective and psychic dimensions of governing life. The course then turns to Arendt's distinction between bios and zoē and Agamben's theory of bare life to explore what it means for life to become the object of political power. The second half of the course examines anthropological responses to these philosophical debates. Through Unfinished: The Anthropology of Becoming and Angela Garcia's ethnography of addiction and dispossession, students explore how people continue to create ethical lives, relationships, and futures amid violence, uncertainty, illness, and marginalization. The course ultimately asks not only how life is governed, but also how life is continually made, inhabited, and transformed.
SOC414.learning_outcomes: 1. Explain the major theoretical contributions of Foucault, Arendt, Agamben, Stevenson, Biehl, Locke, and Garcia. 2. Compare philosophical and anthropological approaches to the politics of life. 3. Apply theoretical concepts to the interpretation of ethnographic case studies. 4. Critically evaluate competing understandings of life, power, care, and ethics. 5. Construct clear, well-argued written and oral analyses that integrate theoretical and ethnographic evidence. 6. Design and complete an independent research paper engaging with the themes of the course.
SOC414.objectives: 1. Explain the major theoretical contributions of Foucault, Arendt, Agamben, Stevenson, Biehl, Locke, and Garcia. 2. SOE4801.introduction: This course is aimed at teaching students what is engineering all about. The diversity of applications and opportunities for Engineers in all walks of life is introduced. What do engineers do for living? Much of the engineering is aimed at answering two key questions: what to make? (Product Engineering) and how to make it? (Process Engineering). Of course, both these objectives must be realised in a sustainable and environmental-friendly manner. Engineers employ a range of tools including electro-mechanical methods, chemical reactions, biology and the whole range of processing operations to convert raw materials into useful desired products. Engineering is a highly interdisciplinary profession. The entire curriculum is aimed at equipping our students with the necessary tools to perform their professional duties in these two areas. The student should develop an awareness and appreciation of the challenges inherent in these two objectives including identifying the need of a product, specifications of the product and to engineer the process to make it in an economical, safe and sustainable manner. Since this is the first course for the UGs, this is more like a storytelling rather than relying on detailed mathematical analysis.
SOE4801.learning_outcomes: On Successful Completion Of This Course, Students Will Be Able To • Identify The Need Of A Product, Define It In Terms Of Technical Measurable Parameters. • Identify The Information Needed. What Kind Of Data Is Required? • What Raw Materials Are Required? In How Much Quantities? • Develop A Tentative Flow Sheet Showing The Elementary Steps Involved For Making A Product. • Identify The Effluents And The Possible Environmental Impact Of A Process, And Life Cycle Analysis Of The Plant. • Evaluate The Technical And Economic Feasibility Of The Overall Process
SOE4801.objectives: The primary objectives of this course are to • Develop an appreciation for the diversity of engineering applications in the modern society. • Develop an understanding of our basic tools used for analysing, synthesising and designing a product (ranging from bulk chemicals, speciality chemicals to all the way to the artificial organs and transplants, mobile phones, public transport system, communication and infrastructure) to tackle the engineering challenges of the new millennium) and to develop the required processes. • Appreciate the highly interdisciplinary nature of the discipline relying upon physics, chemistry, biology, data science and mathematics as the corner stones of engineering. • Engineering is all about answering questions like how much, how big or small, etc., so students should be fully conversant with the conversion of units from one system to another. • Impart the concepts of mechanics (Newton’s laws of motion), conservation of mass and energy and the auxiliary laws like Ohm’s law, quantum mechanical laws, etc. • Identify the constraints arising from thermodynamic aspects or from material properties, etc. • Familiarize with the code of conduct for engineers and develop effective communication strategies.
SOE4801.skill_development: Upon Successful Completion Of The Introduction To Engineering Course, Students Typically Develop A Strong Foundation In Both Technical And Professional Skills Essential For Further Studies And Future Careers In Engineering. Key Skill Areas Include: Fundamental Engineering Knowledge, Design And Innovation Skills, Role Of Sustanibility In Engineering, Basic Tools And Software Proficiency, Project Management And Time Management, Teamwork And Collaboration.

STM2001.learning_outcomes: On successful completion of the course, students will be able to: CLO 1. Explain core concepts, processes, and roles associated with entrepreneurship and early-stage venture creation. CLO 2. Identify and frame entrepreneurial opportunities by analyzing user/customer problems, needs, and contexts. CLO 3. Apply basic tools to assess value proposition, market relevance, alternatives, and early feasibility of a venture idea. CLO 4. STM2001.objectives: Entrepreneurship Primer is a foundational course designed to introduce students to the basic logic, language, and practice of entrepreneurship. Offered alongside TVL 1, the course helps students build the conceptual grounding needed to engage meaningfully in venture exploration and early-stage venture development. It introduces students to entrepreneurial thinking, opportunity recognition, problem identification, customer understanding, value creation, market logic, and basic venture feasibility. Where TVL 1 emphasizes applied team-based venture work, Entrepreneurship Primer provides the analytical and conceptual scaffolding that allows students to approach such work more rigorously. The course combines short lectures, guided discussions, classroom exercises, and applied assignments connected to students’ venture ideas and observations.
STM2001.program_learning_goals: PLO 1. Disciplinary Knowledge Demonstrate foundational knowledge of management, business, and entrepreneurial concepts. PLO 2.
